name: AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Professional
audience: Solutions architects with 2+ years designing and deploying cloud architecture on AWS
format: 75 items (65 scored, 10 unscored) in 180 minutes; multiple choice (1 of 4) and multiple response (2+ of 5+); scaled score 100–1000, pass 720. SAP-C03 replaces SAP-C02 from 17 November 2026.

lessons.title: Event-driven, serverless and container architectures
lessons.summary: Design event-driven systems with the right delivery guarantees, pick between Step Functions and Lambda durable functions, choose container and service-networking options, and isolate tenants.

sections.heading: Delivery guarantees, ordering and idempotency
sections.body:
- **SQS standard** queues deliver **at least once** and do not guarantee order. Consumers must be **idempotent**: record a unique idempotency key (for example an order ID) with a DynamoDB conditional write and skip work already done.
- **SQS FIFO** orders messages **per message group ID**, not per queue. Throughput scales with the number of distinct group IDs, so use a high-cardinality key such as customer ID. High-throughput FIFO adds partitions automatically.
- **Kinesis Data Streams** orders records **per shard**, and the **partition key** picks the shard. A low-cardinality key (for example a country code) creates hot shards.
- **SNS** fans out to many subscribers. **EventBridge** routes events by content-based rules and can target an **event bus in another account or Region**, which is the standard way to centralize events across an organization.

sections.heading: Durable workflows: Step Functions vs Lambda durable functions
sections.body:
- **Step Functions Standard**: runs up to **1 year**, **exactly-once** execution, billed per state transition, supports `.sync` and `.waitForTaskToken` (human approval, callbacks) and Distributed Map. Use it for non-idempotent steps such as payments.
- **Step Functions Express**: runs up to **5 minutes**, **at-least-once** (async) or **at-most-once** (sync), billed by executions, duration and memory. No `.waitForTaskToken` or `.sync`. Use it for high-volume, idempotent event processing.
- The workflow type **cannot be changed** after creation.
- **Lambda durable functions** keep multi-step logic in code inside Lambda for up to one year using **checkpoint/replay**: after an interruption the function reruns and skips completed steps. **Waits suspend execution without compute charges**, which suits human-in-the-loop steps. Choose Step Functions when you orchestrate many AWS services visually; choose durable functions for Lambda-centric code. Combining both is common.

sections.heading: Containers, scaling and service-to-service networking
sections.body:
- **ECS** is the AWS-native orchestrator; **EKS** runs upstream Kubernetes; **Fargate** removes node management for both.
- Scaling: Lambda scales with **concurrency** (reserved/provisioned); Kubernetes uses the **Horizontal Pod Autoscaler** for pods and the **Cluster Autoscaler** for nodes when pods are pending; ECS uses **service auto scaling** through Application Auto Scaling.
- **ECS Service Connect** gives ECS services name-based discovery and traffic metrics inside a namespace.
- **Amazon VPC Lattice** connects services **across VPCs and accounts** through a **service network** shared with AWS RAM. Targets include EC2, IPs, Lambda, ALB, ECS tasks and Kubernetes pods. **IAM auth policies** apply at the service network and service. It **supports overlapping CIDRs** and has no inter-AZ data transfer charges.
- **ECR**: enable image scanning and **lifecycle policies** to expire untagged or old images.

sections.heading: Ingress, edge and real-time APIs
sections.body:
- **ALB** routes HTTP/HTTPS by host and path; **NLB** handles TCP/UDP/TLS with static IPs per AZ; on EKS the **AWS Load Balancer Controller** provisions them from Ingress and Service objects.
- **API Gateway** adds throttling, authorizers and usage plans. **WebSocket APIs** keep persistent connections; store connection IDs (for example in DynamoDB) and post messages back through the connections API.
- **CloudFront Functions**: lightweight JavaScript on viewer request/response only, for header rewrites, redirects and cache-key normalization at very high scale. **Lambda@Edge**: also runs on origin request/response, can make network calls and read the body, for heavier logic.

sections.heading: Multi-tenant isolation
sections.body:
- **Silo**: dedicated resources per tenant (account, database or stack). Strongest isolation, highest cost.
- **Pool**: shared resources with tenant context enforced on every request: put the tenant ID in **Cognito** token claims, propagate it, and enforce **row-level security** in the database or tenant-scoped IAM credentials.
- **Tenant-specific encryption**: a KMS key per tenant lets you revoke or audit one tenant's data independently.
- Mixed tiers are common: pool for standard tenants, silo for premium or regulated tenants.
- Keep compute **stateless**: move session and state to DynamoDB, ElastiCache or S3 so any instance can serve any request.

keyPoints: SQS standard is at-least-once; consumers need idempotency keys.
FIFO ordering and throughput are per message group ID.
Step Functions Standard is exactly-once and up to 1 year; Express is up to 5 minutes and at-least-once (async).
Lambda durable functions use checkpoint/replay and do not charge compute while waiting.
VPC Lattice connects services across accounts and overlapping CIDRs with IAM auth policies.
CloudFront Functions for lightweight viewer logic; Lambda@Edge when you need network calls or origin events.

gotchas.trap: FIFO guarantees order across the whole queue.
gotchas.correct: Order is per message group ID; different groups are processed in parallel.

gotchas.trap: Express workflows can wait for a human approval with a task token.
gotchas.correct: Only Standard workflows support .waitForTaskToken; Express runs at most 5 minutes.

gotchas.trap: You can switch a Standard workflow to Express later to save cost.
gotchas.correct: The workflow type is fixed at creation; create a new state machine.

gotchas.trap: CloudFront Functions can call an external authorization API.
gotchas.correct: CloudFront Functions have no network access; use Lambda@Edge.

lessons.lab: Build an order pipeline: API Gateway -> SQS FIFO (message group = customer ID) -> Lambda with a DynamoDB conditional-write idempotency check -> Step Functions Standard workflow with a .waitForTaskToken approval step. Send duplicate messages and confirm only one order is processed.

lessons.title: Integrating generative AI and ML inference
lessons.summary: Use Amazon Bedrock, Knowledge Bases, AgentCore and SageMaker AI endpoints to build RAG, agents and inference into architectures that span accounts.

sections.heading: Amazon Bedrock as the model layer
sections.body:
- Bedrock gives API access to many foundation models from several providers through `bedrock-runtime`. Architect for model choice: don't hard-code a single model.
- **Cross-Region inference profiles** spread load across Regions. A **geographic** profile (US, EU, APAC) keeps processing in that geography and fits residency rules; a **global** profile is cheaper (about 10%) but can route to any commercial Region. SCPs must allow the destination Regions.
- In multi-account setups, keep model access, guardrails and invocation logging consistent per account and Region; invocation logging is off by default and writes to the same account and Region.

sections.heading: RAG with Knowledge Bases
sections.body:
- **Managed Knowledge Base** (recommended): built-in connectors for S3, SharePoint, Confluence, Google Drive, OneDrive and a web crawler, **document-level ACL filtering**, agentic multi-hop retrieval and AgentCore Gateway integration.
- **Customer-managed** Knowledge Base: bring your own vector store such as OpenSearch Serverless, Aurora or Neptune.
- Both return **citations** and support reranking. Structured data stores are also supported.
- Ingestion chunks and embeds documents into the vector store; retrieval adds the relevant chunks to the prompt.

sections.heading: Agents with Bedrock AgentCore
sections.body:
AgentCore is modular and works with any framework or model:
- **Runtime**: serverless hosting with session isolation (MCP/A2A).
- **Memory**: short- and long-term memory across sessions.
- **Gateway**: turns existing APIs and Lambda functions into **MCP tools**.
- **Identity**: inbound JWT authorization and outbound credentials so agents act on behalf of users.
- **Code Interpreter**, **Browser**, **Observability** (OTEL), **Evaluations**, and **Policy** (deterministic tool-call rules).

sections.heading: SageMaker AI endpoints
sections.body:
- **Real-time endpoints**: persistent, low-latency, auto scaling.
- **Serverless inference**: intermittent traffic, scales to zero, tolerates cold starts.
- **Asynchronous inference**: large payloads or long processing, requests queued, can scale to zero.
- **Batch transform**: offline scoring of whole datasets.
- Use SageMaker AI when you host your own or custom models; use Bedrock for managed foundation models. Model training and fine-tuning are out of scope for this exam.

keyPoints: Managed Knowledge Bases provide connectors and document-level ACL filtering.
AgentCore Gateway exposes existing APIs as MCP tools; Memory persists context; Identity handles user delegation.
Geographic cross-Region inference profiles keep data in a geography; global profiles may use any commercial Region.
Match SageMaker AI inference type to traffic: real-time, serverless, asynchronous or batch transform.

gotchas.trap: Use a global inference profile to meet EU data residency.
gotchas.correct: Use the EU geographic profile; global can route outside the EU.

gotchas.trap: Bedrock invocation logging is on by default.
gotchas.correct: It is disabled by default and must be enabled per account and Region.

gotchas.trap: Build custom ACL filtering for SharePoint documents in application code.
gotchas.correct: Managed Knowledge Bases support document-level ACL filtering.

lessons.lab: Create a Knowledge Base over an S3 prefix, query it with RetrieveAndGenerate, and check the citations. Then expose a Lambda function as an MCP tool through AgentCore Gateway.

lessons.title: Hybrid connectivity, DNS and edge compute
lessons.summary: Build resilient Direct Connect and VPN designs with Transit Gateway, resolve DNS in both directions, move data with DataSync, Storage Gateway and Transfer Family, and place compute on Outposts, Local Zones or Anywhere.

sections.heading: Direct Connect resiliency
sections.body:
- **Maximum resiliency**: separate connections on separate devices in **more than one location** (99.99% SLA).
- **High resiliency**: one connection at each of multiple locations (99.9% SLA).
- **Development/test**: separate devices in a single location; does not survive a location failure.
- **Site-to-Site VPN** is a cheaper backup. With Transit Gateway, when the same prefix arrives over the DX gateway and VPN, **DX is preferred** and VPN is the backup.
- Use one DX gateway for ECMP across transit VIFs. There is no ECMP between different attachment types. TGW **peering attachments use static routes only**.

sections.heading: Hybrid DNS with Route 53 Resolver endpoints (VPC Resolver)
sections.body:
- **Inbound endpoint**: on-premises DNS servers forward queries **into** AWS to resolve private hosted zones.
- **Outbound endpoint + forwarding rules**: VPCs resolve **on-premises** domains through conditional forwarding.
- Share forwarding rules across accounts with AWS RAM. Endpoints work over DX or VPN.
- Split-horizon: the same name answers differently from a public and a private hosted zone.

sections.heading: Data movement and file integration
sections.body:
- **DataSync**: online, scheduled, incremental transfer from NFS/SMB/HDFS/object storage into S3, EFS or FSx, with verification.
- **Storage Gateway**: hybrid access. File Gateway gives NFS/SMB backed by S3 with a local cache; Volume and Tape Gateway serve block and backup use cases.
- **Transfer Family**: managed SFTP/FTPS/FTP/AS2 endpoints in front of S3 or EFS, for partners who keep their file workflows.
- **Legacy integration**: **Amazon MQ** for apps using JMS/AMQP/MQTT/STOMP brokers; API Gateway plus Lambda to transform legacy payloads.
- For offline transfers, new customers use **Data Transfer Terminal** or partners; Snow devices are not available to new customers.

sections.heading: Hybrid and edge compute
sections.body:
- **Outposts**: AWS infrastructure and APIs in your own data center, for local data processing, residency or low latency to on-premises systems.
- **Local Zones**: AWS-run infrastructure in metro areas for single-digit-millisecond latency to end users.
- **EKS Anywhere / ECS Anywhere**: run containers on your own hardware with AWS-consistent tooling.

keyPoints: Maximum DX resiliency = separate devices in more than one location.
With TGW, DX is preferred over VPN for the same prefix.
Inbound endpoint = on-premises resolving AWS; outbound endpoint + rule = AWS resolving on-premises.
Transfer Family for SFTP partners; DataSync for bulk online copies; File Gateway for local cached file access.

gotchas.trap: Two DX connections on two devices in one location give maximum resiliency.
gotchas.correct: That is the dev/test model; maximum needs more than one location.

gotchas.trap: An outbound endpoint lets on-premises servers resolve private hosted zones.
gotchas.correct: That needs an inbound endpoint.

gotchas.trap: Order Snowball Edge for a new customer offline migration.
gotchas.correct: Snow devices are closed to new customers; use Data Transfer Terminal, partners or DataSync.

lessons.lab: Create inbound and outbound Resolver endpoints in a shared-services VPC, share a forwarding rule for corp.example.com with another account through RAM, and test resolution in both directions.

lessons.title: Network design, inspection and global routing
lessons.summary: Connect many VPCs, plan addressing with IPAM, inspect traffic with Network Firewall, WAF and GWLB, adopt IPv6, and route users globally with Route 53, Global Accelerator and Cloud WAN.

sections.heading: Multi-VPC patterns
sections.body:
- **VPC peering**: one-to-one, **non-transitive**, no overlapping CIDRs.
- **Transit Gateway**: Regional hub; route tables segment traffic.
- **PrivateLink**: exposes one service behind an NLB through interface endpoints; one-way, works with overlapping CIDRs. Common for SaaS providers.
- **Gateway endpoints**: S3 and DynamoDB only, free, same Region, via route-table prefix lists. They remove NAT gateway processing charges for that traffic.
- **Cloud WAN**: managed global WAN defined by a **core network policy**. **Segments** are isolated routing domains; attachments map to segments by tag; network function groups steer traffic through firewalls.

sections.heading: Addressing and IPv6
sections.body:
- **VPC IPAM** manages organization-wide pools, allocates non-overlapping CIDRs by rule, and tracks usage and history.
- **Dual-stack** VPCs add IPv6 alongside IPv4. Use an **egress-only internet gateway** for outbound-only IPv6 traffic (the IPv6 equivalent of a NAT gateway's one-way behavior).

sections.heading: Inspection and filtering
sections.body:
- **AWS Network Firewall**: managed stateful firewall. It can **attach natively to Transit Gateway** with appliance mode set automatically, which removes the need to run an inspection VPC.
- **Gateway Load Balancer**: inserts **third-party appliances** transparently using GENEVE, scaling them behind one endpoint.
- **AWS WAF**: layer-7 rules on CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway and others (SQL injection, rate limits, bot control).
- **Security groups** are stateful and attach to ENIs; **NACLs** are stateless subnet rules. **VPC Flow Logs** record traffic metadata.
- With TGW and stateful appliances, enable **appliance mode** so both directions of a flow use the same AZ.

sections.heading: Global routing
sections.body:
- **Route 53 policies**: latency (lowest-latency Region), geolocation (by user location, for content or legal rules), geoproximity (by distance with bias), weighted (split traffic), failover (with health checks), multivalue answer.
- **Global Accelerator**: static **anycast IP addresses**, traffic enters the AWS network at the nearest edge, works for **TCP and UDP**, and fails over between endpoints quickly without DNS caching delays.
- **CloudFront**: caching and edge compute for HTTP(S).

keyPoints: Peering is non-transitive; TGW is the hub; PrivateLink publishes single services across overlapping CIDRs.
Network Firewall can attach directly to Transit Gateway.
GWLB is for third-party appliances; WAF is for layer-7 HTTP rules.
Global Accelerator gives static anycast IPs for TCP/UDP; geolocation routing enforces per-country answers.

gotchas.trap: Latency-based routing guarantees users in Germany reach the EU stack.
gotchas.correct: Use geolocation routing when location must determine the answer.

gotchas.trap: Interface endpoints are the cheapest way to reach S3 privately in-Region.
gotchas.correct: Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free.

gotchas.trap: Use WAF to inspect non-HTTP traffic between VPCs.
gotchas.correct: WAF is HTTP only; use Network Firewall or GWLB appliances.

lessons.lab: Create an IPAM pool for one Region, allocate two VPC CIDRs from it, attach both VPCs and a Network Firewall to a Transit Gateway, and route inter-VPC traffic through the firewall.

lessons.title: Data platforms, databases and caching
lessons.summary: Build lakehouses with S3, Lake Formation and Iceberg, choose analytics and database services, design multi-Region data with Aurora Global Database and DynamoDB global tables, and add caching.

sections.heading: Lakehouse and analytics
sections.body:
- Store data in **S3**, catalog it in the **Glue Data Catalog**, and govern it with **Lake Formation** (fine-grained table, column and row permissions, cross-account sharing).
- **Apache Iceberg** tables add ACID transactions, schema evolution and time travel on S3; Athena, EMR, Glue and Redshift can query them.
- **Redshift Spectrum** queries S3 data from Redshift without loading it.
- **EMR** runs Spark/Hadoop for large batch or streaming jobs; **MSK** is managed Apache Kafka for existing Kafka producers and consumers; **AppFlow** pulls data from SaaS applications.
- **AWS Clean Rooms** lets partners analyze combined data **without sharing or copying raw data**, with analysis rules controlling what queries can run.

sections.heading: Database selection
sections.body:
- **RDS / Aurora**: relational, transactions, SQL joins.
- **DynamoDB**: key-value at any scale with predictable single-digit-millisecond latency.
- **Redshift**: data warehouse for analytical SQL.
- Purpose-built: DocumentDB (documents), Neptune (graph), Keyspaces (Cassandra), Timestream (time series), MemoryDB (durable in-memory).

sections.heading: High availability and multi-Region data
sections.body:
- **RDS Multi-AZ**: synchronous standby for availability; **read replicas** scale reads.
- **Aurora Global Database**: up to 5 secondary Regions, typical lag under 1 second, promote a secondary in under a minute. Fits **write-global** designs (one writer Region); write forwarding is available.
- **DynamoDB global tables**: active-active, **write-local** in every Region, last writer wins on conflicts.

sections.heading: Storage and caching
sections.body:
- **EBS**: block for one instance (or Multi-Attach for specific cases). **EFS**: shared NFS for Linux. **FSx**: Windows File Server (SMB, AD), Lustre (HPC, S3-linked), NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS.
- **ElastiCache** (Redis OSS/Valkey/Memcached): general caching and session store.
- **DAX**: in-memory cache in front of DynamoDB with **microsecond** reads and no application caching logic beyond the DAX client.

keyPoints: Lake Formation adds fine-grained and cross-account governance over the Glue Data Catalog.
Iceberg gives ACID and time travel on S3 tables.
Aurora Global Database = one writer Region, fast promotion; DynamoDB global tables = multi-Region writes, last writer wins.
Clean Rooms enables joint analysis without exposing raw data.

gotchas.trap: Aurora Global Database lets every Region accept writes natively.
gotchas.correct: It has one primary writer Region; use write forwarding or DynamoDB global tables for multi-Region writes.

gotchas.trap: Share raw S3 data with a partner to compute overlapping customers.
gotchas.correct: Use Clean Rooms so neither party sees the other's raw data.

gotchas.trap: Use ElastiCache in front of DynamoDB for microsecond reads with minimal code changes.
gotchas.correct: DAX is API-compatible with DynamoDB and needs only a client swap.

lessons.lab: Create an Iceberg table in the Glue Data Catalog over S3, register the location with Lake Formation, grant column-level access to an analyst role, and query it from Athena.

lessons.title: Workforce, customer and workload identity
lessons.summary: Pick the right identity plane for each caller: IAM Identity Center for the workforce, Cognito for app users, EKS Pod Identity or IRSA for pods, IAM Roles Anywhere for servers outside AWS, and Verified Access for VPN-less app access.

sections.heading: Workforce federation with IAM Identity Center
sections.body:
In a multi-account organization, **IAM Identity Center** is the default answer for human access to AWS accounts.

- Connect an external identity provider (Okta, Microsoft Entra ID and similar) over **SAML 2.0** for sign-in.
- Turn on **SCIM** so users and groups are provisioned and deprovisioned automatically from the IdP. Without SCIM, someone has to create users by hand and leavers can linger.
- Define **permission sets** once and assign them to *groups* on *accounts*. Identity Center creates the matching IAM roles in each account for you.
- Users get short-lived credentials through the access portal or CLI. No IAM users, no long-term keys.

The anti-patterns the exam likes to offer: IAM users in every account, per-account SAML trusts maintained by hand, or Cognito used for employees.

sections.heading: Customer identity with Amazon Cognito
sections.body:
- A **user pool** is a user directory and OIDC/OAuth 2.0 token issuer. It handles sign-up, sign-in, MFA and federation with social or enterprise IdPs, and issues ID and access tokens to your app.
- An **identity pool** exchanges a token (from a user pool or another IdP) for **temporary AWS credentials** tied to an IAM role. Use it when the client must call AWS directly, for example uploading to S3 from a mobile app.
- Scope per-user access with policy variables such as `${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}` in the role policy, so each user can only touch their own prefix.
- For APIs, an API Gateway Cognito authorizer validates user pool tokens. Cognito tokens can also carry tenant context for multi-tenant apps.

sections.heading: Pods, servers and non-AWS workloads
sections.body:
**EKS Pod Identity** maps an IAM role to a Kubernetes service account *without an OIDC provider*. The role trusts the service principal `pods.eks.amazonaws.com`, so the same role can be reused across many clusters without editing its trust policy each time. It needs the Pod Identity Agent DaemonSet and is **not supported on Fargate, Windows nodes, Outposts or EKS Anywhere**. Use **IRSA** (IAM roles for service accounts, OIDC based) there.

**IAM Roles Anywhere** gives workloads outside AWS (on-premises servers, other clouds) temporary credentials in exchange for an **X.509 certificate**:
- A **trust anchor** points to AWS Private CA or your own external CA.
- A **profile** lists the roles that can be assumed and can add a session policy.
- No long-term access keys are stored on the server. The trust boundary is the account, and the resources are Regional.

sections.heading: VPN-less application access with Verified Access
sections.body: **AWS Verified Access** gives users access to internal applications **without a VPN**. Every request is evaluated against **identity** (from your IdP) and **device trust** data, and every access attempt is logged. This is the zero-trust answer when a scenario says "replace the VPN", "check device posture on every request" or "log each access attempt". It is billed per application-hour plus data processed.

keyPoints: Workforce in many accounts: IAM Identity Center + external IdP over SAML 2.0 + SCIM provisioning + permission sets assigned to groups.
App users: Cognito user pool for sign-in and tokens; identity pool when the client needs temporary AWS credentials.
EKS Pod Identity needs no OIDC provider and lets one role serve many clusters; use IRSA on Fargate, Windows, Outposts and EKS Anywhere.
Servers outside AWS: IAM Roles Anywhere with an X.509 trust anchor; no long-term keys.
Replace a VPN with per-request identity and device checks: Verified Access.

gotchas.trap: Use Cognito user pools for employee access to the AWS console.
gotchas.correct: Cognito is for application end users. Workforce access to accounts goes through IAM Identity Center.

gotchas.trap: EKS Pod Identity works everywhere EKS runs.
gotchas.correct: It is not supported on Fargate, Windows nodes, Outposts or EKS Anywhere. Use IRSA there.

gotchas.trap: Rotate IAM user access keys on on-premises servers with a Lambda function.
gotchas.correct: Remove long-term keys entirely with IAM Roles Anywhere and certificates from your PKI.

lessons.lab:
1. In a sandbox organization, enable IAM Identity Center and create two groups and a permission set with ReadOnlyAccess. Assign it to one group on two accounts and sign in through the access portal.
2. Create a Cognito user pool and an identity pool. Attach a role policy that allows `s3:PutObject` only on `arn:aws:s3:::BUCKET/${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}/*` and test from the CLI with a test user.
3. On a small EKS cluster with managed EC2 nodes, install the Pod Identity Agent add-on, create a pod identity association and confirm the pod can list an S3 bucket.
4. Delete the cluster, pools and bucket when finished.

lessons.title: Least privilege, ABAC and data perimeters
lessons.summary: Permissions boundaries, session policies, external IDs and ABAC keep delegated access tight; IAM Access Analyzer, VPC endpoint policies, SCPs and RCPs draw the perimeter around your data.

sections.heading: Policy types that only ever reduce permissions
sections.body:
Effective permissions are the **intersection** of every applicable limit. Only identity-based and resource-based policies grant access. These only cap it:

- **Permissions boundary**: a managed policy attached to a user or role that sets the maximum it can ever have. Classic use: let developers create roles for their Lambda functions, but require (with the condition key `iam:PermissionsBoundary`) that every role they create carries the boundary. This prevents privilege escalation.
- **Session policy**: passed inline or by ARN when calling `AssumeRole` (or in an IAM Roles Anywhere profile). The session gets the intersection of the role's policies and the session policy. A broker that assumes one role for many tenants can scope each session to one tenant prefix. A session policy **cannot add** permissions the role does not already have.
- **SCPs and RCPs** (see the governance lesson) cap principals and resources across accounts.

sections.heading: Cross-account roles and the confused deputy
sections.body: When a third party (a SaaS vendor, a monitoring tool) assumes a role in your account, put the vendor's account in the trust policy **and** require `sts:ExternalId` with a value unique to you. Without it, another customer of the same vendor could trick the vendor into using your role: the **confused deputy** problem.

sections.heading: Attribute-based access control (ABAC)
sections.body:
With ABAC you write a few policies that compare tags instead of one policy per project:

```json
"Condition": {"StringEquals": {"aws:ResourceTag/project": "${aws:PrincipalTag/project}"}}
```

Principal tags can come from IdP session tags through IAM Identity Center or SAML. New projects need new tags, not new policies, so ABAC scales with team growth. Protect the tags themselves: deny changing the `project` tag except through approved roles, for example with an SCP.

sections.heading: Data perimeter tools
sections.body:
- **IAM Access Analyzer** – *external access* findings show resources shared outside your **zone of trust** (an account or the whole organization). *Unused access* findings flag unused roles, keys and permissions. Policy validation and custom policy checks catch problems before deployment.
- **VPC endpoint policies** limit which principals and resources can be reached through an endpoint, for example only buckets in your organization.
- **SCPs** stop *your* principals from acting outside the perimeter. **RCPs** stop *anyone*, including principals outside the org, from reaching your resources unless conditions such as `aws:PrincipalOrgID` match.
- **Verified Access** brings the same idea to application access: identity and device checks per request.

keyPoints: Boundaries, session policies, SCPs and RCPs never grant permissions; they only restrict.
Delegate role creation safely by requiring a permissions boundary with the iam:PermissionsBoundary condition key.
Third-party cross-account roles need sts:ExternalId to prevent the confused deputy problem.
ABAC compares aws:PrincipalTag with aws:ResourceTag so policies do not grow with the number of projects.
IAM Access Analyzer with the organization as zone of trust finds resources shared outside the org; unused access findings support right-sizing.

gotchas.trap: A session policy can give a temporary session extra permissions for one task.
gotchas.correct: Session policies only narrow the role's permissions. The result is an intersection.

gotchas.trap: An SCP can stop principals in other organizations from reading our S3 buckets.
gotchas.correct: SCPs affect only principals in your member accounts. Use an RCP (or bucket policies) to restrict external principals.

gotchas.trap: ABAC means creating one role per project tag.
gotchas.correct: ABAC uses a small number of roles and policies whose conditions match principal tags to resource tags.

lessons.lab:
1. Create a permissions boundary policy that allows only CloudWatch Logs and S3 actions on one bucket.
2. Create a developer role whose policy allows `iam:CreateRole` only when `iam:PermissionsBoundary` equals that boundary ARN. Try to create a role with and without the boundary.
3. Call `aws sts assume-role` with an inline `--policy` that allows only one S3 prefix and confirm other prefixes are denied.
4. Create an IAM Access Analyzer external access analyzer for the account, share a test bucket with another account and review the finding. Clean up afterwards.

lessons.title: Encryption: KMS, certificates, CloudHSM and post-quantum
lessons.summary: How KMS key types and rotation actually behave, when to use ACM, AWS Private CA or CloudHSM, and how to plan TLS 1.3 and post-quantum migration.

sections.heading: KMS keys and rotation rules
sections.body:
Use **customer managed keys** when you need control over the key policy, rotation, grants or cross-account use. AWS managed keys rotate every year and you cannot change that.

Rotation rules worth memorizing:
- **Automatic rotation** works only for **symmetric keys with KMS-generated material**. It is optional. The default period is 365 days and you can set a custom `RotationPeriodInDays`.
- **On-demand rotation** also works for symmetric keys with **imported** (EXTERNAL) material.
- **Asymmetric, HMAC and custom key store keys** can only be rotated **manually**: create a new key and repoint the alias.
- For **multi-Region keys**, rotation is configured on the primary key.
- Rotation **does not re-encrypt data**. KMS keeps earlier key material so old ciphertext still decrypts; new encryptions use the new material.

sections.heading: Certificates: ACM and AWS Private CA
sections.body:
- **ACM public certificates** are for publicly resolvable names and need domain validation. ACM renews them automatically for integrated services such as ELB, CloudFront and API Gateway.
- **AWS Private CA** runs your own private certificate hierarchy for internal names, mutual TLS between services, and device or workload certificates. Private certificates issued through ACM can be renewed by ACM. Private CA can also be the trust anchor for IAM Roles Anywhere.
- Prefer **TLS 1.3** security policies on load balancers, API Gateway and Transfer Family. These policies **do not upgrade on their own**, so set them explicitly in IaC.

sections.heading: CloudHSM vs KMS
sections.body: **AWS CloudHSM** gives you **single-tenant HSMs** in your VPC that only you control, with standard interfaces such as PKCS#11, JCE and OpenSSL. Pick it when a requirement says the customer must have exclusive control of the HSM, or an application needs those cryptographic APIs directly. Otherwise KMS is simpler: it is fully managed, integrated with most AWS services and governed by IAM and key policies. KMS keys in a CloudHSM-backed custom key store can only be rotated manually.

sections.heading: Post-quantum readiness
sections.body:
- The risk is **harvest now, decrypt later**: traffic recorded today could be decrypted by a future quantum computer. Start with data that must stay confidential for **10+ years**.
- Post-quantum key exchange needs **TLS 1.3**. Set TLS policies explicitly in IaC for ELB, API Gateway and Transfer Family, restrict allowed policies with IAM condition keys, and verify the negotiated key exchange in CloudTrail `tlsDetails`.
- KMS offers **ML-DSA** key specs (`ML_DSA_44/65/87`, FIPS 204) for **signing and verification**, and **ML-KEM** key specs (`ML_KEM_512/768/1024`, FIPS 203) with `Encapsulate`/`Decapsulate` for key establishment.
- **SYMMETRIC_DEFAULT (AES-256-GCM)** is considered quantum resistant, so data at rest under symmetric KMS keys does not need a new key type.

keyPoints: Automatic rotation: symmetric KMS-generated keys only, default 365 days, custom period allowed.
Asymmetric, HMAC and custom key store keys rotate manually via a new key and an alias switch.
Rotation never re-encrypts existing data; old material stays available for decryption.
Internal names and mTLS: AWS Private CA. Public endpoints: ACM public certificates.
CloudHSM when you need single-tenant HSMs under exclusive customer control or PKCS#11/JCE.
Post-quantum: TLS 1.3 first, set TLS policies explicitly, ML-DSA for signing, ML-KEM for key encapsulation.

gotchas.trap: Enable automatic rotation on an asymmetric signing key.
gotchas.correct: Asymmetric keys rotate only manually: create a new key and move the alias.

gotchas.trap: After enabling rotation, re-encrypt every object so it uses the new key material.
gotchas.correct: Rotation is transparent. KMS keeps prior material and decrypts old ciphertext automatically.

gotchas.trap: Replace symmetric KMS keys with ML-KEM keys to make S3 data quantum safe.
gotchas.correct: AES-256-GCM symmetric keys are considered quantum resistant. Focus PQ effort on TLS key exchange and long-lived signatures.

gotchas.trap: Load balancer TLS policies will move to the newest post-quantum policy automatically.
gotchas.correct: They do not upgrade on their own. Set the policy explicitly in IaC.

lessons.lab:
1. Create a symmetric customer managed key, enable automatic rotation with a custom period, then call `rotate-key-on-demand` and list rotations with `list-key-rotations`.
2. Encrypt a small file before and after rotation and confirm both ciphertexts decrypt.
3. Create an asymmetric ML-DSA key in a Region where it is offered, sign a digest and verify it.
4. Create an ALB HTTPS listener and set a TLS 1.3 security policy explicitly. Schedule key deletion and delete the ALB when done.

lessons.title: Governing many accounts: Organizations, Control Tower, SCPs and RCPs
lessons.summary: Structure accounts with Organizations and Control Tower, put preventive guardrails in SCPs and RCPs, and centralize detection with org CloudTrail, Config aggregation, GuardDuty, Inspector, Security Hub CSPM and Security Lake.

sections.heading: Account structure and vending
sections.body:
- **AWS Organizations** groups accounts into **OUs** and applies policies at the root, OU or account level. Many security services support a **delegated administrator** account so the management account stays nearly empty.
- **AWS Control Tower** sets up a landing zone (log archive and audit accounts, baseline controls) and provides **Account Factory** to vend new accounts that are already enrolled and governed. Controls come in three behaviors: **preventive** (policies such as SCPs), **detective** (Config rules) and **proactive** (CloudFormation Hooks that check resources before provisioning).
- **AWS RAM** shares resources such as Transit Gateways, subnets (VPC sharing), Route 53 Resolver rules and VPC Lattice service networks with accounts or OUs, so you avoid duplicating network infrastructure.

sections.heading: SCPs vs RCPs
sections.body:
| | SCP | RCP |
|---|---|---|
| Limits | **Principals** in member accounts | **Resources** in member accounts, including access by principals **outside** the org |
| Grants permissions? | No | No |
| Management account | Not affected | Not affected |
| Service-linked roles | Not restricted | Not restricted |

More RCP rules: they need **all features** enabled; they apply to delegated-admin accounts; they **do not apply to AWS managed KMS keys**; they cover a subset of services (including S3, STS, KMS, SQS, Secrets Manager, DynamoDB, ECR, CloudWatch Logs, Cognito, CloudFront, EventBridge, IAM Roles Anywhere, Transfer Family and WAF). **Bedrock is not on the RCP list.** Test RCPs on a test OU before attaching them at the root.

Typical SCPs: deny leaving the organization, deny disabling CloudTrail or GuardDuty, deny Regions outside an approved list using `aws:RequestedRegion` (with exceptions for global services). Typical RCP: deny access to S3 or KMS resources unless `aws:PrincipalOrgID` is your organization (with exceptions for AWS service principals).

sections.heading: Centralized logging and detection
sections.body:
- **Organization trail** in CloudTrail: created in the management account or a delegated admin, logs every member account (including new ones) to a bucket in the log archive account. Member accounts can see it but cannot change or delete it.
- **AWS Config aggregator** with organization scope (from a delegated admin) gives one compliance view; **Config rules** and conformance packs provide automated compliance checks.
- **GuardDuty** with a delegated administrator and **auto-enable** for organization members. It is Regional, so enable it in every Region you use.
- **Amazon Inspector** continuously scans EC2 instances, ECR images and Lambda functions for vulnerabilities, again with a delegated admin.
- **Systems Manager Patch Manager** applies patch baselines through maintenance windows or patch policies across accounts and Regions.
- **Security Hub CSPM** runs posture checks against security standards and aggregates findings. The new **Security Hub** (GA December 2025) correlates GuardDuty, Inspector, Security Hub CSPM and Macie signals into risk prioritization using OCSF.
- **Amazon Security Lake** stores security data in **your account's S3** as **OCSF + Parquet**: CloudTrail management and data events, EKS audit logs, Route 53 resolver query logs, Security Hub CSPM findings, VPC Flow Logs, WAF logs and custom sources. **Rollup Regions** consolidate data, which helps with residency. **Subscribers** get data access or query access, which suits a SIEM.

keyPoints: Control Tower Account Factory vends accounts that land in governed OUs with preventive, detective and proactive controls.
SCPs restrict your principals; RCPs restrict access to your resources, even by outsiders. Neither grants anything.
RCPs skip the management account, service-linked roles and AWS managed KMS keys, and do not cover Bedrock.
One organization trail to a log archive account covers all current and future accounts and cannot be altered by members.
Use delegated administrators plus auto-enable for GuardDuty, Inspector, Config aggregation and Security Hub CSPM.
Security Lake = raw security logs normalized to OCSF in your S3; Security Hub CSPM = posture standards; new Security Hub = correlation and risk prioritization.

gotchas.trap: An SCP attached at the root also restricts the management account.
gotchas.correct: SCPs and RCPs do not affect the management account, so keep workloads out of it.

gotchas.trap: Use an RCP to force Bedrock calls through a guardrail.
gotchas.correct: Bedrock is not on the RCP list. Use an Organizations Amazon Bedrock policy for guardrail enforcement.

gotchas.trap: Deploy a trail in each account with StackSets to centralize logging.
gotchas.correct: An organization trail is simpler and member accounts cannot stop or delete it.

gotchas.trap: GuardDuty enabled once in the delegated admin covers every Region.
gotchas.correct: GuardDuty is Regional. Enable it and auto-enable members in each Region you use.

lessons.lab:
1. In a test organization with all features enabled, create a Sandbox OU and attach an SCP that denies actions outside two approved Regions using `aws:RequestedRegion`, with a `NotAction` list for global services.
2. Attach an RCP to the same OU that denies `s3:*` on its buckets unless `aws:PrincipalOrgID` matches your org (exempt AWS service principals). Test from an account outside the org.
3. Create an organization trail to a bucket in a log archive account and confirm a member account cannot delete it.
4. Designate a delegated admin for GuardDuty and turn on auto-enable. Detach the test policies when you finish.

lessons.title: Compliance: protection, residency, audit trails and evidence
lessons.summary: Turn compliance requirements into controls: Region restrictions and geographic inference profiles for residency, encryption and key control for protection, CloudTrail plus Bedrock invocation logs for audit, AWS Artifact for evidence, and threat modeling early in design.

sections.heading: Data protection and residency
sections.body:
- **Protection**: encrypt at rest with KMS customer managed keys where you need control, encrypt in transit with TLS, classify data, and limit who can use keys through key policies.
- **Residency**: deploy only in approved Regions and **prevent** others with an SCP on `aws:RequestedRegion`. Check that backups, replicas, logs and AI processing stay inside the boundary too.
- **Bedrock cross-Region inference**: a **geographic** profile (US, EU, APAC) keeps processing inside that geography and is the residency choice. A **global** profile is roughly 10% cheaper but can route to any commercial Region. SCPs must allow the destination Regions a profile uses. CloudTrail records the Region that served the request in `additionalEventData.inferenceRegion`.
- **Security Lake rollup Regions** consolidate security data into a Region you choose.

sections.heading: Audit trails, including AI invocations
sections.body:
- **CloudTrail** records API calls: who called what, when and from where. It does **not** capture the full prompt and response of a model call.
- **Bedrock model invocation logging** captures full request and response data plus metadata such as `identity.arn`, token counts and optional `requestMetadata` tags. It is **disabled by default**, must be turned on per Region, and writes to CloudWatch Logs and/or S3 in the **same account and Region only**. Bodies over 100 KB and binary data go to S3 only. It covers only calls through `bedrock-runtime`.
- Centralize afterwards (for example by replicating the S3 logs or subscribing CloudWatch Logs) if auditors need one place to look.

sections.heading: Evidence and threat modeling
sections.body:
- **AWS Artifact** is the self-service portal for AWS compliance **reports** (such as SOC and ISO reports) and **agreements** (such as a HIPAA Business Associate Addendum). Auditors asking for AWS's own attestations get them here.
- **Threat modeling** belongs early in design and repeats as the design changes: identify assets and trust boundaries, enumerate threats (STRIDE is a common framework), and prioritize mitigations. The AWS Well-Architected security pillar recommends identifying threats and prioritizing mitigations with a threat model. For AI workloads, include prompt injection, data leakage through responses and over-privileged agent tools.

keyPoints: Residency is enforced preventively with SCPs on aws:RequestedRegion, not just detected afterwards.
For AI residency use a geographic cross-Region inference profile; global profiles can route anywhere.
Bedrock invocation logging is off by default, Regional, and writes only to the same account and Region.
CloudTrail logs API calls; invocation logs hold prompts and responses.
AWS Artifact supplies AWS compliance reports and agreements such as a BAA.

gotchas.trap: CloudTrail data events are enough to audit model prompts and responses.
gotchas.correct: Enable Bedrock model invocation logging; CloudTrail does not store the request and response bodies.

gotchas.trap: Point Bedrock invocation logging straight at a central security account bucket.
gotchas.correct: Destinations must be in the same account and Region; centralize afterwards with replication or log subscriptions.

gotchas.trap: Use the global inference profile to save money while keeping EU data in the EU.
gotchas.correct: Only a geographic (EU) profile keeps processing inside the EU.

lessons.lab:
1. In a sandbox account, enable Bedrock model invocation logging to an S3 bucket and a CloudWatch Logs group in the same Region.
2. Invoke a foundation model through `bedrock-runtime` with a `requestMetadata` tag, then find the record and its `identity.arn` with CloudWatch Logs Insights.
3. Find the matching CloudTrail event and note which fields it has and which it lacks.
4. Open AWS Artifact and review which reports and agreements are available. Disable logging and delete the bucket when finished.

lessons.title: Responsible AI controls: Guardrails, AgentCore Identity and human approval
lessons.summary: Filter model input and output with Bedrock Guardrails, enforce them across the organization, give agents scoped identities with AgentCore Identity, and pause risky actions for human approval with Step Functions.

sections.heading: Bedrock Guardrails policies
sections.body:
- **Content filters**: Hate, Insults, Sexual, Violence, Misconduct and **Prompt Attack** (jailbreaks and prompt injection).
- **Denied topics** and **word filters**.
- **Sensitive information filters**: block or **mask** PII, plus custom regex patterns.
- **Contextual grounding checks**: catch answers that are not grounded in the retrieved source or not relevant to the query, the classic RAG hallucination control.
- **Automated Reasoning checks**: validate responses against formal rules.
- The **`ApplyGuardrail` API** evaluates any text *without invoking a model*, so you can guard models hosted elsewhere (for example a SageMaker AI endpoint) or check intermediate agent steps.

sections.heading: Enforcing guardrails across accounts
sections.body:
- **Organization level**: an **Amazon Bedrock policy** in AWS Organizations (`BEDROCK_POLICY`, a declarative policy) points to a guardrail created in the management account with a **numbered version** and a resource policy that grants `bedrock:ApplyGuardrail`.
- **Account level**: `PutEnforcedGuardrailConfiguration`.
- Org, account and request guardrails combine as a **union**, so the most restrictive control wins.
- **Automated Reasoning checks are not supported in enforcements.** Guardrails are Regional, so create them in each Region you use. Enforcement can include or exclude specific models.
- RCPs cannot do this job: Bedrock is not on the RCP list.

sections.heading: Agent identity with AgentCore Identity
sections.body:
**Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity** gives agents workload identities.
- **Inbound**: a JWT authorizer validates callers from any IdP (Cognito, Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Auth0).
- **Outbound**: credential providers (OAuth, API keys) let the agent call third-party tools **on behalf of the user**, with an audit trail.

This replaces anti-patterns such as shared service-account API keys in agent code or user refresh tokens in environment variables. AgentCore **Policy** adds deterministic, Cedar-compatible rules on which tool calls an agent may make.

sections.heading: Human approval with Step Functions
sections.body:
For high-impact actions (refunds above a limit, production changes, outbound emails to customers), put a human in the loop:

1. A **Standard** workflow reaches a task using the **`.waitForTaskToken`** integration pattern and sends the task token to an approver (for example through SNS, email or a ticketing system).
2. The execution pauses, for as long as the workflow's limit of up to one year, until the approval app calls `SendTaskSuccess` or `SendTaskFailure` with the token.
3. A Choice state continues or rejects. Add a timeout so stale requests do not wait forever.

**Express workflows do not support `.waitForTaskToken`** and run for at most 5 minutes, so they are wrong for approvals. Lambda durable functions can also wait without paying for compute, when the logic lives in Lambda code.

keyPoints: Prompt injection: Prompt Attack content filter. RAG hallucinations: contextual grounding checks. PII: sensitive information filters with mask or block.
ApplyGuardrail checks text without calling a model, so it works for non-Bedrock models too.
Org-wide guardrails: Organizations Amazon Bedrock policy pointing to a versioned guardrail; most restrictive wins; no Automated Reasoning in enforcements.
AgentCore Identity: inbound JWT from any IdP, outbound OAuth/API-key providers to act on behalf of users.
Human approval: Step Functions Standard with .waitForTaskToken; Express cannot do it.

gotchas.trap: Enforce Automated Reasoning checks for every account through the organization guardrail policy.
gotchas.correct: Automated Reasoning checks are not supported in organization or account enforcements; use them in guardrails that applications specify on their own requests.

gotchas.trap: Use an Express workflow for the approval step because it is cheaper.
gotchas.correct: Express has no .waitForTaskToken and a 5-minute limit. Use Standard.

gotchas.trap: A guardrail created in us-east-1 protects calls in eu-west-1.
gotchas.correct: Guardrails are Regional; create them in each Region used.

lessons.lab:
1. Create a guardrail with the Prompt Attack filter, a denied topic and PII masking for email addresses. Publish a version.
2. Call `ApplyGuardrail` on sample input text containing an email address and a jailbreak attempt and inspect the assessment.
3. Build a Standard Step Functions workflow with a Lambda `.waitForTaskToken` task that writes the token to a DynamoDB table, then complete it from the CLI with `aws stepfunctions send-task-success`.
4. Delete the guardrail, state machine and table when finished.

lessons.title: Pricing models and commitment strategy
lessons.summary: Match each workload to On-Demand, Reserved Instances, Savings Plans (including Database Savings Plans), Spot or Fargate Spot, and use architecture choices such as Graviton, Step Functions Express and Bedrock tiers, batching and caching to lower unit cost.

sections.heading: Rightsize first, then commit
sections.body:
Commitments lock in a spend level, so buy them **after** you remove waste.

1. Use **AWS Compute Optimizer** to find over-provisioned EC2 instances, Auto Scaling groups, EBS volumes, Lambda functions and ECS services on Fargate. It also flags where a Graviton (Arm) instance type would fit.
2. Use **scheduled scaling** for known patterns (for example, office hours) and **target tracking** for variable load, so the baseline you commit to is the true steady state.
3. Cover the steady baseline with commitments, and leave peaks on On-Demand or Spot.

sections.heading: Commitment options
sections.body:
| Option | What it covers | Flexibility |
|---|---|---|
| **Compute Savings Plans** | EC2, Fargate and Lambda | Any instance family, size, OS, tenancy or Region |
| **EC2 Instance Savings Plans** | EC2 in one instance family in one Region | Size, OS and tenancy within that family |
| **Standard Reserved Instances** | A specific instance configuration (also RDS, ElastiCache and others) | Least flexible, deepest discount |
| **Convertible Reserved Instances** | EC2, exchangeable for other configurations | Exchanges allowed, smaller discount |
| **Database Savings Plans** | Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, DocumentDB, Neptune, Keyspaces, Timestream and DMS | Engine, Region, and provisioned vs serverless |

**Database Savings Plans** (launched December 2025) are a **1-year** $/hour commitment. The largest discount applies to serverless usage, with smaller discounts for provisioned instances and for DynamoDB and Keyspaces capacity. Choose them when a database estate is changing engines, Regions or deployment models and a per-instance reservation would be stranded.

sections.heading: Interruptible capacity
sections.body:
- **EC2 Spot** uses spare capacity at a steep discount and can be reclaimed with a two-minute notice. Use it for stateless, fault-tolerant, checkpointed or flexible work such as batch, CI, rendering and big data. Diversify across instance types and AZs, and use a capacity-optimized allocation strategy.
- **Fargate Spot** does the same for ECS tasks on Fargate. Tasks get a two-minute warning (SIGTERM) before they stop. Use a **capacity provider strategy** with a base on regular Fargate and the rest weighted to Fargate Spot, so a minimum stays running if Spot capacity is reclaimed.
- Never put a stateful single-instance database or a workload that cannot tolerate interruption on Spot.

sections.heading: Architecture choices that change unit cost
sections.body:
- **Graviton**: Arm-based EC2, Fargate, Lambda (arm64), RDS and ElastiCache options usually give better price performance. Interpreted and JVM workloads often move with little change.
- **Step Functions**: **Standard** is billed per state transition, runs up to 1 year and is exactly-once. **Express** is billed by executions, duration and memory, runs up to 5 minutes and is at-least-once (async). High-volume, short, idempotent event processing is much cheaper on Express. The type cannot be changed after creation.
- **Lambda**: right-size memory (CPU scales with it), and avoid functions that just wait. For long waits, use Step Functions or Lambda durable functions, whose waits do not incur compute charges.

sections.heading: AI/ML cost levers (Bedrock and SageMaker AI)
sections.body:
- **Bedrock service tiers**: Standard, **Flex** (discounted, for work that can tolerate longer latency), **Priority** (premium, for latency-critical traffic) and Reserved. 
- **Batch inference**: about 50% cheaper than on-demand for supported models. Input is read from S3 and output written to S3. It is for jobs with no real-time need, and it is not supported for provisioned models.
- **Prompt caching**: caches long, repeated prompt prefixes (system prompts, shared documents). Cache reads are cheaper than normal input tokens, cache writes may cost more, and the TTL is usually about 5 minutes and resets on each hit. It works with on-demand inference, **not** batch.
- **Provisioned Throughput**: hourly per model unit, with no-commitment, 1-month or 6-month terms. Use it for steady high volume or when a custom model needs it, not for spiky or low traffic.
- **Cross-Region inference**: a **global** profile is roughly 10% cheaper but may route to any commercial Region; a **geographic** profile (US, EU, APAC) keeps processing in that geography and is the choice when residency matters. There is no extra routing charge.
- **SageMaker AI**: Serverless Inference for intermittent traffic (scales to zero), Asynchronous Inference for large payloads and long processing, Batch Transform for offline scoring, multi-model endpoints to share instances, and SageMaker Savings Plans for steady usage.

keyPoints: Rightsize with Compute Optimizer before buying any commitment.
Compute Savings Plans cover EC2, Fargate and Lambda across families and Regions.
Database Savings Plans are 1-year, span many database services, and allow engine, Region and serverless changes.
Spot and Fargate Spot give a two-minute interruption warning; use them only for interruption-tolerant work.
Step Functions Express is cheaper for high-volume, short, idempotent work; Standard for long or exactly-once work.
Bedrock batch inference is about half the on-demand price; prompt caching cuts the cost of repeated prefixes.

gotchas.trap: Buying a 3-year Standard RI for a database you plan to move to Aurora Serverless next year.
gotchas.correct: Use a Database Savings Plan, which follows usage across engines and between provisioned and serverless.

gotchas.trap: Covering Lambda and Fargate spend with an EC2 Instance Savings Plan.
gotchas.correct: Only Compute Savings Plans apply to Fargate and Lambda.

gotchas.trap: Running millions of short, idempotent events through Step Functions Standard.
gotchas.correct: Use Express workflows, billed by duration and memory instead of per transition.

gotchas.trap: Enabling prompt caching to cut the cost of a Bedrock batch inference job.
gotchas.correct: Prompt caching works with on-demand inference only; batch inference already carries its own discount.

gotchas.trap: Choosing a global cross-Region inference profile for an EU data-residency workload.
gotchas.correct: Use the EU geographic profile; global profiles can route to any commercial Region.

lessons.lab: In a sandbox account, open Compute Optimizer and Cost Explorer Savings Plans recommendations. Note the recommended Compute Savings Plan commitment, then model what changes if you first apply the rightsizing findings. Create a Step Functions Express workflow and compare its billing dimensions with a Standard workflow that does the same work.

lessons.title: Reducing data transfer and network cost
lessons.summary: Cut the hidden network line items: NAT gateway processing, cross-AZ traffic, Transit Gateway and PrivateLink processing, inter-Region replication and origin egress, using endpoints, AZ-aware design and CloudFront.

sections.heading: NAT gateways and VPC endpoints
sections.body:
- A **NAT gateway** charges per hour and **per GB processed**. Traffic to AWS services that flows through NAT pays that processing charge.
- **Gateway endpoints** exist only for **S3 and DynamoDB**. They are **free**, work through route table prefix lists, and are same-Region only. Adding them is often the single biggest network saving for data-heavy private subnets.
- **Interface endpoints** (PrivateLink) charge per endpoint per AZ per hour plus per GB. They are usually cheaper than NAT for heavy service traffic, but not free. Centralizing interface endpoints in a shared services VPC reduces the hourly count but adds Transit Gateway processing for the traffic that reaches them.

sections.heading: AZ-aware design
sections.body:
- Data transfer between AZs in a Region is charged in both directions; within one AZ (private IPs) it is not.
- Put one NAT gateway in **each** AZ and point each private subnet at the NAT in its own AZ. A single shared NAT saves the hourly fee but adds cross-AZ transfer and becomes a single point of failure.
- Keep chatty tiers AZ-local where resilience allows (for example, load balancer cross-zone settings, AZ-affinity routing, read from the local replica).
- **VPC Lattice** has no inter-AZ data transfer charges, which can matter for service-to-service traffic across many VPCs.

sections.heading: Transit Gateway, peering and PrivateLink
sections.body:
- **Transit Gateway** charges per attachment-hour and **per GB processed**. It is the right hub for many VPCs, but a pair of VPCs that exchange very large volumes can be connected directly with **VPC peering**, which has no per-GB processing charge (normal cross-AZ or inter-Region transfer still applies). VPC route tables send that pair's traffic over the peering connection while everything else uses the TGW.
- **PrivateLink** suits publishing one service to many consumers (including overlapping CIDRs). The consumer pays endpoint-hours and per-GB.
- Do not quote exact rates in designs; compare the dimensions (hourly vs per-GB) against the traffic profile.

sections.heading: Edge and inter-Region traffic
sections.body:
- **CloudFront** offloads origin egress and serves cached content close to viewers. Data transfer from AWS origins to CloudFront is not charged.
- **Origin Shield** is an extra caching layer in one Region in front of the origin. It raises cache hit ratio, collapses duplicate requests and reduces origin load and egress. Enable it in the Region with the lowest latency to the origin. It adds a per-request charge and helps little for dynamic or uncacheable content. It suits global audiences, on-premises origins with limited bandwidth, and multi-CDN setups.
- **S3 Cross-Region Replication** costs inter-Region transfer, replication requests and storage in the destination (plus Replication Time Control if enabled). Use **filters (prefix or tag)** to replicate only what needs a second Region.
- **DynamoDB global tables** charge replicated writes in every replica Region plus inter-Region transfer. Add replicas only in Regions that need local reads, writes or recovery.
- **Bedrock cross-Region inference** adds no routing charge; a global profile is cheaper than a geographic one but does not keep processing in one geography.

keyPoints: Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB) are free and remove NAT processing charges for that traffic.
One NAT gateway per AZ avoids cross-AZ charges and removes a single point of failure.
Transit Gateway charges per GB processed; peering a high-volume VPC pair avoids it.
Origin Shield raises cache hit ratio and cuts origin load, but adds per-request cost.
Replicate only what you need: S3 CRR filters, and only the DynamoDB replica Regions you use.

gotchas.trap: Using an interface endpoint for S3 from EC2 in the same Region to save money.
gotchas.correct: A gateway endpoint for S3 is free; interface endpoints add hourly and per-GB charges (they are for on-premises or cross-Region access).

gotchas.trap: Centralizing all egress through one NAT gateway in one AZ to save cost.
gotchas.correct: Cross-AZ transfer and the AZ dependency often outweigh the saved hourly fee; use a NAT per AZ.

gotchas.trap: Enabling Origin Shield for a personalized, uncacheable API.
gotchas.correct: Origin Shield helps cacheable content; for dynamic content it mostly adds request charges.

gotchas.trap: Replicating an entire bucket cross-Region when only one prefix is needed for DR.
gotchas.correct: Use a replication rule filtered by prefix or tag.

lessons.title: Cost allocation, visibility and guardrails
lessons.summary: Attribute every dollar to an owner with tags, tag policies, Cost Categories and split cost allocation data, analyze it with Cost Explorer and CUR, and catch overruns with Budgets and Cost Anomaly Detection, including Bedrock token usage.

sections.heading: Tags and tag governance
sections.body:
- **User-defined cost allocation tags** appear in billing tools only after they are **activated** in the Billing console of the management (payer) account.
- **Tag policies** (Organizations) standardize tag keys, case and allowed values, and can **enforce** compliance for chosen resource types so non-compliant tagging operations fail.
- **SCPs** with `aws:RequestTag` / `aws:TagKeys` conditions can deny creating resources without required tags. **AWS Config** rules (for example `required-tags`) detect untagged resources that already exist.
- Use both: prevent at creation, detect and fix drift afterwards.

sections.heading: Grouping and shared costs
sections.body:
- **Cost Categories** group costs by rules (for example by account, tag or service) into business-friendly buckets such as teams or products. They appear in Cost Explorer, Budgets and CUR, which makes them the usual basis for showback and chargeback.
- **Split cost allocation data** adds per-ECS-task and per-EKS-pod cost to CUR, based on each task or pod's share of CPU and memory of the amortized instance cost. For EKS it also covers GPU and AWS accelerators and adds tags such as `aws:eks:namespace` and `aws:eks:workload-name`. Use it to charge back shared clusters.

sections.heading: Analysis tools
sections.body:
- **Cost Explorer**: interactive analysis, forecasts, and Savings Plans and RI recommendations and coverage reports.
- **Cost and Usage Report (CUR)**: the most detailed line-item data, delivered to S3 and queried with Athena or visualized in QuickSight. Use it for custom chargeback, amortization and split cost allocation.
- **Compute Optimizer**: rightsizing recommendations (see lesson 1).

sections.heading: Alerts and controls
sections.body:
- **AWS Budgets** alerts on actual or forecasted cost, usage, or commitment coverage and utilization against a threshold you set. **Budget actions** can apply an IAM policy or SCP, or stop EC2 or RDS instances when a threshold is crossed.
- **Cost Anomaly Detection** uses machine learning to learn normal spend and alerts on unusual spikes per service, account, Cost Category or tag, without fixed thresholds. Send alerts by email or SNS.
- Use both: Budgets for known limits, Anomaly Detection for surprises.

sections.heading: Generative AI cost attribution
sections.body:
- **Bedrock model invocation logging** is off by default. When enabled, it records token counts, the caller (`identity.arn`) and optional `requestMetadata` tags to CloudWatch Logs or S3 in the same account and Region.
- Pass a team, tenant or feature identifier in `requestMetadata` and aggregate tokens with **CloudWatch Logs Insights** to charge back shared Bedrock usage.
- CloudTrail records that an API was called; it is not the tool for per-team token counts.

keyPoints: Cost allocation tags must be activated in the payer account and only apply going forward from activation by default.
Tag policies standardize and can enforce tags; SCPs can deny untagged creation; Config detects drift.
Cost Categories map costs to teams for showback and chargeback.
Split cost allocation data attributes shared ECS and EKS cluster cost to tasks, pods and namespaces in CUR.
Budgets are threshold-based (with actions); Cost Anomaly Detection is ML-based.
Bedrock token chargeback: invocation logs with identity.arn and requestMetadata, queried in Logs Insights.

gotchas.trap: Expecting a newly applied tag to show up in Cost Explorer without further steps.
gotchas.correct: Activate it as a cost allocation tag in the management account first.

gotchas.trap: Using an SCP to automatically add missing tags.
gotchas.correct: SCPs only deny. Use tag policies and SCP conditions to prevent, and Config or automation to remediate.

gotchas.trap: Splitting a shared EKS cluster bill evenly across teams.
gotchas.correct: Enable split cost allocation data so CUR reflects each pod's actual CPU and memory share.

gotchas.trap: Relying on CloudTrail for Bedrock token usage per team.
gotchas.correct: Use model invocation logging, which includes token counts and requestMetadata.

lessons.lab: Activate a CostCenter cost allocation tag, create a tag policy that limits its values, and build a Cost Category mapping CostCenter values to teams. Create a monthly budget with a forecast alert and an Anomaly Detection monitor for the same scope.

lessons.title: Storage, database and observability cost
lessons.summary: Optimize S3 storage classes and lifecycle, EBS volume types, DynamoDB capacity modes, Aurora Serverless and I/O-Optimized, backup and snapshot lifecycle, and observability spend.

sections.heading: Amazon S3 and EFS
sections.body:
- **S3 Intelligent-Tiering**: moves objects between access tiers automatically based on access, with a small per-object monitoring fee and **no retrieval fees**. Best for unknown or changing access patterns. Small objects are not auto-tiered.
- **Lifecycle rules**: transition by age to Standard-IA, One Zone-IA or Glacier classes, and expire old objects and noncurrent versions. Mind **minimum storage duration** and retrieval charges in the infrequent and archive classes, and avoid transitioning very small objects.
- **Glacier classes**: Instant Retrieval (milliseconds, rarely accessed), Flexible Retrieval (minutes to hours) and Deep Archive (hours, lowest cost) for long retention.
- **EFS lifecycle management** moves files that are not accessed to Infrequent Access or Archive storage classes.

sections.heading: Amazon EBS
sections.body:
- **gp3** lets you set IOPS and throughput **independently of volume size**, with a baseline included, and generally costs less per GB than gp2. On **gp2**, IOPS scale with size, so teams often over-provision capacity just to get IOPS.
- Migrate gp2 to gp3 in place with **Elastic Volumes** (no detach, no downtime).
- Use **io2/io1 (Provisioned IOPS)** only for sustained high IOPS or low-latency needs that gp3 cannot meet.
- Delete unattached volumes and old snapshots; archive rarely needed snapshots to the snapshot archive tier.

sections.heading: Databases
sections.body:
- **DynamoDB on-demand**: pay per request, no capacity planning. Best for new, spiky or unpredictable traffic. **Provisioned with auto scaling**: cheaper for steady or predictable traffic with good utilization, and can be combined with reserved capacity or Database Savings Plans.
- **Aurora Serverless v2**: scales capacity in fine steps with load. Good for variable, intermittent or multi-tenant databases.
- **Aurora I/O-Optimized**: no I/O charges, higher compute and storage price. Choose it when I/O is about **25% or more** of Aurora spend; below that, Aurora Standard is cheaper. You can switch to I/O-Optimized once every 30 days and back at any time.
- **RDS Reserved Instances** or **Database Savings Plans** for steady database usage.

sections.heading: Backups and snapshots
sections.body:
- **AWS Backup**: central, policy-driven backup plans across services and accounts, with lifecycle rules that move eligible recovery points to **cold storage** and expire them. Cold storage has a minimum retention period, so it fits long-term retention.
- **Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM)**: automates creation, retention, copy and deletion of **EBS snapshots and EBS-backed AMIs** by tag, at no additional charge beyond the snapshots. It prevents unbounded snapshot growth.
- Set retention to the real RPO and compliance need; old recovery points are a common hidden cost.

sections.heading: Cost-effective observability
sections.body:
- CloudWatch Logs log groups **never expire by default**. Set a **retention policy** on every log group, and export long-term logs to S3 with lifecycle to archive classes if needed.
- Reduce ingestion at the source: lower log levels in production, filter or sample verbose logs, and do not log full payloads.
- Aggregate metrics: avoid high-cardinality custom metrics (for example a dimension per user or request ID). Use the embedded metric format or metric filters with bounded dimensions.
- Keep high-resolution metrics and detailed monitoring only where they drive decisions.

keyPoints: Intelligent-Tiering for unknown access patterns; lifecycle rules for known, age-based patterns.
gp3 decouples IOPS and throughput from size; migrate from gp2 with Elastic Volumes.
DynamoDB on-demand for spiky or unknown load; provisioned with auto scaling for steady load.
Aurora I/O-Optimized pays off when I/O is roughly 25% or more of Aurora spend.
DLM automates EBS snapshot and AMI lifecycle; AWS Backup centralizes plans and cold storage tiering.
Set CloudWatch Logs retention; default is never expire.

gotchas.trap: Lifecycle-transitioning objects with unpredictable access to Standard-IA after 30 days.
gotchas.correct: Retrieval fees can exceed the savings; use Intelligent-Tiering for unknown patterns.

gotchas.trap: Growing a gp2 volume just to get more IOPS.
gotchas.correct: Move to gp3 and provision IOPS directly.

gotchas.trap: Switching every Aurora cluster to I/O-Optimized.
gotchas.correct: Only when I/O is a large share (about 25% or more) of Aurora cost.

gotchas.trap: Leaving CloudWatch Logs at default retention.
gotchas.correct: Default is never expire; set retention per log group.

lessons.lab: Use S3 Storage Lens to find buckets with no lifecycle rules, then add an Intelligent-Tiering rule to one. Convert a test gp2 volume to gp3 with Elastic Volumes, and create a DLM policy that keeps 7 daily snapshots for volumes tagged Backup=daily.

lessons.title: Planning and Running Large Migrations
lessons.summary: Discovery and wave planning with AWS Transform, choosing among the 7 Rs, rehosting with AWS Transform MGN, moving databases with DMS and Schema Conversion, moving files with DataSync or Data Transfer Terminal, and modernizing incrementally with the strangler fig pattern.

sections.heading: Discovery, dependency mapping, and waves
sections.body:
Large migrations succeed or fail on the portfolio work done before any server moves. You inventory servers and applications, map dependencies (who talks to whom, on which ports), group tightly coupled components into **move groups**, and sequence those groups into **waves**.

**AWS Transform** is the current AWS service for this. It is an agentic AI migration service that covers discovery, wave planning, landing zone and network translation, rehost to EC2 (from VMware, Hyper-V, or bare metal), and containerization to ECS/EKS. Human-in-the-loop approvals are built in, and AWS Transform itself carries no additional charge.

> **Changed recently:** AWS Migration Hub and AWS Application Discovery Service are **closed to new customers** and are not on the SAP-C03 in-scope list. For a new customer, answer with AWS Transform.

sections.heading: The 7 Rs
sections.body:
| Strategy | What it means | Typical example |
|---|---|---|
| **Retire** | Decommission | Zombie apps (under ~5% CPU/memory) and idle apps (roughly 5-20% over 90 days) |
| **Retain** | Keep on premises for now | Recently upgraded or blocked by dependencies |
| **Rehost** | Lift and shift | AWS Transform MGN, Cloud Migration Factory, VM Import/Export |
| **Relocate** | Move a hypervisor-level platform | VMware workloads moved as-is |
| **Repurchase** | Move to SaaS | Replace a self-hosted CRM |
| **Replatform** | Lift, tinker, and shift | SQL Server to RDS for SQL Server, Graviton, App2Container |
| **Refactor / re-architect** | Redesign cloud-native | Monolith to microservices or serverless |

AWS prescriptive guidance for **large** migrations: favor rehost, replatform, relocate, or retire, and **modernize after migrating**. Refactor is the most complex and costly path and should not gate a datacenter exit.

sections.heading: Rehost with AWS Transform MGN
sections.body: **AWS Transform MGN** is the new name (June 2026) of AWS Application Migration Service. Only the name changed. It continuously replicates source servers at the block level into AWS, lets you launch test instances without disrupting the source, and then cut over with a short window. AWS Transform uses it as its replication engine.

sections.heading: Databases: DMS and Schema Conversion
sections.body:
- **AWS DMS** moves **data**: full load plus **change data capture (CDC)** to keep the target in sync until cutover, which keeps downtime low.
- **DMS Schema Conversion** (managed, built on the AWS SCT engine) converts **schema and code objects, not data**. Gen-AI-assisted conversion is available for Oracle, SQL Server, Db2, and SAP ASE sources to PostgreSQL targets.
- Heterogeneous migration pattern: convert schema first, then DMS full load + CDC, then cut over.

sections.heading: Files and bulk data
sections.body:
- **AWS DataSync**: online, managed, incremental transfer from NFS/SMB/HDFS/object storage to S3, EFS, or FSx, with encryption and integrity validation. The default for online bulk copy.
- **Data Transfer Terminal**: physical sites where you reserve a slot, bring your own storage devices, and upload to S3, EFS, or other endpoints. You keep custody of your devices. Use it when network bandwidth cannot meet the deadline.
- **Snowball Edge is not available to new customers** and the Snow Family is not on the C03 in-scope list. Do not choose it for a new customer.

sections.heading: Refactor incrementally: strangler fig
sections.body: The **strangler fig** pattern places a routing facade (for example API Gateway or an ALB with path rules) in front of the monolith. You build new services one capability at a time and shift the matching routes to them, while the monolith keeps serving everything else. Eventually the monolith has nothing left and is retired. It avoids a risky big-bang rewrite and gives a rollback path per route.

sections.heading: Mainframes
sections.body: Mainframe workloads (IBM z/OS, Fujitsu GS21) are not x86 servers, so block replication tools do not apply. **AWS Transform for mainframe** analyzes code and dependencies, and supports modernization (for example COBOL to Java) with human approvals. Data often moves separately through DMS or file transfer.

keyPoints: New customers use AWS Transform for discovery, wave planning, and rehost; Migration Hub and Application Discovery Service are closed to new customers.
AWS Transform MGN is the renamed AWS Application Migration Service: continuous block replication, non-disruptive tests, short cutover.
Large migrations: rehost/replatform/relocate/retire first, modernize after.
DMS Schema Conversion converts schema, not data; DMS full load + CDC moves data with minimal downtime.
DataSync for online bulk transfer; Data Transfer Terminal for physical transfer; never Snowball for new customers.
Strangler fig: a routing facade shifts one capability at a time to new services.

gotchas.trap: Use AWS Application Discovery Service and Migration Hub to plan waves for a new customer.
gotchas.correct: Both are closed to new customers. Use AWS Transform for discovery and wave planning.

gotchas.trap: DMS Schema Conversion migrates the tables and their data.
gotchas.correct: Schema Conversion converts schema and code objects only. DMS tasks move the data.

gotchas.trap: Refactor everything to serverless during the datacenter exit.
gotchas.correct: For large migrations, rehost or replatform first and modernize after migrating.

gotchas.trap: Order a Snowball Edge to ship data for a new AWS customer.
gotchas.correct: Snowball Edge is not available to new customers. Use DataSync online or Data Transfer Terminal physically.

lessons.lab: Sketch a wave plan for a 10-application portfolio: assign each app one of the 7 Rs, group dependent apps into move groups, and choose the transfer tool (Transform MGN, DMS + Schema Conversion, DataSync) for each. Then design a strangler-fig facade with API Gateway that routes /orders to a new service and everything else to the monolith.
