lessons.title: Designing Disaster Recovery
lessons.summary: Matching RTO and RPO to the four DR strategies, failing over with data-plane mechanisms, and using Elastic Disaster Recovery, Application Recovery Controller, Resilience Hub, Route 53, Global Accelerator, and multi-cluster container designs.

sections.heading: RTO, RPO, and cost
sections.body:
- **RPO** (recovery point objective): how much data loss is acceptable, measured backward from the disaster.
- **RTO** (recovery time objective): how long the service may be down.

Lower RTO/RPO means more standing infrastructure and cost. Pick the cheapest strategy that meets both numbers.

sections.heading: The four strategies
sections.body:
| Strategy | State in the DR Region | Traffic ready? |
|---|---|---|
| **Backup & restore** | Backups only; redeploy with IaC | No; slowest, cheapest |
| **Pilot light** | Data replicated live; app tier switched off | **Cannot serve traffic without action** |
| **Warm standby** | Full stack, scaled down | **Can serve traffic immediately** at reduced capacity |
| **Multi-site active/active** (or hot standby) | Full capacity | Yes; near-zero RTO |

Notes from the AWS DR whitepaper:
- **AWS Backup has no scheduled or automatic restore.** Automate restores yourself (for example SNS/EventBridge triggering Lambda with the SDK).
- Warm standby that depends on Auto Scaling to grow is a **control-plane** dependency during the event; hot standby is statically stable.
- Active/active still has **RPO > 0 for data corruption**, because corruption replicates. Keep point-in-time backups.
- AWS recommends one account per Region for DR isolation.

sections.heading: Data plane vs control plane failover
sections.body:
During a regional event, control planes (create, update, configure APIs) are less available than data planes. Design failover to depend only on **data-plane** operations:

- **Route 53 health checks** with failover records (health-check evaluation is data plane).
- **ARC routing controls**: on/off switches backed by a highly available cluster, with safety rules.

Control-plane actions to avoid on the critical path: editing weighted-record weights, changing **Global Accelerator traffic dials**, launching infrastructure with CloudFormation, or waiting for Auto Scaling.

CloudFront origin failover works **per request** (fails over to the secondary origin on configured error codes).

sections.heading: Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC)
sections.body:
Formerly Route 53 ARC. Capabilities:
- **Zonal shift**: you move traffic away from an impaired AZ for a load-balanced resource; it is temporary with an expiry (up to 3 days, extendable).
- **Zonal autoshift**: AWS shifts traffic away from an AZ on your behalf when it detects an impairment.
- **Region switch**: orchestrated multi-Region, multi-account recovery plans.
- **Routing control**: data-plane DNS failover switches with safety rules.
- **Readiness check**: monitors quotas, capacity, and routing configuration. **Not for the failover critical path.**

sections.heading: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS)
sections.body: Block-level continuous replication from on-premises or cloud servers into a low-cost **staging area subnet** (lightweight replication servers and cheap storage). Offers point-in-time recovery (useful against ransomware), non-disruptive drills, launch of recovery instances within minutes, and failback. For AWS-hosted sources it protects **EC2 instances, not RDS** databases; use RDS cross-Region replicas or Aurora Global Database for managed databases.

sections.heading: Resilience Hub, Route 53, Global Accelerator
sections.body:
- **AWS Resilience Hub**: define RTO/RPO policies per application, assess the architecture against them, get recommendations (alarms, SOPs, FIS experiments), and track drift. Integrates with DRS, AWS Backup, and ARC. Use it for **DR testing and continuous validation**.
- **Route 53**: health checks plus failover, latency, weighted, or geolocation routing. Clients cache DNS answers for the record TTL.
- **Global Accelerator**: static anycast IP addresses at the AWS edge; endpoint health checks shift traffic between Regional endpoints without relying on client DNS caches.
- **Aurora Global Database**: secondary Regions with typically sub-second lag; a secondary can be promoted in under a minute.

sections.heading: Multi-cluster EKS and ECS
sections.body: An EKS cluster or ECS cluster is a Regional construct. For Regional resilience, run **independent clusters in each Region** (deployed from the same pipeline and IaC), each spread across multiple AZs, and steer traffic with Route 53 health checks, ARC, or Global Accelerator. Keep state outside the cluster in replicated data stores. Multiple clusters per Region also reduce blast radius for upgrades and misconfiguration.

keyPoints: Pilot light cannot serve traffic without action; warm standby can serve immediately at reduced capacity.
Fail over with data-plane operations: Route 53 health checks and ARC routing controls.
Changing weights or Global Accelerator traffic dials is a control-plane action.
ARC readiness checks are not part of the failover critical path.
Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates servers (EC2 or on-premises), not RDS.
AWS Backup does not restore automatically; automate restores yourself.
Active/active still needs point-in-time backups because corruption replicates.

gotchas.trap: Pilot light gives near-zero RTO because data is already replicated.
gotchas.correct: The app tier must be started and scaled first, so RTO is tens of minutes or more. Warm standby serves immediately.

gotchas.trap: Use an ARC readiness check to trigger failover.
gotchas.correct: Readiness checks monitor preparedness. Use routing controls or health checks to fail over.

gotchas.trap: Protect RDS with Elastic Disaster Recovery.
gotchas.correct: DRS protects EC2 and on-premises servers. Use RDS cross-Region replicas or Aurora Global Database.

gotchas.trap: Run one EKS cluster stretched across two Regions.
gotchas.correct: Clusters are Regional. Run independent clusters per Region and route between them.

lessons.lab: For an ALB + ECS + Aurora app, write a DR design for RTO 10 minutes, RPO 1 minute: choose the strategy, the database replication method, and an ARC routing-control failover with Route 53. Then register the app in Resilience Hub with a matching policy and list the recommendations you would expect.

lessons.title: Business Continuity and Ransomware Resilience
lessons.summary: Centralized cross-account AWS Backup, immutability with Backup Vault Lock, S3 Object Lock and EBS snapshot lock, and validating resilience with Fault Injection Service.

sections.heading: Centralized, cross-account AWS Backup
sections.body:
- Define **backup policies in AWS Organizations** so every account in an OU gets the same plans, applied by tags.
- Copy recovery points to a vault in a **separate, locked-down backup account** (and optionally another Region). A compromised workload account then cannot delete the copies.
- Use a delegated administrator account for day-to-day backup administration instead of the management account.
- Remember restores are not automatic. Script and test them.

sections.heading: AWS Backup Vault Lock
sections.body:
- **Governance mode**: users with the right IAM permissions can remove the lock. Good for testing.
- **Compliance mode**: after a **grace time of at least 3 days (72 hours)** the lock becomes immutable, even for AWS. Optional **minimum and maximum retention** make non-conforming backup jobs fail.
- No extra charge.
- Vault Lock does not block EC2-level `ModifySnapshotAttribute` (for example sharing a snapshot publicly), so deny that with an SCP or IAM policy.

sections.heading: S3 Object Lock
sections.body:
- Requires **versioning**.
- **Compliance mode**: nobody, including the root user, can delete a locked version or shorten its retention.
- **Governance mode**: callers with `s3:BypassGovernanceRetention` who send the bypass header can override.
- **Legal hold**: no expiry; stays until removed.
- A simple DELETE without a version ID only adds a delete marker; locked versions remain.

sections.heading: EBS snapshot lock
sections.body:
- Governance or compliance mode; lock duration from 1 to 36,500 days; no extra cost.
- Compliance mode has an optional **cooling-off period of 1-72 hours**. During it, authorized users can still change or remove the lock; after it ends, the lock cannot be removed or shortened, only extended.

sections.heading: Chaos engineering with AWS Fault Injection Service
sections.body:
1. Define a **steady-state hypothesis** (for example: p99 latency under 300 ms and error rate under 0.1% while one AZ is impaired).
2. Build an **experiment template**: **actions** (what fault), **targets** (which resources), and **stop conditions** (CloudWatch alarms that halt the experiment).
3. Run in pre-production first, then in production with tight stop conditions.
4. Use multi-account experiments for distributed systems. Resilience Hub can recommend and run FIS experiments.

Pair FIS with Route 53 health checks and ARC to prove failover actually works.

keyPoints: Organizations backup policies plus cross-account copy to an isolated backup account protect against account compromise.
Backup Vault Lock compliance mode becomes immutable after a grace time of at least 72 hours.
S3 Object Lock needs versioning; compliance mode cannot be overridden even by root.
EBS snapshot lock compliance mode supports a 1-72 hour cooling-off period.
FIS templates contain actions, targets, and stop conditions tied to CloudWatch alarms.

gotchas.trap: Governance mode is enough to stop an attacker with admin credentials.
gotchas.correct: Privileged users can bypass governance mode. Use compliance mode for ransomware protection.

gotchas.trap: A locked backup vault prevents every way of leaking snapshots.
gotchas.correct: Deny ec2:ModifySnapshotAttribute with an SCP or IAM, because Vault Lock does not block it.

gotchas.trap: Run the first chaos experiment in production without stop conditions.
gotchas.correct: Start in pre-production and always define CloudWatch alarm stop conditions.

lessons.lab: Create a backup vault in a separate backup account, apply Vault Lock in governance mode with min/max retention, add a cross-account copy rule, and add an SCP denying ec2:ModifySnapshotAttribute. Then write an FIS template that stops instances in one AZ with a stop condition on an ALB 5xx alarm.

lessons.title: Governing Infrastructure as Code
lessons.summary: Use CloudFormation and the CDK as the delivery mechanism, layer policy as code at synth, deploy and run time, roll out baselines with StackSets, and keep secrets out of templates.

sections.heading: CloudFormation and the CDK
sections.body:
**AWS CloudFormation** is the provisioning engine: a template declares resources, and a stack is one deployed instance of that template. The **AWS CDK** lets teams define infrastructure in a general-purpose language. It **synthesizes CloudFormation templates**, so everything that governs CloudFormation (Hooks, stack policies, StackSets, change sets) still applies to CDK apps.

Controls that protect stateful resources during updates:
- **Change sets** preview what an update will do, including whether a resource will be **replaced**. Review them before you execute the update.
- **Stack policies** deny update actions such as `Update:Replace` or `Update:Delete` on named logical resources, such as a production database.
- **DeletionPolicy / UpdateReplacePolicy** (`Retain` or `Snapshot`) keep or snapshot data when a resource is deleted or replaced.
- **Termination protection** only blocks deleting the whole stack.
- **Drift detection** reports resources that someone changed outside CloudFormation. It detects drift but does not prevent it.

sections.heading: Policy as code in layers
sections.body:
Task 5.1.2 lists four mechanisms. Each one runs at a different point and has a different bypass risk:

| Layer | When it runs | Strength | Limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CDK aspects** | During `cdk synth`, visiting every construct in a scope | Fastest developer feedback; can also fix things automatically (add tags, set encryption) | Only for CDK apps that include the aspect; developers can skip it |
| **CloudFormation Hooks** | Before provisioning, on resources, stacks, change sets and Cloud Control API calls | Enforced by the service, whatever tool produced the template; set to **fail** or **warn** | Only covers changes that go through CloudFormation or Cloud Control API |
| **AWS Config rules** | After resources exist (detective) | Covers console and CLI changes too; can trigger remediation | Finds problems after deployment |
| **SCPs** | At every API call in member accounts | Hard preventive guardrail that applies to all principals in the account | Coarse: works on API actions and condition keys, not whole template logic |

Hooks can be built from **Guard rules**, **Lambda functions**, custom hook code, or Control Tower **proactive controls**. A mature design uses aspects for quick feedback, Hooks as the server-side gate, Config rules to catch out-of-band changes, and SCPs for absolute prohibitions.

sections.heading: StackSets for multi-account baselines
sections.body:
A **StackSet** deploys one template as stack instances across many accounts and Regions. The StackSet itself is a Regional resource.
- **Self-managed permissions**: you create the administration and execution roles yourself. It works with any accounts, including accounts outside your organization.
- **Service-managed permissions**: integrates with AWS Organizations. You run it from the management account or a **delegated administrator** account. With **automatic deployment**, accounts that join a target OU get the stack instances automatically, and you can choose to retain or delete stacks when an account leaves.
- Rollout controls: **maximum concurrent accounts**, **failure tolerance** per Region, and **sequential or parallel** Region order. Use these to roll out gradually and stop the rollout if failures pile up.

sections.heading: Secrets Manager and Parameter Store
sections.body:
- **AWS Secrets Manager** stores secrets with **built-in rotation**: managed rotation for supported services such as RDS, or a rotation Lambda function for anything else. It supports **resource-based policies** for cross-account access and can **replicate secrets to other Regions**. To share a secret across accounts, encrypt it with a **customer managed KMS key**. The AWS managed key `aws/secretsmanager` cannot be used from another account.
- **Systems Manager Parameter Store** holds hierarchical configuration as String, StringList or **SecureString** (KMS-encrypted) values, in a standard tier and an advanced tier. It has **no native rotation**, so it fits configuration and secrets that rarely change.
- In templates, use **dynamic references** such as `{{resolve:secretsmanager:...}}` so the value is fetched when the stack is deployed and never sits in source control. For RDS and Aurora, `ManageMasterUserPassword` has the database service create and rotate the master password in Secrets Manager.
- A `NoEcho` parameter only hides the value in console and API output. If you put a default value in the template, the secret is still in source control.

keyPoints: The CDK synthesizes CloudFormation, so CloudFormation-level governance covers CDK apps too.
CDK aspects = synth-time feedback; CloudFormation Hooks = enforced pre-provisioning gate; Config rules = detective; SCPs = API-level prevention.
Service-managed StackSets with automatic deployment cover new accounts in target OUs without manual action.
Stack policies and DeletionPolicy/UpdateReplacePolicy protect stateful resources; termination protection covers only stack deletion.
Secrets Manager rotates and shares secrets cross-account (customer managed key plus resource policy); Parameter Store has no native rotation.

gotchas.trap: Relying on a CDK aspect to enforce encryption for every team.
gotchas.correct: Aspects only run in CDK apps that include them. Use a CloudFormation Hook in fail mode as the enforced gate.

gotchas.trap: Enabling termination protection to stop a database from being replaced during a stack update.
gotchas.correct: Termination protection only blocks deleting the stack. Use a stack policy that denies Update:Replace, and review change sets.

gotchas.trap: Sharing a secret encrypted with aws/secretsmanager across accounts.
gotchas.correct: AWS managed keys cannot be used cross-account. Use a customer managed key and a resource policy on the secret.

gotchas.trap: Using self-managed StackSets and manually adding each new account.
gotchas.correct: Service-managed permissions with automatic deployment target OUs and include new accounts automatically.

Deploy a non-compliant template and read the warning, then switch the Hook to fail mode and redeploy. Finally, add a CDK aspect that sets encryption on all buckets and confirm the synthesized template passes.

lessons.title: CI/CD, DevSecOps and Deployment Strategies
lessons.summary: Design CodePipeline-based delivery across accounts and Regions, add vulnerability scanning, signing and AI evaluation gates, and choose blue/green, canary, linear or rolling releases with automatic rollback.

sections.heading: The AWS developer tools
sections.body:
- **CodeCommit**: managed Git repositories. It is back to **general availability and open to new customers** (since late 2025) and is in scope for this exam.
- **CodeBuild**: managed build and test containers driven by a `buildspec`. Typical uses are unit tests, IaC linting, image builds, security scans and evaluation jobs.
- **CodeDeploy**: deploys to EC2/on-premises (in-place or blue/green), **Lambda** (traffic shifting between alias versions) and **ECS** (blue/green with load balancer target groups). It can roll back automatically when **CloudWatch alarms** fire.
- **CodePipeline**: orchestrates source, build, test, approval and deploy stages.

sections.heading: Cross-account and cross-Region pipelines
sections.body:
The usual pattern runs the pipeline in a central **tooling account** and deploys into separate dev, test and prod accounts:
1. Encrypt the pipeline's artifact bucket with a **customer managed KMS key**. The key policy grants the target accounts' roles permission to decrypt. The default AWS managed key cannot be shared across accounts, which is a common reason cross-account deploys fail.
2. Add a bucket policy that lets the target account roles read artifacts.
3. In each target account, create a **cross-account role** that the pipeline assumes. The CloudFormation deploy action can also pass a deployment role that it uses inside the account.
4. For cross-Region actions, CodePipeline needs an **artifact store in each Region** where actions run.

**Promote artifacts. Don't rebuild them.** Build once, then move the same immutable artifact, such as a container image referenced by **digest**, through each environment. If you rebuild per environment, you test one binary and ship a different one.

sections.heading: DevSecOps gates
sections.body:
- **Amazon ECR scanning**: *basic* scanning runs on push or manually. *Enhanced* scanning uses **Amazon Inspector**, scans continuously, and rescans images when new vulnerabilities are published. Inspector also covers EC2 and Lambda.
- **Artifact signing**: sign container images (for example with AWS Signer and Notation) and Lambda code (code signing configurations). Verify signatures before you deploy or at admission time, so only artifacts your pipeline produced can run. Image tag immutability stops tags from being overwritten, but it does not prove where an image came from.
- **Amazon Bedrock Evaluations** (skill 5.2.4): when a gen AI change ships (new model, prompt template or knowledge base), run an evaluation job against a curated prompt dataset. Jobs can score responses automatically or with human reviewers, and knowledge base (RAG) changes can be evaluated the same way. **Fail the pipeline stage when scores drop below a threshold**, just like a failing unit test.

sections.heading: Choosing a deployment strategy
sections.body:
| Strategy | How it works | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| **All-at-once / in-place** | Replace everything at once | Dev/test; downtime is acceptable |
| **Rolling** | Replace capacity in batches | Cost-sensitive; tolerates mixed versions during rollout |
| **Canary** | Small slice first, then the rest (e.g. 10% then 100%) | Want early real-traffic signal with small blast radius |
| **Linear** | Equal increments at fixed intervals | Gradual, predictable ramp |
| **Blue/green** | Full parallel environment, then shift traffic | Fast rollback by switching back; needs double capacity briefly |

Tie every progressive deployment to **CloudWatch alarms** so it rolls back automatically. For ECS, the **deployment circuit breaker** rolls back failed rolling deployments. **ECS native blue/green** (no CodeDeploy needed) adds a **bake time** and **lifecycle hooks** (Lambda or pause) and shifts traffic through ALB, NLB, Service Connect or VPC Lattice. For Lambda, CodeDeploy shifts traffic with weighted aliases using canary, linear or all-at-once configurations.

keyPoints: Cross-account pipelines need a customer managed KMS key for artifacts, a bucket policy, and assumable roles in target accounts.
Build once and promote the same immutable artifact (image digest) through environments.
ECR enhanced scanning (Inspector) is continuous; basic scanning is on push or manual.
Signing plus verification at deploy time proves provenance; tag immutability does not.
Use Bedrock evaluation jobs as a pipeline quality gate for model, prompt and knowledge base changes.
Progressive deployments should roll back automatically when CloudWatch alarms fire.

gotchas.trap: Using the default artifact encryption in a pipeline that deploys to another account.
gotchas.correct: The AWS managed key cannot be shared. Use a customer managed KMS key whose policy grants the target account roles.

gotchas.trap: Rebuilding the image in each environment's pipeline stage.
gotchas.correct: Build once and promote the same digest; rebuilding breaks the guarantee that what you tested is what you ship.

gotchas.trap: Assuming ECS blue/green requires CodeDeploy.
gotchas.correct: ECS now offers native blue/green with bake time and lifecycle hooks; CodeDeploy is one option, not a requirement.

gotchas.trap: Judging a prompt change only by latency metrics after release.
gotchas.correct: Run a Bedrock evaluation job on a fixed dataset before promotion and gate on quality scores.

Use a customer managed KMS key for the artifact bucket. Add a Lambda function deployed through CodeDeploy with a canary configuration tied to an error-rate alarm, then push a faulty version and watch it roll back.

lessons.title: Observability Across Accounts, Users and AI Workloads
lessons.summary: Combine CloudWatch, X-Ray and ADOT for metrics, logs and traces; centralize telemetry across accounts; monitor real and synthetic users; set SLOs with burn-rate alarms; and watch AI inference and model drift.

sections.heading: Metrics, logs and traces
sections.body:
- **CloudWatch metrics and alarms**: static thresholds, **anomaly detection** bands, and **composite alarms** that combine several alarms to reduce noise.
- **CloudWatch Logs**: Logs Insights queries, metric filters, and the embedded metric format for emitting metrics from structured logs.
- **AWS X-Ray**: distributed traces and service maps.
- **AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT)**: AWS's supported OpenTelemetry distribution. You instrument once with vendor-neutral OpenTelemetry APIs and export to X-Ray, CloudWatch or other backends. Choose it when portability matters.
- **Container Insights** collects cluster, node, service/task and pod metrics and logs for ECS and EKS. On EKS, the CloudWatch Observability add-on enables the enhanced observability mode.

sections.heading: Cross-account telemetry and retention
sections.body:
- **CloudWatch cross-account observability**: one or more **monitoring accounts** link to **source accounts** (individually or across an organization). From the monitoring account you can search and query their metrics, logs and traces without copying data.
- **Centralized log archive**: **subscription filters** stream log events to Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon Data Firehose or Lambda. Cross-account delivery goes to a destination in the central account, and **account-level subscription policies** cover every log group in an account. Firehose then writes to S3, where **lifecycle rules move data to archive storage classes** for long, cheap retention.
- Set CloudWatch Logs retention to match how long you actually query the data, and archive older data in S3. Keeping everything forever in CloudWatch Logs is expensive.

sections.heading: Users, synthetics and SLOs
sections.body:
- **CloudWatch Synthetics canaries** are scripted checks that run on a schedule against endpoints and user flows. They **catch failures even when no real users are active**, for example overnight.
- **CloudWatch RUM** collects page load timings, JavaScript errors and sessions from real browsers, broken down by browser, device and location.
- **Application Signals** collects **latency and availability** for instrumented services automatically, and any CloudWatch metric can serve as an SLI. **SLOs** are **period-based or request-based**, have an attainment goal over a rolling or calendar interval, and track an **error budget**. **Burn-rate alarms** fire when the budget is being used up too quickly, which is better than a static error-count threshold. Example: 99% over 30 days of 1-minute periods means 42,768 of 43,200 periods must be healthy.
- **Alerting and response**: alarms publish to **SNS** for people and systems, and alarm state changes go to **EventBridge** to start **Systems Manager Automation** runbooks.

sections.heading: AI and agent observability
sections.body:
- **Amazon Bedrock** publishes CloudWatch runtime metrics for invocations, **invocation latency**, client and server errors, **throttles**, and **input/output token counts**. Use these for capacity alarms and latency SLOs.
- **Model invocation logging is disabled by default.** When enabled, it captures full requests and responses with metadata (caller `identity.arn`, token counts, optional `requestMetadata` tags) and sends them to CloudWatch Logs and/or S3 in the **same account and Region**. CloudTrail records API calls, not prompt and response bodies.
- **AgentCore Observability** emits OpenTelemetry traces for agent steps and tool calls, and **AgentCore Evaluations** adds quality signals.
- **Model drift** on SageMaker AI endpoints: **SageMaker Model Monitor** compares captured inference data with a baseline built from the training data, on a schedule. It covers data quality, model quality, bias drift and feature-attribution drift, and its results feed CloudWatch alarms.

keyPoints: Cross-account observability: monitoring account linked to source accounts; no data copying.
Long-term log archive: subscription filters to Firehose to S3 with lifecycle rules.
Synthetics catches problems with no traffic; RUM measures real user experience.
Application Signals SLOs track error budgets; alert on burn rate.
Bedrock invocation logging is off by default and same account/Region only.
SageMaker Model Monitor detects data and model drift against a baseline.

gotchas.trap: Using CloudTrail to see prompts and responses sent to Bedrock.
gotchas.correct: CloudTrail logs API calls. Enable model invocation logging to capture request and response bodies.

gotchas.trap: Relying on RUM to detect an outage at 3 a.m. when nobody is using the site.
gotchas.correct: RUM only sees real users. Synthetics canaries run on a schedule regardless of traffic.

gotchas.trap: Alerting on a fixed 5xx count for an SLO-driven service.
gotchas.correct: Define an SLO and use burn-rate alarms so pages reflect error budget risk.

gotchas.trap: Retaining all logs indefinitely in CloudWatch Logs for compliance.
gotchas.correct: Stream to S3 and use lifecycle transitions to archive tiers; keep short CloudWatch retention.

lessons.lab: In a sandbox organization, set up CloudWatch cross-account observability with one monitoring account and two source accounts. Deploy a small instrumented service and create an Application Signals availability SLO with a burn-rate alarm. Add a Synthetics canary for its health endpoint, then break the endpoint and watch both signals fire.

lessons.title: Automating Resilience Operations
lessons.summary: Keep workloads within quotas, use backoff, circuit breakers, rate limits and bulkheads to contain failures, scale ahead of demand, and let health checks and runbooks repair systems automatically.

sections.heading: Quotas and event-driven operations
sections.body:
- **Service Quotas** shows applied and default quotas and handles increase requests. For quotas that publish usage metrics, create **CloudWatch alarms on utilization** so you hear about limits before you hit them. A **quota request template** in AWS Organizations automatically requests your standard increases when new accounts are created.
- **EventBridge** rules react to alarms, AWS Health events, Config compliance changes and service events, then call **Systems Manager Automation**, Lambda or Step Functions.

sections.heading: Failure containment patterns
sections.body:
- **Retries with exponential backoff and jitter**: wait longer after each failure and randomize the delay so clients don't retry in sync. Cap the number of attempts. AWS SDKs already include retry with backoff. Immediate retries with no limit turn a slowdown into a **retry storm**.
- **Circuit breaker**: after repeated failures, stop calling the unhealthy dependency for a while and **fail fast** or serve a fallback. Then send probe requests to check whether it has recovered.
- **Rate limiting and throttling**: API Gateway stage and method throttling and **usage plans** with per-client API keys, plus AWS WAF **rate-based rules**. These protect the backend from one noisy client.
- **Bulkheads**: split resources so a failure in one part cannot drain the rest. Examples are separate queues or worker pools per workload, cell-based architectures, and Lambda **reserved concurrency** per function, which both guarantees and caps that function's share of account concurrency.
- **Idempotency**: retries are only safe if repeating an operation has no extra side effects. Use idempotency keys.

sections.heading: Scaling ahead of demand
sections.body:
- **Target tracking** keeps a metric (for example average CPU or requests per target) near a target value and is the default choice.
- **Step scaling** adds or removes capacity in steps based on how far an alarm is breached.
- **Scheduled scaling** handles known calendar events, but someone has to keep the schedule up to date.
- **Predictive scaling** uses machine learning on historical load to **forecast** daily and weekly patterns and **launches capacity before demand arrives**. It helps most when instances take a long time to initialize. Start in **forecast-only** mode to check the forecasts, and **combine it with target tracking** for anything the forecast misses.
- **Application Auto Scaling** applies the same policy types to ECS services, DynamoDB, Aurora replicas, Lambda provisioned concurrency and others.

sections.heading: Self-healing and automated runbooks
sections.body:
- **Auto Scaling group health checks**: EC2 status checks by default. Turn on **ELB health checks** so the group replaces instances that fail application-level checks.
- **ECS** service schedulers replace tasks that stop or fail container or load balancer health checks.
- **Lambda asynchronous invocations** are retried twice by default. Configure **on-failure destinations** or a DLQ, and set the maximum event age, so failed events are kept instead of lost. Event source mappings have their own retry and partial-batch settings.
- **Automated runbooks**: Systems Manager **Automation** runbooks fix problems (restart, resize, reconfigure). **Patch Manager** with patch baselines and **maintenance windows** handles patching. **Config rules with automatic remediation** run Automation documents when a resource falls out of compliance. **Alarm or EventBridge triggers** start runbooks without waiting for a person.

keyPoints: Alarm on quota utilization; use quota request templates for new accounts.
Exponential backoff with jitter plus capped retries prevents retry storms; circuit breakers fail fast.
Bulkheads (reserved concurrency, separate queues, cells) contain noisy neighbors.
Predictive scaling launches capacity before forecast peaks; pair with target tracking.
ASGs need ELB health checks to replace instances that are up but unhealthy at the application level.
Config auto-remediation and EventBridge-triggered Automation runbooks close the loop without humans.

gotchas.trap: Increasing retry counts and removing delays when a dependency is slow.
gotchas.correct: Use capped retries with exponential backoff and jitter, plus a circuit breaker.

gotchas.trap: Expecting an ASG to replace instances whose application returns errors.
gotchas.correct: With only EC2 status checks it will not; set the health check type to include ELB.

gotchas.trap: Using scheduled scaling for a pattern that shifts gradually every week.
gotchas.correct: Predictive scaling learns the pattern without manual schedule maintenance.

gotchas.trap: Letting failed asynchronous Lambda events disappear after retries.
gotchas.correct: Configure an on-failure destination or DLQ and make handlers idempotent.

lessons.lab: Create an Auto Scaling group behind an ALB with ELB health checks and a target tracking policy, then add predictive scaling in forecast-only mode. Break the application's health endpoint on one instance and watch the group replace it. Add an EventBridge rule that starts an Automation runbook when a CloudWatch alarm enters ALARM.

flashcards.front: What delivery guarantee does an SQS standard queue provide?
flashcards.back: At-least-once delivery with best-effort ordering. Consumers must be idempotent.

flashcards.front: In SQS FIFO, what is the unit of ordering?
flashcards.back: The message group ID. Messages in one group are ordered; different groups are processed in parallel.

flashcards.front: How do you scale throughput on an SQS FIFO queue while keeping per-customer order?
flashcards.back: Use a high-cardinality message group ID (such as customer ID) and high-throughput FIFO, which adds partitions.

flashcards.front: What decides which shard a Kinesis Data Streams record lands on?
flashcards.back: The partition key. A low-cardinality key creates hot shards.

flashcards.front: Common idempotency pattern for Lambda consumers?
flashcards.back: Write an idempotency key with a DynamoDB conditional write; if it already exists, skip the side effect.

flashcards.front: Step Functions Standard: duration and execution semantics?
flashcards.back: Up to 1 year, exactly-once, billed per state transition, supports .sync and .waitForTaskToken.

flashcards.front: Step Functions Express: duration and execution semantics?
flashcards.back: Up to 5 minutes; async is at-least-once, sync is at-most-once; no .waitForTaskToken.

flashcards.front: What are Lambda durable functions?
flashcards.back: Multi-step workflows in Lambda code for up to one year using checkpoint/replay; waits suspend execution without compute charges.

flashcards.front: How do you route events from many accounts to a central account?
flashcards.back: EventBridge rules that target the event bus in the central account (cross-account and cross-Region targets are supported).

flashcards.front: What is a VPC Lattice service network?
flashcards.back: The logical boundary that groups services and VPCs, shared via RAM, with IAM auth policies at network and service level.

flashcards.front: Does VPC Lattice work with overlapping VPC CIDRs?
flashcards.back: Yes. It also has no inter-AZ data transfer charges.

flashcards.front: ECS Service Connect is used for what?
flashcards.back: Name-based service discovery and service-to-service traffic with metrics between ECS services in a namespace.

flashcards.front: EKS pods are Pending because nodes are full. Which component adds nodes?
flashcards.back: The Cluster Autoscaler. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler only changes pod counts.

flashcards.front: CloudFront Functions vs Lambda@Edge?
flashcards.back: CloudFront Functions: lightweight JS on viewer events, no network access. Lambda@Edge: viewer and origin events, network calls, heavier logic.

flashcards.front: How do you push messages to connected clients with API Gateway?
flashcards.back: Use a WebSocket API, store connection IDs (for example in DynamoDB), and post to connections through the management API.

flashcards.front: Silo vs pool tenancy?
flashcards.back: Silo: dedicated resources per tenant. Pool: shared resources with tenant context enforced (Cognito claims, row-level security, scoped credentials).

flashcards.front: Which Knowledge Base type offers SharePoint/Confluence connectors and document-level ACL filtering?
flashcards.back: The Managed Knowledge Base.

flashcards.front: AgentCore Gateway does what?
flashcards.back: Turns existing APIs and Lambda functions into MCP tools that agents can call.

flashcards.front: Which AgentCore component stores context across agent sessions?
flashcards.back: AgentCore Memory (short- and long-term).

flashcards.front: Cross-Region inference profile for EU data residency?
flashcards.back: The EU geographic profile. A global profile may route to any commercial Region.

flashcards.front: SageMaker AI inference for large payloads with long processing and queued requests?
flashcards.back: Asynchronous inference.

flashcards.front: Direct Connect maximum resiliency model?
flashcards.back: Separate connections on separate devices in more than one location (99.99% SLA).

flashcards.front: Same prefix learned over DX gateway and VPN on a Transit Gateway: which wins?
flashcards.back: Direct Connect; VPN becomes the backup.

flashcards.front: Route 53 Resolver inbound vs outbound endpoints?
flashcards.back: Inbound: on-premises queries into AWS. Outbound + forwarding rules: AWS queries to on-premises DNS.

flashcards.front: Managed SFTP endpoint into S3 for external partners?
flashcards.back: AWS Transfer Family.

flashcards.front: Outposts vs Local Zones?
flashcards.back: Outposts: AWS infrastructure in your data center. Local Zones: AWS-run infrastructure in metro areas near users.

flashcards.front: How can Network Firewall inspect Transit Gateway traffic without an inspection VPC?
flashcards.back: Attach Network Firewall natively to the TGW; appliance mode is enabled automatically.

flashcards.front: Gateway Load Balancer is used for what?
flashcards.back: Inserting third-party virtual appliances (firewalls, IDS) transparently and at scale using GENEVE.

flashcards.front: Which VPC endpoints are free and which services do they cover?
flashcards.back: Gateway endpoints, for S3 and DynamoDB only, in the same Region.

flashcards.front: What does Global Accelerator provide?
flashcards.back: Static anycast IP addresses, entry at the nearest AWS edge, TCP/UDP support, and fast endpoint failover.

flashcards.front: Cloud WAN segments?
flashcards.back: Isolated routing domains (like VRFs) defined in the core network policy; attachments map to segments by tag.

flashcards.front: Outbound-only internet access for IPv6 instances?
flashcards.back: An egress-only internet gateway.

flashcards.front: Aurora Global Database key numbers?
flashcards.back: Up to 5 secondary Regions, typical replication lag under 1 second, promotion in under a minute.

flashcards.front: DynamoDB global tables conflict resolution?
flashcards.back: Every replica Region accepts writes; with the default eventually consistent mode, conflicts resolve by last writer wins.

flashcards.front: What does AWS Clean Rooms solve?
flashcards.back: Joint analysis of combined datasets without sharing or copying raw data.

flashcards.front: Microsecond read cache for DynamoDB with minimal code change?
flashcards.back: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX).

flashcards.front: Which service is the default for workforce access to many AWS accounts, and which two protocols connect it to an external IdP?
flashcards.back: IAM Identity Center. SAML 2.0 handles sign-in and SCIM provisions and deprovisions users and groups automatically. Access is granted with permission sets assigned to groups on accounts.

flashcards.front: Cognito user pool vs identity pool?
flashcards.back: A user pool is a user directory and OIDC/OAuth 2.0 token issuer (sign-up, sign-in, MFA, federation). An identity pool exchanges tokens for temporary AWS credentials through IAM roles.

flashcards.front: How do you restrict each Cognito identity to its own S3 prefix?
flashcards.back: Use the policy variable ${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub} in the identity pool role policy resource ARN.

flashcards.front: EKS Pod Identity: what does the role trust, and why does that help?
flashcards.back: The service principal pods.eks.amazonaws.com. No per-cluster OIDC provider is needed, so one role can be reused across clusters without editing its trust policy.

flashcards.front: Where is EKS Pod Identity not supported?
flashcards.back: Fargate, Windows nodes, Outposts and EKS Anywhere. Use IRSA (OIDC-based IAM roles for service accounts) there.

flashcards.front: IAM Roles Anywhere: trust anchor vs profile?
flashcards.back: The trust anchor points to the CA (AWS Private CA or an external CA) that issued the workload X.509 certificates. The profile lists the roles that can be assumed and an optional session policy.

flashcards.front: What does AWS Verified Access evaluate and log?
flashcards.back: Each request to an application is evaluated against identity and device trust data, without a VPN, and every access attempt is logged.

flashcards.front: Can a permissions boundary or session policy grant permissions?
flashcards.back: No. Both only cap permissions. The effective result is the intersection with identity-based policies.

flashcards.front: How do you let developers create IAM roles without privilege escalation?
flashcards.back: Allow iam:CreateRole only with the condition iam:PermissionsBoundary equal to an approved boundary policy ARN, and deny removing or changing that boundary.

flashcards.front: What problem does sts:ExternalId solve?
flashcards.back: The confused deputy problem: a third party that assumes roles for many customers cannot be tricked into using your role on behalf of someone else.

flashcards.front: Core ABAC condition for project isolation?
flashcards.back: Compare aws:ResourceTag/project with ${aws:PrincipalTag/project}. New projects need new tags, not new policies.

flashcards.front: IAM Access Analyzer: external access vs unused access findings?
flashcards.back: External access findings show resources shared outside the zone of trust (account or organization). Unused access findings show unused roles, access keys, passwords and permissions.

flashcards.front: SCP vs RCP in one line each?
flashcards.back: SCP: maximum permissions for principals in member accounts. RCP: maximum permissions on resources in member accounts, including requests from principals outside the org.

flashcards.front: Four things RCPs do not affect or cover?
flashcards.back: The management account, service-linked roles, AWS managed KMS keys, and services not on the supported list (Bedrock is not on it).

flashcards.front: Which KMS keys support automatic rotation?
flashcards.back: Only symmetric keys with KMS-generated material. Default 365 days, with a custom RotationPeriodInDays allowed. Imported symmetric keys support on-demand rotation.

flashcards.front: How do you rotate an asymmetric, HMAC or custom key store KMS key?
flashcards.back: Manually: create a new key and point the alias to it.

flashcards.front: Does KMS key rotation re-encrypt existing data?
flashcards.back: No. KMS keeps the previous key material so old ciphertext still decrypts; only new encryptions use the new material.

flashcards.front: Where is rotation configured for a KMS multi-Region key?
flashcards.back: On the primary key.

flashcards.front: ML-DSA vs ML-KEM in KMS?
flashcards.back: ML-DSA (FIPS 204, ML_DSA_44/65/87) is for signing and verification. ML-KEM (FIPS 203, ML_KEM_512/768/1024) does key encapsulation with Encapsulate/Decapsulate.

flashcards.front: Why is TLS 1.3 central to post-quantum migration on AWS?
flashcards.back: Post-quantum hybrid key exchange requires TLS 1.3. ELB, API Gateway and Transfer Family TLS policies do not upgrade on their own, so set them explicitly and verify the key exchange in CloudTrail tlsDetails.

flashcards.front: When is CloudHSM the right choice over KMS?
flashcards.back: When you need single-tenant HSMs under your exclusive control, or applications need standard cryptographic APIs such as PKCS#11, JCE or OpenSSL.

flashcards.front: ACM public certificate vs AWS Private CA?
flashcards.back: ACM public certificates are for publicly resolvable names and need domain validation. AWS Private CA issues certificates for internal names, mTLS and workloads, and can be a Roles Anywhere trust anchor.

flashcards.front: Three control behaviors in AWS Control Tower?
flashcards.back: Preventive (policies such as SCPs), detective (Config rules) and proactive (CloudFormation Hooks that check resources before provisioning).

flashcards.front: What makes an organization CloudTrail trail better than per-account trails?
flashcards.back: It automatically covers all current and new member accounts, and member accounts can see but not modify or delete it.

flashcards.front: What does Amazon Security Lake store and in what format?
flashcards.back: Security logs and findings (CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, Route 53 resolver query logs, EKS audit logs, WAF, Security Hub CSPM findings, custom sources) in your own S3, as OCSF in Parquet.

flashcards.front: Security Hub CSPM vs the new Security Hub?
flashcards.back: Security Hub CSPM checks posture against security standards. The new Security Hub (GA December 2025) correlates GuardDuty, Inspector, Security Hub CSPM and Macie into risk prioritization.

flashcards.front: What does Amazon Inspector scan?
flashcards.back: EC2 instances, ECR container images and Lambda functions, continuously, for software vulnerabilities (and network exposure for EC2).

flashcards.front: What does AWS RAM let you share in a multi-account network?
flashcards.back: Resources such as Transit Gateways, VPC subnets, Route 53 Resolver rules and VPC Lattice service networks, with accounts or OUs.

flashcards.front: Bedrock model invocation logging: default state and destinations?
flashcards.back: Disabled by default. Writes to CloudWatch Logs and/or S3 in the same account and Region only. Bodies over 100 KB and binary data go to S3 only.

flashcards.front: Which Bedrock cross-Region inference profile satisfies data residency?
flashcards.back: A geographic profile (US, EU or APAC), which keeps processing in that geography. A global profile can route to any commercial Region.

flashcards.front: What is AWS Artifact for?
flashcards.back: Self-service download of AWS compliance reports (for example SOC and ISO) and acceptance of agreements such as a HIPAA BAA.

flashcards.front: Which Bedrock Guardrails features target prompt injection and RAG hallucination?
flashcards.back: The Prompt Attack content filter for prompt injection and jailbreaks; contextual grounding checks for ungrounded or irrelevant answers.

flashcards.front: How do you enforce one guardrail across all accounts in an organization?
flashcards.back: An AWS Organizations Amazon Bedrock policy that references a versioned guardrail in the management account with a resource policy granting bedrock:ApplyGuardrail. Most restrictive wins; Automated Reasoning is not supported in enforcements.

flashcards.front: What does the ApplyGuardrail API do?
flashcards.back: It evaluates content against a guardrail without invoking a foundation model, so it can protect models hosted outside Bedrock or intermediate agent steps.

flashcards.front: AgentCore Identity: inbound vs outbound?
flashcards.back: Inbound: a JWT authorizer accepts tokens from any IdP. Outbound: OAuth or API-key credential providers let the agent call tools on behalf of the user, with an audit trail.

flashcards.front: Which Step Functions pattern implements human approval?
flashcards.back: A Standard workflow task using .waitForTaskToken; the approver app calls SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure. Express workflows do not support it.

flashcards.front: Which Savings Plan covers EC2, Fargate and Lambda across instance families and Regions?
flashcards.back: Compute Savings Plans. EC2 Instance Savings Plans are limited to one instance family in one Region and do not cover Fargate or Lambda.

flashcards.front: What do Database Savings Plans cover, and what term do they use?
flashcards.back: A 1-year $/hour commitment that applies across Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, DocumentDB, Neptune, Keyspaces, Timestream and DMS, flexible across engine, Region, and provisioned vs serverless. The largest discount applies to serverless usage.

flashcards.front: Why rightsize before buying Savings Plans or Reserved Instances?
flashcards.back: A commitment locks in a spend level. Rightsizing first (Compute Optimizer, scaling policies) sizes the commitment to the real steady baseline so you do not pay for idle capacity.

flashcards.front: How much warning does Fargate Spot give before stopping a task, and how do you keep a minimum running?
flashcards.back: A two-minute warning (SIGTERM). Use a capacity provider strategy with a base on regular Fargate and the remaining weight on Fargate Spot.

flashcards.front: Step Functions Standard vs Express billing?
flashcards.back: Standard is billed per state transition (up to 1 year, exactly-once). Express is billed by executions, duration and memory (up to 5 minutes, at-least-once async), so it is cheaper for high-volume short work.

flashcards.front: Bedrock batch inference: price and constraints?
flashcards.back: About 50% cheaper than on-demand for supported models. Input and output are in S3, there is no real-time response, and it is not supported for provisioned models.

flashcards.front: When does Bedrock prompt caching save money?
flashcards.back: When many requests share a long, repeated prompt prefix. Cache reads are cheaper than normal input tokens. TTL is usually about 5 minutes and resets on each hit. It works with on-demand inference, not batch.

flashcards.front: Bedrock global vs geographic cross-Region inference profile?
flashcards.back: Global is roughly 10% cheaper but may route to any commercial Region. Geographic (US, EU, APAC) keeps processing in that geography, so use it for residency. Neither adds a routing charge.

flashcards.front: Which VPC endpoints are free, and for which services?
flashcards.back: Gateway endpoints, available only for S3 and DynamoDB, same Region. Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) charge hourly per AZ plus per GB.

flashcards.front: How do you avoid cross-AZ charges for NAT traffic?
flashcards.back: Deploy one NAT gateway per AZ and route each private subnet to the NAT in its own AZ.

flashcards.front: What does CloudFront Origin Shield do for cost?
flashcards.back: Adds a central caching layer in one Region in front of the origin, raising cache hit ratio and collapsing duplicate requests, which reduces origin load and egress. It adds a per-request charge and helps little for uncacheable content.

flashcards.front: When is VPC peering cheaper than Transit Gateway for a VPC pair?
flashcards.back: When two VPCs exchange large volumes: Transit Gateway charges per GB processed, while peering has no processing charge (normal cross-AZ or inter-Region transfer still applies).

flashcards.front: What must happen before a user-defined tag appears in Cost Explorer?
flashcards.back: It must be activated as a cost allocation tag in the Billing console of the management (payer) account.

flashcards.front: What does split cost allocation data add to CUR?
flashcards.back: Per-ECS-task and per-EKS-pod cost based on each one's CPU and memory share of the amortized instance cost (EKS also covers GPU and accelerators), with tags such as aws:eks:namespace.

flashcards.front: AWS Budgets vs Cost Anomaly Detection?
flashcards.back: Budgets alert (and can act) when actual or forecasted spend crosses a threshold you set. Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning to flag unusual spend without fixed thresholds.

flashcards.front: How do you charge back Bedrock token usage across teams that share an account?
flashcards.back: Enable model invocation logging, pass a team identifier in requestMetadata, and aggregate token counts by identity.arn or metadata with CloudWatch Logs Insights.

flashcards.front: When is Aurora I/O-Optimized cheaper than Aurora Standard?
flashcards.back: When I/O charges are about 25% or more of total Aurora spend. You can switch to I/O-Optimized once every 30 days and back at any time.

flashcards.front: Why move gp2 volumes to gp3?
flashcards.back: gp3 sets IOPS and throughput independently of size and is generally cheaper per GB, so you stop over-provisioning capacity for IOPS. Elastic Volumes converts in place without downtime.

flashcards.front: DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned capacity?
flashcards.back: On-demand: pay per request, best for new, spiky or unpredictable traffic. Provisioned with auto scaling: cheaper for steady, predictable traffic with high utilization.

flashcards.front: What does Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager automate?
flashcards.back: Creation, retention, cross-Region or cross-account copy, and deletion of EBS snapshots and EBS-backed AMIs, targeted by tags.

flashcards.front: Default retention of a CloudWatch Logs log group?
flashcards.back: Never expire. Set a retention policy on each log group to control storage cost.

flashcards.front: List the 7 Rs of migration.
flashcards.back: Retire, Retain, Rehost, Relocate, Repurchase, Replatform, Refactor (re-architect).

flashcards.front: What is AWS Transform MGN?
flashcards.back: The renamed AWS Application Migration Service: continuous block-level replication for rehost migrations, with non-disruptive test launches and short cutovers. It is the replication engine behind AWS Transform.

flashcards.front: Which service should a new customer use for discovery and wave planning?
flashcards.back: AWS Transform. Migration Hub and Application Discovery Service are closed to new customers.

flashcards.front: Does DMS Schema Conversion move data?
flashcards.back: No. It converts schema and code objects. DMS tasks (full load + CDC) move the data.

flashcards.front: Online bulk file transfer vs physical transfer for a new customer?
flashcards.back: Online: AWS DataSync. Physical: Data Transfer Terminal (bring your own devices to an AWS site). Snowball Edge is not available to new customers.

flashcards.front: What is the strangler fig pattern?
flashcards.back: A routing facade in front of a monolith shifts one capability at a time to new services until the monolith can be retired.

flashcards.front: Pilot light vs warm standby?
flashcards.back: Pilot light: data live, app tier off, cannot serve traffic without action. Warm standby: scaled-down full stack that can serve traffic immediately.

flashcards.front: Which failover mechanisms are data-plane operations?
flashcards.back: Route 53 health-check-based failover and ARC routing controls. Changing record weights or Global Accelerator traffic dials are control-plane actions.

flashcards.front: What does AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery replicate, and where to?
flashcards.back: Servers (on-premises or cloud, and EC2 for AWS sources, not RDS) at the block level into a low-cost staging area subnet, with point-in-time recovery, drills, and failback.

flashcards.front: Name the main ARC capabilities.
flashcards.back: Zonal shift, zonal autoshift, Region switch, routing control, and readiness check (readiness check is not on the failover critical path).

flashcards.front: What does AWS Resilience Hub do?
flashcards.back: Defines RTO/RPO policies per app, assesses the app against them, recommends improvements and FIS experiments, and tracks resilience drift. Integrates with DRS, Backup, and ARC.

flashcards.front: Does AWS Backup restore automatically in a DR Region?
flashcards.back: No. There is no scheduled or automatic restore; automate restores with the SDK (for example Lambda triggered by events).

flashcards.front: Backup Vault Lock compliance mode: when does it become immutable?
flashcards.back: After the grace time (minimum 3 days / 72 hours). Then nobody, including AWS, can remove it.

flashcards.front: S3 Object Lock compliance vs governance mode?
flashcards.back: Compliance: nobody, even root, can delete or shorten retention. Governance: users with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention and the bypass header can override. Both need versioning.

flashcards.front: EBS snapshot lock cooling-off period?
flashcards.back: Optional 1-72 hours in compliance mode; afterwards the lock cannot be removed or shortened, only extended.

flashcards.front: What are the parts of an FIS experiment template?
flashcards.back: Actions, targets, and stop conditions (CloudWatch alarms).

flashcards.front: Why does active/active still need backups?
flashcards.back: Data corruption or ransomware replicates to every Region, so RPO for corruption is greater than zero without point-in-time backups.

flashcards.front: How do you get Regional resilience for EKS or ECS?
flashcards.back: Run independent clusters per Region (each multi-AZ) from the same IaC and pipeline, keep state in replicated data stores, and route with Route 53, ARC, or Global Accelerator.

flashcards.front: Why might Global Accelerator fail over faster for clients than DNS failover?
flashcards.back: Clients use static anycast IPs, and Global Accelerator shifts traffic between healthy endpoints at the edge, so client DNS caching (TTL) does not delay failover.

flashcards.front: What gap does Backup Vault Lock leave that an SCP should close?
flashcards.back: It does not block ec2:ModifySnapshotAttribute (for example sharing snapshots); deny it with an SCP or IAM policy.

flashcards.front: CDK aspects vs CloudFormation Hooks: when does each run?
flashcards.back: CDK aspects run during synthesis inside a CDK app and give quick feedback or automatic fixes. CloudFormation Hooks run in the service before provisioning, for any template or Cloud Control API call, and either fail the operation or warn.

flashcards.front: What can a CloudFormation Hook inspect?
flashcards.back: Individual resources, whole stacks, change sets, and Cloud Control API operations, before provisioning.

flashcards.front: Ways to implement CloudFormation Hooks
flashcards.back: Control Tower proactive controls, CloudFormation Guard rules, Lambda functions, or custom hook code.

flashcards.front: StackSets: self-managed vs service-managed permissions
flashcards.back: Self-managed: you create the admin and execution roles, and it works for any accounts. Service-managed: AWS Organizations integration, run from the management account or a delegated administrator, with automatic deployment to accounts added to target OUs.

flashcards.front: StackSet rollout controls
flashcards.back: Maximum concurrent accounts, failure tolerance per Region, sequential or parallel Region order, and retaining stacks when accounts are removed.

flashcards.front: What protects a database from replacement during a stack update?
flashcards.back: Review change sets for replacement, set a stack policy that denies Update:Replace on that resource, and set UpdateReplacePolicy/DeletionPolicy to Retain or Snapshot. Termination protection only blocks deleting the stack.

flashcards.front: Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store
flashcards.back: Secrets Manager: built-in rotation, cross-account resource policies, and replication to other Regions. Parameter Store: hierarchical config and SecureString values with no native rotation, good for config and secrets that rarely change.

flashcards.front: Requirement for sharing a Secrets Manager secret across accounts
flashcards.back: A resource-based policy on the secret plus a customer managed KMS key whose key policy allows the other account. The AWS managed key aws/secretsmanager cannot be used cross-account.

flashcards.front: How do you keep secrets out of CloudFormation templates?
flashcards.back: Use dynamic references (for example to Secrets Manager) resolved at deploy time, or have RDS/Aurora manage the master password in Secrets Manager. NoEcho with a default value still leaves the secret in source.

flashcards.front: Cross-account CodePipeline essentials
flashcards.back: A customer managed KMS key for the artifact store, a bucket policy for target roles, and a cross-account role in each target account that the pipeline assumes. Cross-Region actions need an artifact store in each Region.

flashcards.front: Why promote artifacts instead of rebuilding per environment?
flashcards.back: Promoting the same immutable artifact, such as an image digest, guarantees that production runs exactly what was tested.

flashcards.front: ECR basic vs enhanced scanning
flashcards.back: Basic: on push or manual. Enhanced: powered by Amazon Inspector, continuous, and rescans images when new vulnerabilities are published.

flashcards.front: What does artifact signing add beyond image tag immutability?
flashcards.back: Provenance. Verifying a signature at deploy or admission time proves the artifact came from your trusted pipeline. Immutability only stops tags from being overwritten.

flashcards.front: Role of Amazon Bedrock Evaluations in CI/CD
flashcards.back: A quality gate. Run an evaluation job (automatic or human scoring) on a curated dataset when a model, prompt or knowledge base changes, and fail promotion when scores drop below a threshold.

flashcards.front: Canary vs linear vs blue/green
flashcards.back: Canary: a small slice of traffic, then the rest. Linear: equal increments at fixed intervals. Blue/green: a full parallel environment, then a traffic switch with fast rollback. All should be tied to alarm-based rollback.

flashcards.front: ECS native blue/green features
flashcards.back: Bake time, lifecycle hooks (Lambda or pause), and managed traffic shifting for ALB, NLB, Service Connect or VPC Lattice, with no CodeDeploy needed.

flashcards.front: CloudWatch cross-account observability
flashcards.back: Monitoring accounts are linked to source accounts (or a whole organization) so their metrics, logs and traces can be searched centrally without copying the data.

flashcards.front: Centralized, low-cost long-term log retention
flashcards.back: Subscription filters (or account-level subscription policies) send logs to a cross-account destination, Firehose writes them to S3, and lifecycle rules move them to archive storage classes.

flashcards.front: Synthetics vs RUM
flashcards.back: Synthetics canaries run scripted checks on a schedule, even with no users. RUM measures real users' page loads, errors and sessions by browser, device and location.

flashcards.front: Application Signals SLO building blocks
flashcards.back: An SLI (automatic latency/availability or any CloudWatch metric), period-based or request-based evaluation, an attainment goal over a rolling or calendar interval, an error budget, and burn-rate alarms.

flashcards.front: Bedrock model invocation logging defaults
flashcards.back: Disabled by default. When enabled, it logs full requests and responses with identity.arn and token counts to CloudWatch Logs and/or S3 in the same account and Region.

flashcards.front: How do you detect model drift on a SageMaker AI endpoint?
flashcards.back: SageMaker Model Monitor compares captured inference data with a training baseline on a schedule (data quality, model quality, bias, feature attribution) and sends results to CloudWatch alarms.

flashcards.front: Exponential backoff with jitter
flashcards.back: Retry delays grow after each failure and are randomized, with a cap on attempts, so clients do not retry in sync and overload a recovering dependency.

flashcards.front: Circuit breaker vs bulkhead
flashcards.back: Circuit breaker: stop calling a failing dependency and fail fast until probe requests succeed. Bulkhead: split resources (pools, queues, reserved concurrency, cells) so one failure cannot drain everything.

flashcards.front: Predictive scaling
flashcards.back: ML forecasts of recurring load that launch capacity before the forecast peak. Validate in forecast-only mode and pair with target tracking.

flashcards.front: Service Quotas automation
flashcards.back: CloudWatch alarms on quota utilization, and quota request templates in Organizations that automatically request increases for new accounts.

flashcards.front: Why set an ASG health check type to ELB?
flashcards.back: EC2 status checks only catch instance-level failures. ELB health checks let the group replace instances whose application fails health checks.

flashcards.front: Lambda async invocation failure handling
flashcards.back: Two retries by default, configurable retry count and maximum event age, and on-failure destinations or a DLQ to keep failed events.

questions.scenario: A retailer processes orders from an SQS standard queue with Lambda. During a traffic spike, some customers were charged twice for the same order. Logs show the same message was delivered to two invocations.
questions.stem: What is the MOST reliable fix?
options: Increase the queue visibility timeout so the same message is never delivered twice.
Record the order ID with a DynamoDB conditional write before charging, and skip processing when the record already exists.
Set the Lambda reserved concurrency to 1 so only one invocation runs at a time.
Enable long polling on the queue to reduce duplicate receives.
questions.explanation: SQS standard queues deliver at least once, so duplicates can occur regardless of tuning. An idempotency key stored with a conditional write makes the charge happen only once. The other options reduce the chance of duplicates or throughput but do not remove them.
rationales: A longer visibility timeout reduces redelivery after slow processing but cannot prevent at-least-once duplicates.
Correct. A conditional write on the order ID makes the side effect idempotent.
Serializing processing cuts throughput and still processes a duplicate message twice.
Long polling reduces empty receives; it does not change the delivery guarantee.

questions.scenario: A bank sends account events to an SQS FIFO queue. Events for each account must be processed in order. The queue uses a single message group ID, and throughput has hit a ceiling while consumers sit idle.
questions.stem: Which change raises throughput while keeping the ordering requirement?
options: Switch to an SQS standard queue and sort events by timestamp in the consumer.
Add more consumers to the queue without other changes.
Use the account ID as the message group ID and enable high-throughput mode for the FIFO queue.
Use a random message group ID for each message to spread the load.
questions.explanation: FIFO ordering is per message group ID, and parallelism comes from having many groups. Using the account ID keeps per-account order and lets many groups process at once, and high-throughput FIFO scales partitions. One group serializes everything, and random groups lose per-account order.
rationales: Standard queues do not guarantee order, and timestamp sorting in consumers is fragile.
With one message group, only one message is in flight at a time, so extra consumers stay idle.
Correct. Per-account groups preserve the required order and allow parallel processing.
Random groups break ordering for events of the same account.

questions.scenario: A clickstream pipeline writes events to Kinesis Data Streams using the visitor's country code as the partition key. Most traffic comes from two countries, and two shards are throttled while others are nearly idle.
questions.stem: What should the architect change?
options: Use a high-cardinality partition key such as session ID.
Double the number of shards in the stream.
Switch the consumer to enhanced fan-out.
Move the data to an SQS standard queue.
questions.explanation: The partition key decides the shard, so a low-cardinality key creates hot shards. A high-cardinality key spreads records evenly. Adding shards does not help when the same few keys still map to the same shards.
rationales: Correct. A high-cardinality key distributes writes across shards.
More shards do not help when only two key values carry most of the traffic.
Enhanced fan-out improves read throughput per consumer, not write hot spots.
An SQS standard queue drops per-key ordering and stream replay, and it does not fix the partition key design.

questions.scenario: A payment workflow calls a card processor (not idempotent), waits up to 5 days for a fraud analyst to approve high-value transactions, and then updates the ledger.
questions.stem: Which orchestration choice meets these requirements?
options: A Step Functions Express workflow with a Wait state for the approval.
An SQS delay queue that re-checks the approval status every 15 minutes.
An EventBridge Scheduler schedule that polls a DynamoDB approval table.
A Step Functions Standard workflow that uses a .waitForTaskToken step for the analyst approval.
questions.explanation: Standard workflows run up to a year with exactly-once execution, which suits non-idempotent payment calls. The task token pattern pauses until the analyst sends success or failure. Express workflows are limited to 5 minutes and do not support task tokens.
rationales: Express workflows run at most 5 minutes and are at-least-once when asynchronous.
Polling with delay queues adds custom state handling and is not a durable workflow.
Polling with a scheduler works but adds custom code and lacks workflow state and history.
Correct. Standard plus .waitForTaskToken gives exactly-once execution and a durable human approval.

questions.scenario: A media company receives about 50,000 small JSON events per second. Each event goes through three short, idempotent transformation steps that finish in under a second. Cost is the main concern.
questions.stem: Which workflow type should the architect choose?
options: Step Functions Express workflows.
Step Functions Standard workflows.
Step Functions Standard workflows with a Distributed Map state per event.
An Amazon MQ broker with one queue per transformation step.
questions.explanation: Express workflows are designed for high-volume, short, idempotent processing and are billed by executions, duration and memory. Standard workflows bill per state transition, which is expensive at this volume.
rationales: Correct. Express suits high-volume, short, idempotent steps.
Standard bills per state transition and is costly at tens of thousands of events per second.
Distributed Map processes large datasets in parallel; per event it adds cost and complexity.
MQ is for broker-protocol compatibility, not serverless orchestration.

questions.scenario: A development team writes most of its business logic in Lambda. A new onboarding process runs several steps, then waits up to two weeks for a customer to upload documents before continuing. The team wants to keep the logic in code and not pay for compute while waiting.
questions.stem: Which approach fits BEST?
options: A single Lambda function that sleeps in a loop until documents arrive.
An EC2 instance running a cron job that resumes onboarding.
A Lambda durable function that checkpoints completed steps and suspends while waiting.
A Step Functions Express workflow with a Wait state.
questions.explanation: Lambda durable functions run multi-step code for up to a year with checkpoint/replay, and waits suspend execution without compute charges. A sleeping function hits the Lambda timeout and pays while idle, and Express is limited to 5 minutes.
rationales: A Lambda invocation has a maximum timeout and would bill for idle time.
A cron server adds infrastructure to manage and pays continuously.
Correct. Durable functions keep the logic in code and do not charge compute while waiting.
Express workflows run for at most 5 minutes.

questions.scenario: A company has 60 workload accounts. The security team wants all EC2 state-change and GuardDuty-related events delivered to a central security account for processing, with minimal custom code.
questions.stem: What should the architect do?
options: Deploy a Lambda function in every account that polls EventBridge and writes to an S3 bucket.
In each account, create an EventBridge rule whose target is the event bus in the central account, and allow those accounts in the central bus resource policy.
Create an SNS topic in each account and subscribe a central SQS queue to all 60 topics.
Enable CloudTrail in each account and query events with Athena every 5 minutes.
questions.explanation: EventBridge rules can target an event bus in another account, and the target bus's resource policy controls who can send. This centralizes events with no custom code. Polling and batch querying add latency and code.
rationales: Custom polling code is unnecessary; EventBridge pushes events.
Correct. Cross-account event bus targets are the native pattern.
This works but adds 60 topics and subscriptions to manage and does not use content-based routing.
Batch querying CloudTrail adds latency and is not event-driven.

questions.scenario: An enterprise runs microservices on ECS, EKS and Lambda across 25 accounts. Several VPCs have overlapping CIDR ranges. Teams want service-to-service calls with IAM-based authorization and without managing peering, Transit Gateway routes or sidecar proxies.
questions.stem: Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Peer all VPCs and use security groups to restrict calls.
Expose every service through its own PrivateLink endpoint service and create interface endpoints in every consumer VPC.
Attach all VPCs to a Transit Gateway and use NACLs for authorization.
Create a VPC Lattice service network, share it with AWS RAM, associate the VPCs and services, and apply auth policies.
questions.explanation: VPC Lattice connects services across accounts and VPCs, supports overlapping CIDRs, and enforces IAM auth policies at the service network and service. Targets include ECS tasks, Kubernetes pods and Lambda. Peering and TGW cannot route overlapping CIDRs, and per-service PrivateLink does not scale well for many-to-many calls.
rationales: Peering does not work with overlapping CIDRs and gives no IAM authorization.
PrivateLink works with overlapping CIDRs but needs an endpoint per service per consumer, which is a lot of overhead.
TGW cannot route overlapping CIDRs, and NACLs are not identity-aware.
Correct. VPC Lattice handles overlapping CIDRs, cross-account sharing and IAM auth.

questions.scenario: A CloudFront distribution serves a global web app. The team needs to (1) normalize query strings and add security headers on every request with minimal latency, and (2) on cache misses, call an external entitlement API before forwarding to the origin.
questions.stem: Which combination is MOST appropriate?
options: Lambda@Edge for both tasks on viewer request.
CloudFront Functions for both tasks.
CloudFront Functions for header and query-string work, and Lambda@Edge on origin request for the entitlement call.
AWS WAF rules for both tasks.
questions.explanation: CloudFront Functions are built for lightweight, high-volume viewer-event logic such as header manipulation and cache-key normalization. They have no network access and do not run on origin events, so the external API call needs Lambda@Edge on origin request, which runs only on cache misses.
rationales: This works but runs heavier, costlier code on every request for simple header logic.
CloudFront Functions cannot make network calls or run on origin events.
Correct. Each tool is used for what it is designed for.
WAF filters requests; it does not rewrite query strings or call external APIs.

questions.scenario: A trading platform must push price updates to tens of thousands of browser clients in real time. The team wants a serverless design.
questions.stem: Which architecture fits BEST?
options: An API Gateway REST API that clients poll every second.
An API Gateway WebSocket API, with connection IDs stored in DynamoDB and a Lambda function posting updates to each connection.
An SNS topic with a browser subscription per client.
An ALB with sticky sessions in front of EC2 instances that hold connections in memory.
questions.explanation: WebSocket APIs keep persistent two-way connections, and storing connection IDs externally lets stateless Lambda functions push updates to clients. Polling wastes requests and adds latency, and in-memory connection state on EC2 is not serverless.
rationales: Polling adds latency and cost and is not real time.
Correct. This is the serverless real-time push pattern.
SNS does not deliver directly to browser sessions.
This is not serverless, and state kept in instance memory makes scaling harder.

questions.scenario: A SaaS provider runs a pooled multi-tenant application on Aurora PostgreSQL with Cognito user pools. Standard-tier tenants share all resources. A new regulated customer requires that its data be encrypted with a key that can be revoked independently and that it cannot be affected by other tenants' load.
questions.stem: Which TWO actions should the architect take? (Select two.)
options: Deploy a siloed stack (dedicated database and compute) for the regulated tenant, encrypted with a tenant-specific KMS customer managed key.
Put the tenant ID in Cognito token claims and enforce row-level security in the pooled database for standard tenants.
Move all tenants into one shared table and filter by tenant ID only in the UI.
Give every tenant the same IAM role and rely on application code for isolation.
Create a separate Cognito user pool for each standard tenant and keep the shared database without row-level security.
questions.explanation: A silo with its own KMS key gives the regulated tenant independent key revocation and protection from noisy neighbors. Standard tenants stay pooled, with tenant context carried in Cognito claims and enforced by row-level security. UI-only filtering and shared roles do not enforce isolation.
rationales: Correct. Silo plus a tenant-specific key meets the isolation and revocation requirements.
