questions.scenario: A company runs 180 AWS accounts in AWS Organizations and uses Okta as its corporate identity provider. Today, each account has IAM users created by a ticket process, and leavers often keep access for weeks.
questions.stem: Which solution gives employees single sign-on to the accounts and removes access automatically when someone leaves Okta?
options: Create an Amazon Cognito user pool federated with Okta and grant console access through the identity pool roles
Create a SAML identity provider in IAM in every account, and use a nightly script to create matching IAM roles and remove roles for leavers
Enable IAM Identity Center, connect Okta as the external IdP with SAML 2.0, enable SCIM provisioning, and assign permission sets to Okta groups on accounts
Keep IAM users but enforce MFA and an access key rotation policy, and use IAM Access Analyzer to find unused users
questions.explanation: IAM Identity Center with an external IdP centralizes workforce access across the organization. SAML 2.0 handles sign-in and SCIM keeps users and groups in sync, so a user disabled in Okta loses access without manual steps. Permission sets are defined once and deployed as roles to each assigned account.
rationales: Cognito is for application end users, not workforce access to AWS accounts and the console.
Per-account SAML trusts work but need 180 configurations and a custom script; deprovisioning still depends on that script.
Correct. Identity Center plus SAML and SCIM gives SSO and automatic deprovisioning across all accounts.
IAM users keep long-term credentials and still require manual deprovisioning; detection with Access Analyzer does not fix the process.

questions.scenario: A mobile photo app must let signed-in users upload images directly to Amazon S3 without passing through the backend. Each user must be able to write only under their own prefix in the bucket.
questions.stem: Which design meets these requirements with the least operational overhead?
options: Authenticate users with a Cognito user pool, exchange the token through a Cognito identity pool for temporary credentials, and scope the role policy with the ${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub} variable
Embed an IAM user access key with s3:PutObject in the app and validate the user ID in an S3 event notification Lambda function
Federate users through IAM Identity Center and assign a permission set that allows s3:PutObject on the bucket
Store a shared access key in AWS Secrets Manager and let the app retrieve it after login
questions.explanation: A Cognito identity pool exchanges the user pool token for temporary AWS credentials, so the client can call S3 directly. Using the identity ID policy variable in the resource ARN confines each user to their own prefix. No long-term credentials ship with the app.
rationales: Correct. User pool for sign-in, identity pool for temporary credentials, and a policy variable for per-user scoping.
Long-term keys in a mobile app can be extracted, and after-the-fact validation does not prevent writes to other prefixes.
IAM Identity Center is for workforce access, not consumer app users.
A shared key gives every user the same permissions and is still a long-term credential.

questions.scenario: A platform team runs 14 Amazon EKS clusters on managed EC2 node groups across several accounts. Each new cluster today requires updating the trust policies of dozens of IAM roles to add the cluster's OIDC provider. The team wants pods to keep using least-privilege IAM roles.
questions.stem: Which approach removes the per-cluster trust policy updates?
options: Attach all required permissions to the node instance role so every pod inherits them
Keep IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA) and use a wildcard for the OIDC provider in the trust policy
Store access keys for each role in Kubernetes Secrets and mount them into the pods
Use EKS Pod Identity: install the Pod Identity Agent and create pod identity associations to roles that trust pods.eks.amazonaws.com
questions.explanation: EKS Pod Identity roles trust the pods.eks.amazonaws.com service principal instead of a cluster-specific OIDC provider. The same role can be associated with service accounts in any cluster without editing its trust policy. Managed EC2 node groups are supported.
rationales: Node roles give every pod on the node the same broad permissions, breaking least privilege.
IRSA trust policies are tied to specific OIDC providers; a wildcard approach is not how IRSA trust is meant to work and would weaken the trust boundary.
Long-term keys in Secrets must be rotated and can leak; temporary credentials are preferred.
Correct. Pod Identity removes the OIDC provider dependency and lets roles be reused across clusters.

questions.scenario: A company is moving a batch service to Amazon EKS. The pods will run on AWS Fargate profiles, and they must read from one Amazon SQS queue and write to one S3 bucket using a dedicated IAM role.
questions.stem: How should the pods obtain AWS credentials?
options: Create an EKS Pod Identity association for the service account and install the Pod Identity Agent DaemonSet
Use IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA): create the cluster OIDC provider and annotate the service account with a role that trusts it
Attach the policy to the Fargate pod execution role
Use IAM Roles Anywhere with a certificate issued to each pod
questions.explanation: EKS Pod Identity is not supported on Fargate, so IRSA is the supported way to give Fargate pods a dedicated role. IRSA uses the cluster OIDC provider and a service account annotation. The pod execution role is for pulling images and logging, not application permissions.
rationales: Pod Identity and its agent DaemonSet are not supported on Fargate.
Correct. IRSA works on Fargate and gives each service account its own role.
The pod execution role is used by the Fargate infrastructure (image pulls, logs) and would not isolate application permissions.
Roles Anywhere is for workloads outside AWS, not pods running in EKS.

questions.scenario: A manufacturer has 300 on-premises Linux servers that upload telemetry to Amazon S3. They use IAM user access keys stored in configuration files. A security audit forbids long-term AWS credentials on servers. The company already operates an enterprise PKI that issues X.509 certificates to every server.
questions.stem: Which solution meets the requirement?
options: Configure IAM Roles Anywhere with a trust anchor for the enterprise CA and a profile that maps to a role allowing the S3 uploads
Rotate the access keys every 30 days with a Lambda function and store them in AWS Secrets Manager
Create an Amazon Cognito identity pool and let each server authenticate as an unauthenticated identity
Place the servers behind AWS Verified Access and allow the Verified Access endpoint to write to S3
questions.explanation: IAM Roles Anywhere lets workloads outside AWS exchange an X.509 certificate from a trusted CA for temporary credentials. The trust anchor references the existing enterprise CA and the profile limits which roles can be assumed. No long-term keys remain on the servers.
rationales: Correct. Certificates from the existing PKI become the identity, and the servers receive only temporary credentials.
Rotated keys are still long-term credentials stored on servers, and fetching them from Secrets Manager needs credentials too.
Unauthenticated Cognito identities provide no strong server identity and are meant for app guests.
Verified Access controls user access to applications; it does not issue credentials for S3 calls.

questions.scenario: A company wants to retire its client VPN for 40 internal web applications hosted behind ALBs in private subnets. Security requires that each request is checked against the user's corporate identity and the device's security posture, and that every access attempt is logged.
questions.stem: Which AWS service should the architect use?
options: AWS Client VPN with authorization rules per security group
Public ALBs with Amazon Cognito authentication actions
AWS Verified Access with the corporate IdP as identity trust provider and a device trust provider
AWS PrivateLink endpoint services shared to each employee laptop
questions.explanation: Verified Access provides VPN-less access to applications and evaluates every request against identity and device trust data. It logs every access attempt, which meets the audit requirement. This is the zero-trust pattern the scenario describes.
rationales: Client VPN is the thing being retired and does not evaluate device posture per request.
Cognito authentication on a public ALB checks identity but not device posture, and exposes the apps publicly.
Correct. Verified Access checks identity and device trust on each request and logs all attempts.
PrivateLink connects VPCs to services; it cannot be shared to individual laptops.

questions.scenario: Developers in a workload account need to create IAM roles for their own Lambda functions without waiting for the security team. Security must ensure that no role a developer creates can ever have more permissions than an approved set, and that developers cannot escalate their own privileges.
questions.stem: Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Require developers to pass a session policy when they assume their role so created roles inherit the session limits
Attach an SCP that denies iam:CreateRole in the workload account and have the security team create roles on request
Grant developers AdministratorAccess and review CloudTrail weekly for unusual role creation
Grant developers iam:CreateRole and iam:AttachRolePolicy only when the iam:PermissionsBoundary condition equals an approved boundary policy, and deny changing or deleting that boundary
questions.explanation: A permissions boundary caps what any role can do, and the iam:PermissionsBoundary condition key forces developers to attach it whenever they create a role. Denying edits to the boundary closes the escalation path. This delegates role creation safely.
rationales: Session policies limit only the current session; they are not inherited by roles that session creates.
This is secure but removes the self-service the scenario asks for.
Detective review after the fact does not prevent privilege escalation.
Correct. The required boundary limits every created role, and the deny protects the boundary itself.

questions.scenario: A SaaS cost-analysis vendor needs read access to billing data in thousands of customer AWS accounts. Each customer creates an IAM role in its own account that the vendor's AWS account assumes.
questions.stem: What should each customer add to the role trust policy to prevent the vendor from being tricked into accessing one customer's account on behalf of another?
options: A condition on aws:SourceIp limited to the vendor's published IP ranges
A condition that requires sts:ExternalId to equal a unique value the vendor assigns to that customer
A permissions boundary on the role
A condition requiring aws:PrincipalOrgID to match the customer's organization
questions.explanation: This is the confused deputy problem. Requiring a unique external ID per customer means the vendor only assumes a customer's role when acting for that customer. The other options do not tie the request to the specific customer relationship.
rationales: IP conditions confirm the call comes from the vendor, but every customer's request comes from the same vendor IPs.
Correct. A unique sts:ExternalId per customer prevents the confused deputy.
A boundary limits permissions, not who can assume the role or for whom.
The vendor's principal is outside the customer's organization, so this condition would block the vendor entirely.

questions.scenario: A research institute has 60 project teams that share one AWS account. Each team must access only its own S3 objects, DynamoDB items and Secrets Manager secrets. New projects start every month, and the IAM team is tired of writing a new policy for each one. Users sign in through IAM Identity Center, which passes a project attribute from the IdP.
questions.stem: Which approach scales best?
options: Create one IAM role and one customer managed policy per project, listing that project's resource ARNs
Use resource-based policies on every bucket and secret that list each team member's IAM Identity Center user
Use ABAC: pass the project attribute as a session tag, tag resources with project, and write policies that allow access when aws:ResourceTag/project matches aws:PrincipalTag/project
Create a permissions boundary per project and attach it to each user
questions.explanation: Attribute-based access control compares the principal's tag with the resource's tag, so one set of policies covers every project. New projects only need tags, not new policies. Identity Center can pass IdP attributes as session tags.
rationales: Role-per-project RBAC works but grows linearly and is exactly the overhead the institute wants to avoid.
Listing users in resource policies is hard to maintain and some services have policy size limits.
Correct. ABAC with matching principal and resource tags scales without new policies.
Boundaries per project still require a new policy for each project and do not grant access.

questions.scenario: A multi-tenant document service runs in one AWS account. Tenant data is stored in one S3 bucket under a prefix per tenant. A broker service assumes a single role, TenantDataAccess, which can read the whole bucket, before it processes each tenant request.
questions.stem: How can the architect ensure that each request's credentials can only reach the current tenant's prefix, without creating a role per tenant?
options: Call AssumeRole with an inline session policy that allows s3:GetObject only on the current tenant's prefix
Add a session policy that grants s3:GetObject on the tenant prefix and remove S3 permissions from the role
Attach an RCP that denies access to other tenants' prefixes
Enable S3 Object Ownership with bucket owner enforced
questions.explanation: A session policy passed at AssumeRole narrows the session to the intersection of the role's policy and the session policy. The broker can scope each session to one tenant prefix dynamically. Session policies cannot grant permissions the role lacks, so the role must keep the broad read access.
rationales: Correct. Per-request session policies scope the credentials to one tenant prefix.
Session policies cannot grant permissions; with S3 removed from the role, the intersection would allow nothing.
An RCP is an organization-wide guardrail and does not know which tenant a given request is for.
Object Ownership controls ACL ownership; it does not limit access by tenant.

questions.scenario: The security team of a 90-account organization must find every S3 bucket, KMS key and IAM role that is shared with principals outside the organization, and must also identify IAM roles and permissions that nobody has used for months.
questions.stem: Which actions meet these requirements? (Select two.)
options: Create an IAM Access Analyzer external access analyzer with the organization as the zone of trust from a delegated administrator account
Create an IAM Access Analyzer unused access analyzer for the organization
Enable Amazon GuardDuty S3 Protection in all accounts
Enable AWS Config and deploy the managed rule that checks for S3 buckets without default encryption
Create an AWS Organizations tag policy that requires a "shared" tag on every S3 bucket, KMS key and IAM role
questions.explanation: External access findings report resources that grant access to principals outside the zone of trust; setting the zone to the organization targets sharing outside the org. Unused access findings identify roles, keys and permissions that are not being used. GuardDuty detects threats and the encryption rule checks configuration, neither reports sharing or unused access.
rationales: Correct. External access findings with an organization zone of trust show resources shared outside the org.
Correct. Unused access findings flag unused roles and permissions across the organization.
GuardDuty S3 Protection looks for suspicious activity, not for resource policies shared outside the org.
That rule checks encryption settings, not cross-organization sharing or unused permissions.
Tag policies standardize tags; they do not detect cross-organization sharing or unused permissions.

questions.scenario: An organization wants to guarantee that data in S3 buckets and secrets in AWS Secrets Manager across all member accounts can never be read by principals outside the organization, even if a developer adds a bad bucket policy. AWS services that act on the company's behalf must keep working.
questions.stem: Which preventive control meets this requirement with the least ongoing effort?
options: An SCP attached at the root that denies s3:GetObject and secretsmanager:GetSecretValue unless aws:PrincipalOrgID matches the organization
A permissions boundary on every IAM role in the organization
IAM Access Analyzer external access findings with an EventBridge rule that notifies the security team
A resource control policy (RCP) attached at the root that denies those actions unless aws:PrincipalOrgID matches the organization, with an exception for AWS service principals
questions.explanation: RCPs restrict what can be done to resources in member accounts, including by principals outside the organization, and S3 and Secrets Manager are supported. An SCP only limits principals inside the organization, so it cannot stop outsiders. Access Analyzer detects rather than prevents, and boundaries affect only your own principals.
rationales: SCPs apply only to principals in member accounts; external principals are not affected.
Permissions boundaries cap your own principals and do nothing about outside principals.
This is detective; data could be read before anyone responds.
Correct. An RCP sets a preventive perimeter on resources that even a permissive bucket policy cannot override.

sources.title: Cross-account secret access — Secrets Manager docs

questions.scenario: A security architect attaches a resource control policy (RCP) at the organization root. It denies kms:Decrypt unless the calling principal belongs to the organization. All features are enabled in the organization.
questions.stem: Which statements about the effect of this RCP are correct? (Select two.)
options: It does not restrict KMS keys in the management account
It does not apply to AWS managed KMS keys
It grants kms:Decrypt to every principal in the organization
It also restricts actions taken by service-linked roles in member accounts
A key policy in a member account that explicitly allows a principal from another organization overrides this RCP
questions.explanation: RCPs do not affect resources in the management account and do not apply to AWS managed KMS keys. Like SCPs, they never grant permissions and they do not restrict service-linked roles. Principals still need identity or key policy permissions to decrypt.
rationales: Correct. RCPs do not affect the management account.
Correct. AWS managed KMS keys are out of RCP scope.
RCPs only restrict; access still needs an allow from a key policy or identity policy.
RCPs do not restrict service-linked roles.
An explicit deny in an RCP cannot be overridden by an allow in a key policy, so the external principal is still denied.

sources.title: What is AWS KMS — KMS docs

questions.scenario: A European bank must ensure that no workload in its production OU can create resources outside eu-central-1 and eu-west-1. Some global services such as IAM must keep working. The control must prevent violations, not only report them.
questions.stem: Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Deploy an AWS Config rule that flags resources in other Regions and auto-remediates by deleting them
Attach an SCP to the production OU that denies all actions when aws:RequestedRegion is not one of the two Regions, using NotAction to exempt required global services
Attach a permissions boundary to every IAM role in the production accounts that allows only the two Regions
Enable an Amazon EventBridge rule that alerts the security team when CloudTrail logs a call in another Region
questions.explanation: An SCP with a deny on aws:RequestedRegion prevents actions outside approved Regions for every principal in the OU. NotAction keeps global services such as IAM working. Config rules and EventBridge alerts are detective, and boundaries must be attached to every role and can be missed.
rationales: Detect-and-delete still lets resources exist and process data in other Regions for a while.
Correct. A Region-deny SCP is the standard preventive residency guardrail.
Boundaries would have to be on every principal, and any role without one would be unrestricted.
Alerts do not prevent the violation.

questions.scenario: A German insurer is building a claims assistant on Amazon Bedrock. Regulators require that inference requests are processed only in EU Regions. Traffic is bursty, and the team wants to use cross-Region inference for capacity.
questions.stem: Which configuration should the architect choose?
options: Use the EU geographic cross-Region inference profile and make sure SCPs allow the EU destination Regions the profile uses
Use the global cross-Region inference profile for the extra capacity and lower price
Use the global profile and add an SCP that denies aws:RequestedRegion values outside the EU
Disable cross-Region inference and send all requests to a single Region's on-demand endpoint with client-side retries
questions.explanation: A geographic inference profile keeps processing inside that geography, so the EU profile meets residency while adding burst capacity. SCPs must allow the destination Regions or requests are denied. The global profile can route to any commercial Region, which breaks the requirement.
rationales: Correct. The EU geographic profile keeps processing in the EU while spreading load.
The global profile can route requests outside the EU.

With a global profile the requested Region is "unspecified", so an EU-only Region SCP would block those requests rather than confine their routing; the global profile itself can still route outside the EU.
This keeps data in one Region but gives up the burst capacity the team needs.

questions.scenario: A compliance standard requires all encryption keys to be rotated at least every 180 days. The company uses three kinds of KMS customer managed keys: symmetric keys with KMS-generated material for S3 and EBS, asymmetric RSA keys for document signing, and HMAC keys for token verification.
questions.stem: Which approach meets the requirement with the least operational effort?
options: Enable automatic rotation with a 180-day period on all three key types
Re-import new key material into every key every 180 days
Enable automatic rotation with RotationPeriodInDays set to 180 on the symmetric keys; for the asymmetric and HMAC keys, create new keys on a schedule and move the aliases
Switch all keys to AWS managed keys, which rotate automatically
questions.explanation: Automatic rotation with a custom period is available only for symmetric keys with KMS-generated material. Asymmetric and HMAC keys must be rotated manually by creating a new key and updating the alias that applications use. AWS managed keys rotate yearly and cannot be changed, and they do not support signing or HMAC.
rationales: Asymmetric and HMAC keys do not support automatic rotation.
Key material can be imported only into keys created without KMS-generated material, so this does not work for these keys, and manual re-imports across every key add heavy operational work.
Correct. Automate what KMS supports and use alias swaps for the rest.
AWS managed keys rotate once a year (too slowly) and are symmetric encryption keys only.

questions.scenario: A media company enabled automatic rotation on the KMS customer managed key that protects 3 PB of objects in S3 using SSE-KMS. The storage team plans a large batch job to re-encrypt every object after each rotation.
questions.stem: What should the architect tell them?
options: The job is required, because objects encrypted under old key material can no longer be decrypted after rotation
The job is unnecessary, because rotation automatically re-encrypts all data keys stored with the objects
The job is required only for objects larger than 4 KB
The job is unnecessary, because KMS keeps prior key material and decrypts older ciphertext transparently while new encryptions use the new material
questions.explanation: Key rotation in KMS does not re-encrypt data. KMS retains every earlier version of the key material under the same key ID, so existing objects keep decrypting normally. Only new encryptions use the current material.
rationales: Old key material is kept, so old ciphertext still decrypts.
Rotation does not touch existing encrypted data keys or data.
Object size has no bearing on rotation behavior.
Correct. Rotation is transparent; no re-encryption is needed.

questions.scenario: A payments processor must run a custom cryptographic application that calls an HSM directly through PKCS#11. Auditors require that the HSMs are single-tenant and that the company, not AWS, has exclusive control over the key material.
questions.stem: Which service should the architect use?
options: AWS KMS customer managed keys with a strict key policy
AWS CloudHSM clusters in the company's VPC
AWS KMS with imported key material
AWS Secrets Manager with a customer managed KMS key
questions.explanation: CloudHSM provides single-tenant HSMs that the customer controls exclusively and supports standard interfaces such as PKCS#11. KMS is a managed multi-tenant service accessed through its own API, even with imported material. Secrets Manager stores secrets but is not an HSM interface.
rationales: KMS keys are used through the KMS API, not PKCS#11, and the HSMs are AWS-managed.
Correct. CloudHSM meets the single-tenant, exclusive control and PKCS#11 requirements.
Importing material changes key origin but not the API or the tenancy model.
Secrets Manager does not provide HSM operations.

sources.title: What is AWS CloudHSM — CloudHSM docs

questions.scenario: A company runs 200 microservices on Amazon ECS behind internal ALBs with names such as orders.corp.internal. Security now requires TLS everywhere, including mutual TLS for some services, with certificates that renew automatically and no self-signed certificates.
questions.stem: Which solution meets the requirements?
options: Request ACM public certificates for the .corp.internal names using DNS validation
Generate certificates with OpenSSL in a build pipeline and import them into ACM every year
Create an AWS Private CA hierarchy and issue private certificates through ACM for the internal ALBs and services
Use AWS CloudHSM to generate a self-managed root and issue certificates with a script
questions.explanation: AWS Private CA issues certificates for private names and supports mTLS between workloads. Private certificates issued through ACM for integrated services such as ALB can be renewed automatically. Public certificates require publicly resolvable, validated domains.
rationales: ACM public certificates need domain validation of public names and cannot cover a private .internal zone.
Imported certificates are not renewed by ACM and this is effectively self-managed PKI.
Correct. Private CA plus ACM provides managed private certificates with renewal.
Building a CA with scripts on CloudHSM adds heavy operational work and no automatic renewal.

questions.scenario: A healthcare company stores genomic data that must remain confidential for 30 years. Its security team worries that encrypted traffic captured today could be decrypted by future quantum computers. Public APIs run on Application Load Balancers and Amazon API Gateway, all defined in AWS CloudFormation.
questions.stem: Which action should the architect prioritize first?
options: Replace the SYMMETRIC_DEFAULT KMS keys that protect data at rest with ML-KEM keys
Wait for the load balancers and API Gateway to adopt post-quantum TLS policies automatically

Set TLS 1.3 security policies that include post-quantum hybrid key exchange explicitly in the CloudFormation templates, restrict allowed policies with IAM condition keys, and verify the negotiated key exchange in CloudTrail tlsDetails
Downgrade to TLS 1.2 with the strongest cipher suites for broad compatibility
questions.explanation: The harvest-now-decrypt-later risk is to data in transit, and post-quantum key exchange requires TLS 1.3. AWS guidance is to set TLS policies explicitly in IaC because ELB and API Gateway policies do not upgrade on their own, then verify with CloudTrail tlsDetails. AES-256-GCM symmetric keys are already considered quantum resistant.
rationales: Symmetric AES-256-GCM keys are considered quantum resistant; ML-KEM is for key encapsulation, not bulk S3 encryption.
TLS policies do not upgrade on their own.
Correct. Explicit TLS 1.3 PQ policies in IaC address the in-transit risk.
Post-quantum key exchange needs TLS 1.3, so TLS 1.2 moves in the wrong direction.

sources.title: What is AWS Certificate Manager — ACM docs

questions.scenario: A software vendor signs firmware images that will stay in the field for 20 years. It wants signatures that remain secure against future quantum attacks and wants the private key to never leave AWS KMS.
questions.stem: Which KMS key should the vendor create?
options: A symmetric KMS key with automatic rotation enabled
An asymmetric KMS key with an ML-KEM key spec, used with Encapsulate and Decapsulate
An HMAC KMS key used with GenerateMac
An asymmetric KMS key with an ML-DSA key spec, used with the Sign and Verify operations
questions.explanation: ML-DSA (FIPS 204) is the post-quantum digital signature algorithm offered in KMS for signing and verification. ML-KEM (FIPS 203) is for key encapsulation, not signatures. HMAC and symmetric keys do not produce publicly verifiable signatures.
rationales: Symmetric keys cannot produce public-key signatures.
ML-KEM establishes shared secrets; it does not sign.
An HMAC requires the verifier to hold the secret key, which is unsuitable for field devices.
Correct. ML-DSA provides post-quantum signatures with the private key held in KMS.

questions.scenario: A company with 250 accounts must capture API activity from every current and future account in one immutable location. Account administrators in member accounts must not be able to stop or delete the logging.
questions.stem: Which solution meets these requirements with the least operational overhead?
options: Use CloudFormation StackSets to deploy a trail in each account that writes to a central bucket
Create an organization trail from the management account or a delegated administrator that delivers to an S3 bucket in a dedicated log archive account with S3 Object Lock
Create an AWS Config aggregator for the organization
Configure CloudWatch Logs cross-account subscriptions from each account to the security account
questions.explanation: An organization trail automatically covers every member account, including new ones, and member accounts cannot modify or delete it. Delivering to a locked bucket in a separate log archive account protects the logs. Per-account trails could be stopped by local administrators unless additional controls are added.
rationales: Per-account trails add drift and can be stopped by account admins without extra SCPs.
Correct. An org trail into a protected log archive account is the standard pattern.
Config records resource configuration, not every API call.
Log subscriptions need setup per account and do not capture CloudTrail by themselves.

questions.scenario: A security team must enable Amazon GuardDuty threat detection for all 120 existing accounts in the organization and for every new account created in the future, in each of the four Regions the company uses. They do not want to run security tools from the management account.
questions.stem: Which approach should they take?
options: Ask each account owner to enable GuardDuty and verify with a Config rule
Enable GuardDuty in the management account in one Region; it covers the organization globally
Designate a security tooling account as GuardDuty delegated administrator and enable auto-enable for organization members in each of the four Regions
Use StackSets to enable GuardDuty once and invite new accounts manually each month
questions.explanation: GuardDuty supports a delegated administrator, so the management account stays out of day-to-day security work. Auto-enable turns GuardDuty on for new members automatically. GuardDuty is Regional, so this setup is repeated in each Region in use.
rationales: Relying on account owners is unreliable and only detects gaps.
GuardDuty is Regional and the management account should not host security tooling.
Correct. Delegated admin plus auto-enable in every Region covers current and future accounts.
Manual invitations do not scale and leave new accounts unprotected for a while.

questions.scenario: A financial firm wants one place to store security logs from 70 accounts: CloudTrail management and data events, VPC Flow Logs, Route 53 resolver query logs and Security Hub CSPM findings. Data must be normalized to an open schema, stored in the firm's own S3 buckets, consolidated in an EU rollup Region, and queried by a third-party SIEM.
questions.stem: Which service meets these requirements?
options: AWS Security Hub CSPM with cross-Region aggregation
Amazon CloudWatch Logs with cross-account subscriptions to a central account
Amazon Security Lake with a rollup Region and a query-access subscriber for the SIEM
Amazon GuardDuty with a delegated administrator
questions.explanation: Security Lake collects these log sources and findings into the customer's own S3 as OCSF in Parquet. Rollup Regions consolidate data in a chosen Region, which helps with residency, and subscribers get data or query access for tools such as a SIEM. Security Hub CSPM handles findings and posture, not raw logs.
rationales: Security Hub CSPM aggregates findings, not raw CloudTrail, Flow Log or DNS data.
CloudWatch Logs does not normalize to OCSF and would need custom work for each source.
Correct. Security Lake normalizes to OCSF in your S3 with rollup Regions and subscribers.
GuardDuty analyzes logs for threats; it does not provide a queryable security data lake.

sources.title: What is Security Lake — Security Lake docs

questions.scenario: A CISO wants two capabilities across the organization: continuous checks of every account against the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices and CIS benchmarks, and a single prioritized view that correlates GuardDuty threats, Inspector vulnerabilities and posture findings to show which exposures matter most.
questions.stem: Which combination of services provides these capabilities?
options: AWS Trusted Advisor for standards checks, and AWS Artifact for prioritization
Amazon Inspector for standards checks, and Amazon Detective for prioritization
AWS Config conformance packs for prioritization, and Amazon Security Lake for standards checks
Security Hub CSPM for standards-based posture checks, and the new AWS Security Hub for correlation and risk prioritization
questions.explanation: Security Hub CSPM is the posture and standards service that runs controls such as the Foundational Security Best Practices. The new Security Hub, generally available since December 2025, correlates GuardDuty, Inspector, Security Hub CSPM and Macie signals into risk prioritization. Neither Inspector nor Artifact does posture standards checks.
rationales: Artifact provides AWS compliance reports, not risk prioritization.
Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities, not account posture standards.
Security Lake stores data; it does not run standards checks.
Correct. CSPM for standards, the new Security Hub for correlation and prioritization.

questions.scenario: A network team owns a Transit Gateway and a shared services VPC in a central networking account. Forty application accounts in two OUs need to attach their VPCs to the Transit Gateway, and some small teams should deploy into subnets owned by the networking account rather than run their own VPCs.
questions.stem: Which approach meets these needs?
options: Create a Transit Gateway in each application account and peer them
Use AWS RAM to share the Transit Gateway with the two OUs, and share selected subnets through RAM for VPC sharing
Use VPC peering from each application VPC to the shared services VPC
Create cross-account IAM roles that let application accounts create attachments in the networking account
questions.explanation: AWS RAM shares a Transit Gateway with accounts or OUs so their VPCs can attach to it, and it shares subnets so participant accounts can launch resources into a centrally owned VPC. Sharing with OUs means new accounts in those OUs get access automatically. This avoids duplicated Transit Gateways and peering meshes.
rationales: Many Transit Gateways with peering add cost and routing complexity.
Correct. RAM is the mechanism for sharing TGWs and subnets across the organization.
Peering is non-transitive and does not scale to 40 VPCs with central routing.
Attachments are created in the VPC owner's account after the TGW is shared; roles are not the sharing mechanism.

questions.scenario: An operations team must continuously find software vulnerabilities on EC2 instances, container images in Amazon ECR and Lambda functions across all accounts, and must patch EC2 instances automatically on a schedule using approved baselines.
questions.stem: Which actions meet these requirements? (Select two.)
options: Enable Amazon Inspector for the organization through a delegated administrator
Use AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager with patch baselines and maintenance windows or patch policies across the accounts
Enable Amazon Macie in every account
Enable GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring to install missing patches
Deploy AWS Config conformance packs that install missing operating system patches on EC2 instances
questions.explanation: Inspector continuously scans EC2, ECR images and Lambda functions for vulnerabilities and supports a delegated administrator. Patch Manager applies approved patch baselines on a schedule across accounts and Regions. Macie discovers sensitive data and GuardDuty detects threats; neither patches.
rationales: Correct. Inspector covers EC2, ECR and Lambda vulnerability scanning organization-wide.
Correct. Patch Manager automates patching with baselines and schedules.
Macie finds sensitive data in S3, not software vulnerabilities.
GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring detects threats; it does not install patches.
Config rules and conformance packs evaluate configuration; they do not scan for software vulnerabilities or install patches.

questions.scenario: A company creates around 15 new AWS accounts per month. Every new account must start with centralized logging, baseline preventive and detective controls, and IAM Identity Center access, without manual steps by the cloud team.
questions.stem: Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Call the Organizations CreateAccount API from a script, then run a checklist manually
Create accounts manually in the console and attach AdministratorAccess for the requester
Use AWS Control Tower Account Factory to vend accounts into enrolled OUs that have the required controls enabled
Create accounts with Organizations and rely on a Config aggregator to report what is missing
questions.explanation: Control Tower Account Factory creates accounts that are enrolled in the landing zone, with centralized logging, Identity Center access and the controls of the target OU. Preventive, detective and proactive controls apply automatically to accounts in governed OUs. Scripts and detective-only approaches leave gaps.
rationales: A manual checklist is error-prone and slow at 15 accounts a month.
This skips the required baseline and over-grants permissions.
Correct. Account Factory vends governed accounts with baselines applied.
An aggregator only reports gaps; it does not set up the baseline.

questions.scenario: An auditor asks a bank to produce, for every Amazon Bedrock call in its claims assistant, the full prompt, the full model response, the calling IAM principal and the token counts. The application runs in one account in eu-west-1. The bank currently has CloudTrail enabled with management events only.
questions.stem: What should the architect do?
options: Do nothing; Bedrock logs invocations to CloudWatch Logs by default
Enable CloudTrail data events for Bedrock; they include the prompt and response bodies
Configure model invocation logging to deliver directly to an S3 bucket in the central security account in us-east-1
Enable Bedrock model invocation logging in eu-west-1 with an S3 bucket (and optionally CloudWatch Logs) in the same account and Region
questions.explanation: Model invocation logging captures full request and response data with metadata such as identity.arn and token counts. It is disabled by default and delivers to CloudWatch Logs and/or S3 in the same account and Region. CloudTrail records API activity but not the prompt and response bodies.
rationales: Invocation logging is disabled by default.
CloudTrail records that the call happened, not the full prompt and response.
Destinations must be in the same account and Region; centralize afterwards.
Correct. Invocation logging in the same account and Region captures what the auditor asked for.

questions.scenario: A hospital group wants to run patient-facing workloads on AWS and must sign a HIPAA Business Associate Addendum with AWS. Its external auditor also wants AWS's current SOC 2 report.
questions.stem: Where can the compliance team obtain both?
options: AWS Config conformance packs
AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS Security Hub CSPM
AWS Artifact
questions.explanation: AWS Artifact is the self-service portal for AWS compliance reports, such as SOC reports, and for agreements such as the HIPAA BAA. The other services assess your own resources rather than providing AWS attestations or agreements.
rationales: Conformance packs evaluate your resources against rules; they do not provide AWS reports or agreements.
Trusted Advisor gives best-practice recommendations, not audit reports or agreements.
Security Hub CSPM checks your accounts against standards; it does not provide AWS attestations.
Correct. Artifact provides both reports and agreements.

questions.scenario: An architecture team is designing a new agentic customer-service application that can issue refunds and read customer records. The CISO wants security considered before any code is written and wants the analysis kept current as the design changes.
questions.stem: Which practice best addresses this?
options: Run a penetration test after the application reaches production

Build a threat model during design: map assets, data flows and trust boundaries, enumerate threats such as prompt injection and over-privileged tools, prioritize mitigations, and revisit it when the design changes
Enable GuardDuty and rely on its findings to discover design weaknesses
Download the AWS SOC 2 report from AWS Artifact to cover the application's risks
questions.explanation: Threat modeling identifies threats and prioritizes mitigations early, when changes are cheap, and should be updated as the design evolves; the Well-Architected security pillar recommends it. For agentic AI this includes prompt injection, data leakage and over-privileged tools. Penetration tests and GuardDuty come later and find different things.
rationales: A test after production is too late to shape the design.
Correct. An iterative threat model during design is the recommended practice.
GuardDuty detects threats in running environments, not design flaws.
AWS reports cover AWS's side of the shared responsibility model, not this application.

questions.scenario: A company with 60 accounts uses Amazon Bedrock in two Regions. The responsible AI board requires that every model call in every account is checked by the same approved guardrail, regardless of what developers pass in requests. Developers may add stricter guardrails of their own.
questions.stem: Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Create the guardrail once in us-east-1 and enforce it with account-level configuration in every account
Attach an RCP that denies bedrock:InvokeModel unless a guardrail identifier is present
Publish the guardrail ID on the internal wiki and ask developers to include it in every request

Create the guardrail with a numbered version and a resource policy granting bedrock:ApplyGuardrail in the management account in each Region, and attach an AWS Organizations Amazon Bedrock policy that enforces it
questions.explanation: An Organizations Amazon Bedrock policy enforces a versioned guardrail from the management account across member accounts, and the guardrail needs a resource policy granting bedrock:ApplyGuardrail. Guardrails are Regional, so one is needed in each Region. Org, account and request guardrails combine, so developers' stricter guardrails still apply.
rationales: Guardrails are Regional, so a us-east-1 guardrail does not cover the second Region.
Bedrock is not supported by RCPs.
Voluntary inclusion does not guarantee enforcement.
Correct. Organization-level enforcement with a versioned, shared guardrail in each Region.

questions.scenario: A legal research assistant built on Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases sometimes gives answers that are not supported by the retrieved documents. Users have also tried to make it ignore its instructions by pasting "ignore previous instructions" text.
questions.stem: Which Amazon Bedrock Guardrails features address these two problems? (Select two.)
options: Contextual grounding checks
The Prompt Attack content filter
Word filters with a list of legal terms
Sensitive information filters with masking
A denied topic that blocks all questions about legal advice
questions.explanation: Contextual grounding checks flag responses that are not grounded in the source content or not relevant to the query, which targets RAG hallucinations. The Prompt Attack filter detects jailbreak and prompt injection attempts. Word filters and PII masking solve different problems.
rationales: Correct. Grounding checks catch answers that the retrieved documents do not support.
Correct. Prompt Attack targets jailbreaks and prompt injection.
Blocking legal terms would break the app and does not detect ungrounded answers.
PII masking protects sensitive data, not grounding or injection.
Denying legal topics would block the assistant's core purpose and does not detect ungrounded answers or injection attempts.

questions.scenario: A company hosts a fine-tuned open-weight model on an Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint and also calls a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock. It wants the same content and PII policies applied to the inputs and outputs of both models.
questions.stem: What is the most efficient way to apply one policy set to both?
options: Rebuild the SageMaker AI model as a Bedrock agent
Write regex filters in each application and keep them in sync manually
Create one Bedrock guardrail and call the ApplyGuardrail API on the SageMaker AI inputs and outputs, while attaching the same guardrail to Bedrock calls
Use AWS WAF rules on the SageMaker AI endpoint to filter PII
questions.explanation: ApplyGuardrail evaluates text against a guardrail without invoking a Bedrock model, so the same guardrail can screen content for models hosted elsewhere. Attaching that guardrail to Bedrock calls keeps one policy set for both paths.
rationales: Re-platforming the model is unnecessary to apply content policies.
Hand-maintained filters drift and lack features such as prompt attack detection.
Correct. ApplyGuardrail lets one guardrail cover models outside Bedrock.
WAF inspects HTTP requests; it does not filter model responses for PII or harmful content.

questions.scenario: An AI agent built with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore must read and update each signed-in employee's calendar and CRM records in third-party SaaS tools. Employees authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID. Security forbids shared service-account credentials and requires that every tool call is attributable to the user it was made for.
questions.stem: Which design meets these requirements?
options: Store a shared SaaS API key in the agent's environment variables and log the user name in application logs
Give the agent an IAM role with AdministratorAccess and rely on CloudTrail for attribution
Create an IAM user per employee and give the agent their access keys
Use AgentCore Identity with an inbound JWT authorizer for Entra ID tokens and outbound OAuth credential providers so the agent calls the SaaS APIs on behalf of each user
questions.explanation: AgentCore Identity validates inbound JWTs from any IdP, including Entra ID, and uses outbound credential providers such as OAuth so the agent acts on behalf of the specific user. This removes shared credentials and keeps an audit trail per user. IAM roles and users do not grant access to third-party SaaS APIs.
rationales: A shared key cannot enforce per-user permissions and violates the policy.
AWS permissions do not apply to SaaS tools, and AdministratorAccess breaks least privilege.
IAM users are long-term credentials and do not authenticate to third-party SaaS.
Correct. Inbound JWT plus outbound OAuth delegation gives per-user access and attribution.

questions.scenario: A fintech company uses an AI agent to propose customer refunds. Refunds above a limit must wait for a human approver, who may take up to three days to respond. The rest of the process is orchestrated with AWS Step Functions.
questions.stem: How should the architect implement the approval step?
options: Use an Express workflow with a Wait state that polls a DynamoDB table for the approval
Use a Standard workflow with a task that uses the .waitForTaskToken pattern to send the token to the approver; the approval app calls SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure
Use an Express workflow with the .waitForTaskToken pattern to minimize cost
Let the agent issue the refund and send the approver a notification to reverse it if needed
questions.explanation: The callback pattern pauses a Standard workflow until the approval app returns the task token with SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure. Standard workflows can run for up to one year, which easily covers a three-day wait. Express workflows last at most 5 minutes and do not support .waitForTaskToken.
rationales: Express workflows cannot run for three days.
Correct. Standard plus the task token callback is the human approval pattern.
Express workflows do not support .waitForTaskToken.
Acting before approval defeats the control.

questions.scenario: A security architect is hardening the logging foundation of a 100-account organization. An organization CloudTrail trail already exists. A recent review found that an administrator in a member account could, in theory, tamper with security tooling or the logs themselves.
questions.stem: Which measures protect the logging foundation from tampering by member account administrators? (Select two.)
options: Attach an SCP to the workload OUs that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging, cloudtrail:DeleteTrail and disabling GuardDuty
Deliver the organization trail to an S3 bucket in a dedicated log archive account with S3 Object Lock in compliance mode
Attach an IAM policy in each member account that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging to the account's administrators
Attach a permissions boundary to the management account's root user
Enable S3 Versioning, without Object Lock, on a log bucket in each member account
questions.explanation: An SCP is a preventive guardrail that member account administrators cannot remove, so it stops them from disabling security services. Storing logs in a separate log archive account with Object Lock in compliance mode means nobody can delete or shorten retention on the stored logs. IAM policies inside member accounts can be changed by those same administrators.
rationales: Correct. SCPs cap every principal in the member accounts, including administrators.
Correct. A separate account and compliance-mode Object Lock make the logs immutable.
Local administrators could edit or detach a policy in their own account.
Permissions boundaries cannot be attached to the root user, and the management account is not where the risk lies.
Administrators of the account that owns a bucket can still permanently delete object versions, and per-account buckets are not a central, protected store.

questions.scenario: A team is writing a key management standard for AWS KMS and wants to state only behaviors that KMS actually supports.
questions.stem: Which statements are correct? (Select two.)
options: Symmetric keys with KMS-generated material support automatic rotation with a custom rotation period
For a multi-Region key, rotation is configured on the primary key
Asymmetric keys support automatic rotation every 365 days
The rotation period of AWS managed keys can be shortened to 90 days
Automatic rotation re-encrypts existing ciphertext with the new key material
questions.explanation: Automatic rotation applies to symmetric keys with KMS-generated material, with a default of 365 days and a configurable RotationPeriodInDays. Multi-Region keys are rotated by configuring rotation on the primary key. Asymmetric keys rotate only manually, and AWS managed keys rotate yearly with no option to change the period.
rationales: Correct. Custom rotation periods are supported for these keys.
Correct. Rotation for multi-Region keys is set on the primary.
Asymmetric keys must be rotated manually with a new key and an alias change.
AWS managed key rotation cannot be changed.
Rotation does not re-encrypt data; KMS keeps earlier key material so existing ciphertext still decrypts.

questions.scenario: A company runs a steady baseline of EC2 instances that it expects to move from x86 to Graviton families over the next year. It also runs ECS tasks on Fargate and a growing set of Lambda functions. Finance wants a single commitment that keeps applying through these changes.
questions.stem: Which purchase option best meets the requirement?
options: Standard Reserved Instances for the current instance types
Spot Instances for the baseline with On-Demand as fallback
EC2 Instance Savings Plans for the current instance families
Compute Savings Plans sized to the steady combined baseline
questions.explanation: Compute Savings Plans apply across instance families, sizes, OS and Regions, and also cover Fargate and Lambda. The other commitments are tied to a family or configuration and would not follow the Graviton move or cover serverless compute.
rationales: Tied to specific instance attributes and does not cover Fargate or Lambda.
Spot is interruptible and is not a commitment for a steady baseline.
Locked to one instance family per Region and does not cover Fargate or Lambda.
Correct. Covers EC2, Fargate and Lambda and stays applicable when families change.

questions.scenario: An enterprise runs a mix of RDS for PostgreSQL, provisioned Aurora clusters and DynamoDB tables. Over the next 12 months it plans to move several RDS databases to Aurora Serverless v2 and to shift some workloads to another Region. It wants a discount on database spend without stranding commitments.
questions.stem: Which approach is most cost-effective?
options: Stay On-Demand until the migrations finish, then buy Aurora Reserved Instances
Purchase 3-year RDS Reserved Instances for the current RDS instances
Purchase a 1-year Database Savings Plan sized to the steady database spend
Purchase Compute Savings Plans, which also apply to managed databases

rationales: Forgoes a year of discount, and Reserved Instances do not apply to Aurora Serverless capacity.
RIs are tied to engine, Region and instance class, so they would be stranded by the migration.

Compute Savings Plans cover EC2, Fargate and Lambda, not managed databases.

questions.scenario: A platform team wants to cut its AWS bill. Cost Explorer recommends a large Compute Savings Plan. Compute Optimizer shows that about 40% of instances are over-provisioned, and several Auto Scaling groups keep a fixed minimum sized for daytime peaks around the clock.
questions.stem: What should the team do first?
options: Buy the recommended Savings Plan immediately to lock in the discount
Apply the rightsizing findings and scheduled or target tracking scaling, then size the Savings Plan to the new baseline
Move all instances to Spot to avoid any commitment
Buy 3-year Convertible Reserved Instances so they can be exchanged after rightsizing
questions.explanation: A commitment based on today's over-provisioned usage would lock in waste for the whole term. Rightsizing and better scaling first lowers the steady baseline, and the commitment then covers only real demand.
rationales: Commits to spend that rightsizing would remove.
Correct. Remove waste first, then commit to the real baseline.
Not every workload tolerates interruption, and this ignores the rightsizing finding.
Still commits based on over-provisioned usage, for a longer term.

questions.scenario: A media company processes millions of short device events per hour with a workflow that validates, enriches and stores each event. Each run finishes in under 10 seconds and every step is idempotent. The workflow currently runs on Step Functions Standard and its cost is dominated by state transitions.
questions.stem: Which change reduces cost the most?
options: Change the existing workflow type from Standard to Express in place
Add a Wait state to batch events inside each Standard execution
Move the workflow to Standard with Distributed Map
Recreate the workflow as a Step Functions Express workflow
questions.explanation: Express workflows are billed by executions, duration and memory rather than per state transition, which suits high-volume, short, idempotent work. The workflow type cannot be changed after creation, so a new Express state machine is needed.
rationales: The workflow type cannot be changed after creation.
Adds transitions and duration without changing the billing model.
Distributed Map runs large parallel dataset processing from a Standard parent; it does not fit a continuous stream of independent short events, and the parent still bills per state transition.
Correct. Express pricing fits short, high-volume, idempotent processing.

questions.scenario: An analytics team runs nightly ECS jobs on Fargate that process files from S3. Each job checkpoints progress to S3 and can restart safely. Jobs must finish by morning, but individual task interruptions are acceptable.
questions.stem: Which configuration lowers cost while keeping the jobs reliable?
options: Buy a Compute Savings Plan sized to the nightly peak
Move the jobs to Step Functions Standard with Wait states
Run all tasks on Fargate Spot only
Use a capacity provider strategy with a small base on Fargate and the remaining weight on Fargate Spot
questions.explanation: Fargate Spot is much cheaper and gives a two-minute warning before stopping a task, which checkpointed jobs can handle. A base on regular Fargate keeps a minimum running if Spot capacity is reclaimed, so the jobs still finish.
rationales: A commitment sized to a short nightly peak would be idle most of the day.
Does not change the compute cost of the processing tasks.
Cheapest, but if Spot capacity is unavailable no tasks run and the deadline is at risk.
Correct. Spot savings with a guaranteed base for progress.

questions.scenario: A company must summarize several million archived support tickets with a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock. Results are needed within a few days. There is no user waiting on any individual response.
questions.stem: Which approach is most cost-effective?
options: Enable prompt caching and run the batch inference job with cached prefixes
Call the on-demand API in a loop with the Priority service tier
Purchase 6-month Provisioned Throughput for the model
Submit a Bedrock batch inference job with input and output in Amazon S3
questions.explanation: Batch inference reads prompts from S3, writes results to S3, and is about 50% cheaper than on-demand for supported models. It fits large offline workloads with no real-time need.
rationales: Prompt caching does not apply to batch inference.
Priority is a premium tier for latency-critical traffic, the opposite of this need.
A multi-month commitment for a one-off job is wasteful.
Correct. Offline, high-volume work at a batch discount.

questions.scenario: A customer-support assistant on Amazon Bedrock sends the same 20,000-token policy document and system instructions with every user turn. Traffic is steady through the business day, and the input token bill is far larger than the output bill.
questions.stem: Which change most directly reduces cost?
options: Move the workload to batch inference
Switch to a global cross-Region inference profile only
Increase the model's maximum output tokens to reduce the number of turns
Enable prompt caching on the repeated prefix
questions.explanation: Prompt caching stores a long, repeated prefix so later requests read it at a lower cache-read rate instead of paying full input price. The cache TTL resets on each hit, which suits steady traffic.
rationales: Interactive chat needs real-time responses.
Gives a modest discount but leaves the repeated input tokens at full rate.
Raises output cost and does not reduce repeated input.
Correct. Targets the repeated input tokens that dominate the bill.

questions.scenario: A bank in the EU runs a generative AI application on Amazon Bedrock. Regulators require that inference processing stays within the EU. The team wants to reduce cost and handle traffic bursts beyond a single Region's capacity.
questions.stem: Which design meets both requirements?
options: Use Provisioned Throughput through a global inference profile
Replicate the application into a US Region and route bursts there
Use a global cross-Region inference profile because it is cheaper
Use the EU geographic cross-Region inference profile and allow the EU destination Regions in SCPs
questions.explanation: A geographic profile keeps processing inside that geography and spreads load across its Regions with no extra routing charge. The SCPs must allow those destination Regions. A global profile is roughly 10% cheaper but can route to any commercial Region, which breaks the residency rule.
rationales: Provisioned Throughput is not supported through inference profiles, and global breaks residency.
Processes data outside the EU.
Can route outside the EU.
Correct. Residency and burst handling with no routing charge.

questions.scenario: EC2 instances in private subnets read and write several hundred terabytes per month to Amazon S3 buckets in the same Region. All traffic currently flows through NAT gateways, and NAT data processing is now the largest network charge.
questions.stem: Which change reduces the cost most?
options: Add an S3 interface endpoint in each AZ
Add an S3 gateway endpoint and associate it with the private subnets' route tables
Replace the NAT gateways with NAT instances
Route S3 traffic through a Transit Gateway to a central egress VPC
questions.explanation: Gateway endpoints for S3 have no charge and send S3 traffic through route table prefix lists instead of the NAT gateway. That removes the per-GB NAT processing charge for this traffic.
rationales: Works, but interface endpoints charge hourly and per GB, while a gateway endpoint is free.
Correct. Free and removes NAT processing for S3 traffic.
Avoids the per-GB NAT gateway charge but adds instance cost, throughput limits and operational burden; a free gateway endpoint takes S3 traffic off the NAT path entirely.
Adds Transit Gateway processing on top of NAT processing.

questions.scenario: A workload runs in three AZs. All private subnets route internet-bound and AWS service traffic to a single NAT gateway in AZ A. Most of that traffic goes to DynamoDB in the same Region. Cost reports show high NAT processing and inter-AZ data transfer charges.
questions.stem: Which two changes reduce these charges? (Select two.)
options: Move all instances into AZ A to remove cross-AZ traffic
Create a DynamoDB gateway endpoint and add it to the private route tables
Deploy a NAT gateway in each AZ and point each subnet's route table to the NAT in its own AZ
Replace the NAT gateway with a Transit Gateway attachment to a central egress VPC
Move the NAT gateway to a larger instance size to lower the per-GB processing charge
questions.explanation: A DynamoDB gateway endpoint is free and takes DynamoDB traffic off the NAT gateway. A NAT gateway per AZ with AZ-local routes removes cross-AZ transfer for the remaining egress and removes the single-AZ dependency.
rationales: Removes high availability; cost should not override the resilience design.
Correct. Free endpoint removes NAT processing for DynamoDB traffic.
Correct. AZ-local NAT avoids inter-AZ transfer.
Adds Transit Gateway processing charges and still pays NAT processing centrally.
NAT gateways have no instance sizes to choose; data processing is charged per GB regardless, so this changes nothing.

questions.scenario: A video platform serves a large on-demand catalog to viewers worldwide through CloudFront. The origin is an on-premises cluster with limited internet bandwidth. Many edge locations miss cache at the same time when new titles are released, overloading the origin.
questions.stem: Which change best reduces origin load and egress?
options: Add Lambda@Edge to rewrite every request to the origin
Replace CloudFront with Global Accelerator
Enable CloudFront Origin Shield in the AWS Region closest to the origin
Lower the cache TTLs so content refreshes more often
questions.explanation: Origin Shield adds a central caching layer that collapses duplicate requests from many edge locations into one origin fetch and raises the cache hit ratio. Placing it in the Region with the lowest latency to the origin is the recommended setup.
rationales: Adds cost and does not reduce origin fetches.
Global Accelerator does not cache; every request still reaches the origin.
Correct. Fewer, collapsed requests reach the constrained origin.
Lower TTLs increase origin fetches.

questions.scenario: A company connects 40 VPCs with a Transit Gateway. Two of them, an analytics VPC and a data-lake VPC in the same Region, exchange tens of terabytes per month. All other VPC traffic is light. Transit Gateway data processing charges have become significant.
questions.stem: Which change reduces cost with the least disruption?
options: Add a VPC peering connection between the two high-volume VPCs and route their traffic over it, keeping the Transit Gateway for everything else
Expose the data-lake VPC through PrivateLink to all 40 VPCs
Move both VPCs to a second Transit Gateway
Replace the Transit Gateway with a full mesh of VPC peering connections
questions.explanation: Transit Gateway charges per GB processed, while VPC peering has no processing charge. Peering only the high-volume pair and pointing their route table entries at the peering connection removes most of the processing cost and keeps the hub for the rest.
rationales: Correct. Targets the expensive flow only.
PrivateLink has its own hourly and per-GB charges and changes the access model for every VPC.
A second Transit Gateway still charges per GB processed.
A 40-VPC mesh is hard to operate and unnecessary for light traffic.

questions.scenario: Several teams share an Amazon EKS cluster on EC2 nodes. Finance wants each team charged for the CPU and memory its pods actually use, by Kubernetes namespace, in the Cost and Usage Report.
questions.stem: Which solution meets the requirement with the least custom work?
options: Tag each EC2 node with the team that runs the most pods on it
Enable split cost allocation data for EKS and report on the namespace tags in CUR
Divide the cluster bill evenly across teams with a Cost Category
Run one node group per team and tag the node groups
questions.explanation: Split cost allocation data splits the amortized instance cost by each pod's CPU and memory share and adds tags such as aws:eks:namespace to CUR. That gives usage-based chargeback without changing the cluster layout.
rationales: Nodes run pods from many teams, so node tags misattribute cost.
Correct. Usage-based per-pod cost by namespace in CUR.
An even split ignores real usage.
Works but reduces bin-packing efficiency and adds cost and operational overhead.

questions.scenario: A company with AWS Organizations wants every resource to carry a CostCenter tag from an approved list, and wants costs grouped by CostCenter in Cost Explorer for chargeback.
questions.stem: Which two actions are required? (Select two.)
options: Enable Cost Anomaly Detection for each member account
Create a tag policy that defines the CostCenter key and allowed values, with enforcement for the relevant resource types
Activate CostCenter as a user-defined cost allocation tag in the management account's Billing console
Create an SCP that automatically adds a default CostCenter tag to new resources
Switch Cost Explorer to hourly granularity for all member accounts
questions.explanation: Tag policies standardize the key and allowed values and can block non-compliant tagging for enforced resource types. A user-defined tag only appears in Cost Explorer after it is activated as a cost allocation tag in the management account. Tag policy enforcement blocks non-compliant values but does not by itself require the tag to be present; pair it with an SCP that denies creation without the tag (aws:RequestTag/aws:TagKeys) or Config detection if presence must be guaranteed.
rationales: Detects spend spikes but does not enforce tags or group costs.
Correct. Standardizes and enforces the CostCenter values.
Correct. Required for the tag to appear in billing tools.
SCPs can only deny actions; they never add tags.
Hourly granularity changes how finely data is shown; it neither standardizes CostCenter values nor groups costs by the tag.

questions.scenario: Several product teams call Amazon Bedrock through a shared service in one account. Finance needs monthly token usage per team so it can charge back the cost.
questions.stem: Which approach meets the requirement?
options: Enable model invocation logging, have the service pass the team identifier in requestMetadata, and aggregate token counts with CloudWatch Logs Insights
Filter Cost Explorer by the Amazon Bedrock service
Create an AWS Budget per team with Bedrock as the service filter
Use CloudTrail management events to count InvokeModel calls per team
questions.explanation: Model invocation logging records token counts with the caller identity and any requestMetadata tags. Aggregating those logs by team identifier gives per-team usage for chargeback. Invocation logging is disabled by default, so it must be turned on.
rationales: Correct. Token counts tagged by team.
Shows total Bedrock spend for the account, not per team.
