Correct: delegated administrator plus OU targeting with automatic deployment covers new accounts automatically.
Custom loop code repeats what StackSets already does and must be maintained.
Decentralized manual deployment is error-prone and cannot be enforced.

questions.scenario: Application teams deploy infrastructure with a mix of the AWS CDK, raw CloudFormation templates and Terraform that calls the Cloud Control API. Security requires that no S3 bucket or EBS volume is provisioned without encryption. Non-compliant deployments must be stopped before any resource is created, whatever tool a team uses.
questions.stem: Which control BEST meets this requirement?
options: A CDK aspect in the shared construct library that fails synthesis for unencrypted buckets and volumes
AWS Config managed rules for S3 and EBS encryption with automatic remediation
A peer review checklist enforced on pull requests
A CloudFormation Hook in fail mode that evaluates S3 bucket and EBS volume resources before provisioning, including Cloud Control API operations
questions.explanation: CloudFormation Hooks are enforced by the service before provisioning. They cover CloudFormation stacks (including those synthesized by the CDK) and Cloud Control API operations, and in fail mode they stop non-compliant changes. CDK aspects only run in CDK apps that include them, and Config rules detect problems after the resource exists.
rationales: Aspects only run in CDK apps that use the library; raw templates and Cloud Control API calls skip them.
Config rules are detective and run after the resource is created.
Manual review cannot reliably enforce a security requirement.
Correct: an enforced pre-provisioning gate covering CloudFormation and Cloud Control API.

questions.scenario: An application in account A must read database credentials stored in AWS Secrets Manager in account B. The credentials must rotate every 30 days with no application downtime. The secret is currently encrypted with the AWS managed key aws/secretsmanager.
questions.stem: What should the solutions architect do?
options: Re-encrypt the secret with a customer managed KMS key whose key policy allows account A's role, add a resource-based policy on the secret allowing that role, and enable rotation
Add a resource-based policy on the secret that allows account A's role and keep the AWS managed key
Copy the secret into a Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString in account A and rotate it with a cron job
Store the credentials in an encrypted environment variable on the application in account A
questions.explanation: Cross-account access to a secret needs a resource-based policy on the secret and a customer managed KMS key that the other account can use, because AWS managed keys cannot be used from another account. Secrets Manager rotation then keeps the credentials current. Copying the secret or putting it in environment variables loses central rotation.
rationales: Correct: a customer managed key, a resource policy and native rotation.
The AWS managed key cannot be used from account A, so decryption fails.
Parameter Store has no native rotation, and copies drift from the source.
Environment variables need redeployment for every rotation and spread the secret around.

sources.title: Cross-account secret access — Secrets Manager docs

questions.scenario: A team's CloudFormation template creates an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL instance. Today, the master password is a template parameter with NoEcho set and a default value committed to the Git repository. Auditors want the password removed from source control and rotated automatically.
questions.stem: Which options would each, on its own, meet these requirements? (Select two.)
options: Set ManageMasterUserPassword so RDS creates and rotates the master password in AWS Secrets Manager
Keep NoEcho but move the default value into a separate parameters file in the same repository
Reference a Secrets Manager secret through a CloudFormation dynamic reference and configure rotation on that secret
Store the password as a plain String parameter in Parameter Store and reference it from the template
Encrypt the template file in the Git repository with a customer managed KMS key
questions.explanation: Both RDS-managed master passwords and Secrets Manager dynamic references keep the value out of the template and source control, and both support rotation. NoEcho only masks output, so a committed parameters file still exposes the secret. A plain String parameter is not encrypted and does not rotate.
rationales: Correct: RDS manages and rotates the password in Secrets Manager.
The secret is still in source control; NoEcho only hides console and API output.
Correct: the value is resolved at deploy time from a secret that can rotate.
Plain String parameters are not encrypted and have no rotation.
The password is still stored in source control, just encrypted, and nothing rotates it.

sources.title: Cross-account secret access — Secrets Manager docs

questions.scenario: During a routine CloudFormation update, a developer changed a property on a production Amazon Aurora cluster that requires replacement. The cluster was replaced and data was lost. Leadership wants to stop this from happening again while still allowing normal in-place updates to the stack.
questions.stem: Which combination of controls should the solutions architect implement?
options: Enable termination protection on the stack and run drift detection weekly
Move the cluster to a separate account and deploy it manually from the console
Apply a stack policy that denies Update:Replace and Update:Delete on the cluster's logical ID, set UpdateReplacePolicy and DeletionPolicy to Snapshot, and require change set review before execution
Use a CDK aspect that adds Retain to all resources in the application
questions.explanation: A stack policy blocks replacement or deletion of the protected resource during updates while other updates continue. Snapshot policies keep a recovery copy if replacement is ever allowed, and change sets show replacements before they happen. Termination protection only stops deleting the whole stack, and drift detection does not prevent anything.
rationales: Termination protection does not cover resource replacement during updates, and drift detection is not preventive.
Manual console management gives up IaC and adds drift risk.
Correct: targeted update protection, data-preserving policies, and change previews.
Retain stops deletion of the old resource but does not stop the update from replacing it with an empty cluster.

questions.scenario: A platform team publishes an internal CDK construct library used by 40 teams. They want developers to see, on their laptops and before any deployment, that S3 buckets are missing required tags and server access logging. The fix should be applied automatically where possible.
questions.stem: What should the platform team use?
options: CloudFormation Hooks in warn mode
CDK aspects packaged in the shared library and applied to each app's scope
AWS Config conformance packs
Service control policies that deny s3:CreateBucket without tags
questions.explanation: CDK aspects visit every construct during synthesis, so developers get feedback locally before any deployment. Aspects can also change constructs, for example by adding tags. Hooks and Config run in AWS at deploy time or later, and SCPs only deny API calls.
rationales: Hooks run during deployment in AWS, not on the developer's machine at synth time.
Correct: synth-time checks that can also fix constructs automatically.
Config evaluates deployed resources after the fact.
SCPs block API calls at deploy time and give no local feedback or automatic fixes.

questions.scenario: A CodePipeline in a central tooling account builds a CloudFormation artifact and deploys it to a production account. The deploy action fails with an access denied error when the production account's CloudFormation role tries to read the artifact from the pipeline's S3 artifact bucket. The bucket uses the pipeline's default encryption with the AWS managed key for S3.
questions.stem: Which change resolves the issue?
options: Grant the production role s3:GetObject in the artifact bucket policy only
Make the artifact bucket public for the duration of the deployment
Replicate the artifact bucket to the production account with S3 Cross-Region Replication
Configure the artifact store with a customer managed KMS key whose key policy allows the production account roles to decrypt, and add a bucket policy granting those roles read access
questions.explanation: Cross-account pipelines need a customer managed KMS key for the artifact store, because the AWS managed key cannot be shared with another account. The key policy and bucket policy together let the target account's role decrypt and read artifacts. A bucket policy alone still fails at decryption.
rationales: Without KMS permissions on a shareable key, the object cannot be decrypted.
Making the bucket public is a serious security anti-pattern and still does not solve KMS decryption.
Replication adds complexity and does not fix the problem: the deploy role still needs a KMS key it is allowed to use.
Correct: a shareable customer managed key plus a bucket policy for the target roles.

questions.scenario: A payments team deploys AWS Lambda functions behind API Gateway. They want each new version to receive a small share of production traffic first, and to roll back automatically if the error rate rises, without changing client configuration.
questions.stem: Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Use CodeDeploy with a Lambda canary deployment configuration that shifts alias traffic and rolls back on CloudWatch alarms
Publish a new version and update the alias to point to it all at once, then monitor dashboards
Create a second API Gateway stage and ask clients to switch to it gradually
Use Route 53 weighted records between two Regions
questions.explanation: CodeDeploy's Lambda canary configurations shift a percentage of alias traffic to the new version first and then the rest. CloudWatch alarms trigger automatic rollback. Clients keep calling the same alias through API Gateway.
rationales: Correct: alias traffic shifting with alarm-based rollback.
All-at-once updates expose all traffic, and rollback is manual.
This requires client changes and has no automatic rollback.
DNS weighting across Regions does not stage Lambda versions and is slow to change.

sources.title: What is AWS CodeDeploy — CodeDeploy docs

questions.scenario: A team runs services on Amazon ECS behind an Application Load Balancer. They want blue/green releases that keep the new version at full capacity for a bake period, run an automated smoke-test Lambda function before production traffic shifts, and roll back quickly. They want to avoid adding CodeDeploy to their tooling.
questions.stem: Which deployment approach should they use?
options: ECS rolling updates with the deployment circuit breaker enabled
Two separate ECS clusters with manual Route 53 record updates
ECS native blue/green deployments with a lifecycle hook that invokes the smoke-test Lambda function and a configured bake time
Recreate the service with the new task definition during a maintenance window
questions.explanation: ECS native blue/green deployments support lifecycle hooks (Lambda or pause), a bake time, and managed traffic shifting for ALB, without CodeDeploy. The deployment circuit breaker rolls back failed rolling deployments, but it does not create a parallel green environment or run hook-based tests.
rationales: Rolling updates replace tasks in place; the circuit breaker does not provide blue/green bake or test hooks.
Manual DNS changes are slow, error-prone and have no automated test gate.
Correct: native blue/green with hooks and bake time.
Recreating the service causes downtime and gives no safe rollback path.

questions.scenario: A security team requires that container images deployed to Amazon EKS and ECS are checked for vulnerabilities continuously, including CVEs disclosed after the image was pushed. Only images produced by the company's trusted build pipeline may run.
questions.stem: Which actions meet these requirements? (Select two.)
options: Enable Amazon ECR enhanced scanning with Amazon Inspector for continuous scanning
Enable ECR basic scanning on push only
Sign images in the pipeline (for example with AWS Signer) and verify signatures before deployment or at admission
Enable image tag immutability on the repositories as proof of provenance
Rely on Amazon GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring for the EKS and ECS workloads
questions.explanation: Enhanced scanning uses Inspector to scan continuously and rescans images when new vulnerabilities are published. Signing in the pipeline and verifying at deploy or admission time ensures only trusted artifacts run. Scan-on-push misses later CVEs, and tag immutability does not prove where an image came from.
rationales: Correct: continuous scanning that catches newly disclosed CVEs.
On-push scans check the image once and do not catch CVEs disclosed later.
Correct: signature verification enforces provenance.
Immutability stops tags from being overwritten but does not prove where an image came from.
Runtime Monitoring detects threats in running workloads; it does not scan images for CVEs or verify where an image came from.

sources.title: What is Amazon Inspector — Inspector docs

questions.scenario: A company's pipeline rebuilds its container image from source in each of the dev, staging and production stages, using the same Dockerfile. A production incident was traced to a base-image update that arrived between the staging and production builds.
questions.stem: What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Pin the base image tag to latest in the Dockerfile
Build the image once, push it to ECR, and promote the same image digest through staging and production
Add a manual approval before each rebuild
Run the production build at the same time as the staging build
questions.explanation: Building once and promoting the immutable digest guarantees production runs the exact artifact that was tested. Rebuilding per stage allows dependencies to change between environments. Approvals or timing tricks do not remove that variability.
rationales: The latest tag makes builds even less reproducible.
Correct: build-once, promote-by-digest.
Approvals do not stop the content of the rebuild from changing.
Builds at the same moment can still pull different dependencies, and this does not make the process sound.

sources.title: What is AWS CodePipeline — CodePipeline docs

questions.scenario: A customer-support assistant uses a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock with a knowledge base. Prompt templates and retrieval settings change several times a week through CodePipeline. Two recent releases reduced answer quality, and nobody noticed for days.
questions.stem: What is the MOST effective way to catch these regressions before release?
options: Ask a team member to try a few prompts manually after each deployment
Create a CloudWatch alarm on InvocationLatency after deployment
Increase the guardrail content filter strength for every release
Add a CodeBuild stage that runs an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job against a curated dataset with expected answers and fails the stage when scores fall below a threshold
questions.explanation: An automated evaluation job over a fixed dataset measures quality the same way every time and can block promotion when scores drop. Latency metrics and stricter content filters do not measure answer quality. Manual spot checks are inconsistent and happen after release.
rationales: Ad hoc manual checks are inconsistent and happen too late.
Latency says nothing about answer correctness, and the check runs after release.
Content filters block harmful content; they do not measure answer quality.
Correct: a repeatable pre-release quality gate in the pipeline.

questions.scenario: A company has 250 AWS accounts in AWS Organizations. The operations team wants one place where engineers can search metrics, logs and X-Ray traces from every workload account, including accounts created in the future, without copying data or switching roles.
questions.stem: Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Configure CloudWatch cross-account observability with a central monitoring account linked to source accounts across the organization
Create CloudWatch dashboards in every account and share them by URL
Export all metrics and logs to S3 daily and query them with Athena
Create IAM users in each account for the operations team
questions.explanation: CloudWatch cross-account observability links source accounts, including organization-wide, to a monitoring account. Engineers can then search metrics, logs and traces centrally without copying data. The other options are fragmented, delayed or insecure.
rationales: Correct: an organization-wide link to a central monitoring account.
Per-account dashboards do not give a single place to search.
Daily exports are delayed and do not include trace analysis.
IAM users in each account are a security anti-pattern and still need role switching.

questions.scenario: Regulations require application logs from 120 accounts to be kept for 7 years in a central account that workload teams cannot modify. Logs are queried often for 30 days and almost never after that. Costs must be minimized.
questions.stem: Which design meets these requirements?
options: Set every CloudWatch Logs log group retention to 7 years in each account
Have each account export logs to its own S3 bucket monthly with CreateExportTask

Use account-level subscription policies to send logs to a cross-account destination in the log archive account, deliver them through Amazon Data Firehose to S3, set short CloudWatch Logs retention, and use S3 lifecycle rules to move objects to archive storage classes
Stream all logs to a Lambda function that writes them to a DynamoDB table
questions.explanation: Subscription policies stream logs continuously to the central account, where Firehose writes them to S3. S3 lifecycle rules move rarely read data to low-cost archive storage, while short CloudWatch retention covers the frequent 30-day queries. Keeping logs for 7 years in CloudWatch Logs costs much more, and per-account buckets are not centrally protected.
rationales: Long CloudWatch Logs retention is expensive and data stays in accounts that workload teams control.
Per-account monthly exports are not central, not continuous and are open to tampering.
Correct: central, tamper-resistant, tiered archive.
DynamoDB is a costly, poor fit for bulk log archives.

sources.title: Real-time processing with subscriptions — CloudWatch Logs docs

questions.scenario: An e-commerce company's checkout flow broke at 3 a.m. and nobody noticed until customers complained hours later. Separately, the product team wants page-load and JavaScript error data from real customers, broken down by browser and country.
questions.stem: Which actions meet these requirements? (Select two.)
options: Create CloudWatch Synthetics canaries that script the checkout flow on a schedule and alarm on failure
Increase the X-Ray sampling rate to 100%
Add the CloudWatch RUM web client to the storefront
Enable Container Insights on the ECS cluster
Enable VPC Flow Logs on the storefront subnets
questions.explanation: Synthetics canaries test the checkout flow on a schedule even when no customers are active, so failures are caught overnight. CloudWatch RUM records real users' page loads and errors by browser and location. More trace sampling or container metrics do not exercise the flow or capture what happens in the browser.
rationales: Correct: proactive scripted checks that work without real traffic.
Tracing only records requests that actually happen; with no users, nothing is traced.
Correct: real-user monitoring by browser and location.
Container metrics show infrastructure health, not end-to-end flow failures or browser experience.
Flow logs record IP traffic metadata; they do not exercise the checkout flow or capture page loads and JavaScript errors in the browser.

questions.scenario: An API team has committed to 99.9% availability over a rolling 28-day window. Their current alarm fires on any minute with more than 50 HTTP 5xx errors, which pages engineers constantly during harmless short spikes but missed a slow, steady degradation last month.
questions.stem: What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Raise the static threshold to 500 errors per minute
Define a request-based availability SLO in CloudWatch Application Signals and create burn-rate alarms on the error budget
Replace the alarm with a daily email report of error counts
Add more instances so that error rates fall
questions.explanation: An SLO with an error budget measures how much unreliability the commitment allows. Burn-rate alarms fire when the budget is being used up too fast, which catches slow degradation and ignores short spikes. Static thresholds are either too noisy or too blunt.
rationales: A higher threshold still ignores the slow degradation.
Correct: alerting based on the error budget and burn rate.
Daily reports are too late for operational response.
Adding capacity does not fix the alerting design and may not fix the cause of errors.

questions.scenario: A company runs microservices on EKS, ECS and Lambda. It wants distributed traces and metrics in AWS X-Ray and CloudWatch today, but must be able to send the same telemetry to another backend later without re-instrumenting code.
questions.stem: Which instrumentation approach should the company choose?
options: Enable VPC Flow Logs for all subnets
Write custom log lines and parse them with metric filters
Use only CloudWatch Container Insights
Use vendor-neutral OpenTelemetry instrumentation with AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) collectors exporting to X-Ray and CloudWatch
questions.explanation: ADOT is AWS's supported OpenTelemetry distribution. Code instrumented once with OpenTelemetry can export to X-Ray and CloudWatch, and the collector can be pointed at another backend later. The other options either do not produce traces or are tied to a single backend.
rationales: Flow Logs record network flows, not application traces.
Log parsing does not produce distributed traces.
Container Insights gives container metrics but not request-level traces across Lambda.
Correct: portable instrumentation with AWS-supported exporters.

sources.title: AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry — X-Ray docs
What is AWS X-Ray — X-Ray docs

questions.scenario: Operators of a multi-tenant Amazon EKS cluster need CPU and memory utilization per pod, node and namespace, plus container logs in CloudWatch, with as little custom setup as possible.
questions.stem: What should they do?
options: Install the Amazon CloudWatch Observability add-on to enable Container Insights with enhanced observability
Create custom metrics with PutMetricData from each application
Use CloudTrail data events for the cluster
Enable detailed monitoring on the worker node EC2 instances only
questions.explanation: Container Insights collects cluster, node, namespace and pod metrics and container logs, and the CloudWatch Observability add-on enables it for EKS with little setup. Custom metrics take engineering work, CloudTrail records API activity, and EC2 detailed monitoring has no pod-level detail.
rationales: Correct: managed collection of pod-level metrics and logs.
Custom metrics take significant per-application effort.
CloudTrail records API calls, not resource utilization.
Instance metrics cannot be broken down by pod or namespace.

questions.scenario: A company runs a generative AI application on Amazon Bedrock. Finance wants token usage charged back by business unit. Operations wants alerts when requests are throttled or latency rises. Today, the only Bedrock telemetry is CloudTrail.
questions.stem: Which solution meets both requirements?
options: Query CloudTrail for prompt and response sizes by user
Turn on VPC Flow Logs for the Bedrock interface endpoint and estimate tokens from bytes

Enable Bedrock model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs with requestMetadata tags per business unit and analyze identity and token counts with Logs Insights; create CloudWatch alarms on the Bedrock invocation throttle and latency metrics
Enable AWS Config recording for Bedrock resources
questions.explanation: Invocation logging is disabled by default. Once enabled, it records the caller identity, token counts and optional request metadata, which supports chargeback through Logs Insights. Bedrock's CloudWatch runtime metrics cover throttles and latency for alarms. CloudTrail records API calls, not token-level details.
rationales: CloudTrail does not capture prompt and response bodies or token counts for chargeback.
Network bytes are not a reliable proxy for tokens and miss identity details.
Correct: invocation logs for chargeback and runtime metrics for alarms.
Config tracks resource configuration, not invocation usage.

questions.scenario: A fraud-scoring model is hosted on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. Over time the distribution of input features changes as customer behavior shifts, and model accuracy declines without anyone noticing.
questions.stem: How should the solutions architect detect this automatically?
options: Apply Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to the endpoint
Configure SageMaker Model Monitor with data capture, a baseline from the training data, and a monitoring schedule that publishes violations to CloudWatch alarms
Create a CloudWatch anomaly detection alarm on endpoint CPU utilization
Retrain the model every hour regardless of performance
questions.explanation: Model Monitor compares captured inference data against a training baseline on a schedule and reports data and model quality drift, which can trigger alarms. CPU usage does not reflect feature drift, and Guardrails filter content for Bedrock. Blind retraining wastes resources and does not detect anything.
rationales: Guardrails are content safety controls for generative AI, not drift detection.
Correct: scheduled drift detection against a baseline.
Infrastructure metrics do not show changes in input data distribution.
Retraining on a fixed schedule gives no visibility into drift and is costly.

questions.scenario: A company frequently hits regional quotas when launching new workloads, and each new account created through Organizations needs the same set of quota increases that the team currently requests by hand.
questions.stem: Which solution reduces these incidents with the LEAST manual effort?
options: Deploy all workloads into the management account to share quotas
Open a support case for each quota every quarter
Write a script that calls each service's Describe APIs nightly and emails the results
Create CloudWatch alarms on Service Quotas utilization metrics and configure a Service Quotas quota request template for new accounts in the organization
questions.explanation: Service Quotas utilization alarms warn before a limit is reached. A quota request template automatically requests the standard increases when new accounts are created in the organization. The other options are manual, incomplete or break account isolation.
rationales: Running workloads in the management account violates multi-account best practice.
Periodic manual cases do not keep up with demand and do not scale.
A custom script repeats a managed capability and needs maintenance.
Correct: proactive alarms plus automatic increases for new accounts.

sources.title: What is Service Quotas — Service Quotas docs

questions.scenario: During a partial outage of a downstream inventory service, thousands of order-service instances retried failed calls immediately and without limit. The extra load kept the inventory service down long after its original problem was fixed.
questions.stem: Which changes should the solutions architect make to the order service? (Select two.)
options: Use capped retries with exponential backoff and jitter
Increase client timeouts to several minutes so calls eventually succeed
Add a circuit breaker that stops calling the inventory service after repeated failures and returns a fallback until probes succeed
Double the number of order-service instances
Retry each failed call immediately up to 10 times before giving up
questions.explanation: Exponential backoff with jitter and capped attempts spreads out retries and limits extra load. A circuit breaker stops traffic to a failing dependency so it can recover, and fails fast in the meantime. Longer timeouts and more callers make the overload worse.
rationales: Correct: retries that are spread out, randomized and capped.
Long timeouts hold resources and add pressure without helping recovery.
Correct: fail fast and give the dependency room to recover.
More instances means more retry traffic against the struggling service.
Immediate retries with no delay are what amplified the outage; a fixed count without backoff still floods the dependency.

sources.title: Control and limit retry calls — Well-Architected Reliability Pillar

questions.scenario: In a shared AWS account, a batch Lambda function occasionally scales out and uses all available account concurrency. Customer-facing API Lambda functions are then throttled.
questions.stem: What should the solutions architect do to isolate the workloads?
options: Configure reserved concurrency on the customer-facing functions and on the batch function to cap it
Increase the memory size of the API functions
Configure provisioned concurrency on the batch function
Add retries to the API clients
questions.explanation: Reserved concurrency acts as a bulkhead. It guarantees capacity to the functions that have it and also caps the batch function. Memory changes or client retries do not prevent the batch function from using up concurrency.
rationales: Correct: concurrency bulkheads that guarantee and cap capacity.
Memory affects performance per invocation, not concurrency isolation.
Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes environments; it does not cap the batch function's scaling.
Retries add load and do not stop the throttling.

questions.scenario: A web application on an EC2 Auto Scaling group has a strong daily and weekly traffic pattern that shifts gradually over the seasons. Instances take about 10 minutes to initialize, so target tracking scales out too late each morning. The team does not want to maintain schedules by hand.
questions.stem: Which solution should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Replace target tracking with step scaling using a lower threshold
Create scheduled actions for each weekday morning and update them every month
Add predictive scaling, first in forecast-only mode to check the forecasts, then in forecast-and-scale mode alongside the existing target tracking policy
Keep the group at peak capacity at all times
questions.explanation: Predictive scaling learns recurring patterns from history and launches capacity before the forecast peak, which hides long initialization times without manual schedules. Running alongside target tracking handles anything the forecast misses. Scheduled actions need ongoing maintenance, and staying at peak capacity wastes money.
rationales: Step scaling is still reactive and cannot avoid the 10-minute initialization delay.
Schedules work but must be updated by hand as the pattern changes.
Correct: forecast-driven scaling that adapts as the pattern shifts, backed by target tracking.
Static peak capacity is highly cost-inefficient.

sources.title: Predictive scaling — EC2 Auto Scaling docs

questions.scenario: Instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer sometimes have a hung application process. The ALB marks them unhealthy and stops routing to them, but the Auto Scaling group never replaces them, so capacity stays reduced.
questions.stem: What is the MOST likely fix?
options: Enable detailed monitoring on the instances
Enable ELB health checks on the Auto Scaling group
Increase the ALB idle timeout
Add a lifecycle hook for instance launch
questions.explanation: By default, an Auto Scaling group uses only EC2 status checks, which pass while the operating system is healthy. Adding ELB health checks lets the group replace instances that fail application-level checks. The other options do not change how the group decides an instance is unhealthy.
rationales: More frequent metrics do not trigger replacement.
Correct: the group then acts on the load balancer's health checks.
Idle timeout affects connection handling, not health.
Launch hooks run at launch and do not detect unhealthy running instances.

sources.title: Health checks for Auto Scaling instances — EC2 Auto Scaling docs

questions.scenario: A company wants security groups that allow SSH from 0.0.0.0/0 to be corrected automatically within minutes in every account. It also wants EC2 fleets patched monthly with an approved list of patches, with no manual steps.
questions.stem: Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Use an SCP that denies ec2:AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress for all principals
Have the security team review security groups weekly and patch instances by hand
Use CloudTrail to log security group changes and send a monthly report

Deploy an AWS Config rule for unrestricted SSH with automatic remediation that runs a Systems Manager Automation runbook, and use Patch Manager with patch baselines and maintenance windows for patching
questions.explanation: Config rules with automatic remediation run Automation runbooks as soon as a resource falls out of compliance. Patch Manager applies approved patches during maintenance windows. Manual reviews and reports are slow, and a blanket SCP would block all legitimate ingress changes.
rationales: Denying all ingress changes breaks normal operations and does not handle patching.
Manual processes do not meet the within-minutes requirement.
Logging and reports do not remediate anything.
Correct: detective control plus automated runbook remediation and scheduled patching.

sources.title: Systems Manager Automation — Systems Manager docs

questions.scenario: An order-processing Lambda function is invoked asynchronously by Amazon EventBridge. During a database outage, some events failed every retry and were lost. The business needs failed events kept for reprocessing, without duplicate side effects when they are replayed.
questions.stem: What should the solutions architect do?
options: Disable retries so failures surface sooner
Increase the function timeout to the maximum
Switch to synchronous invocation from EventBridge
Configure an on-failure destination (for example an SQS queue) for the asynchronous invocations and make the handler idempotent using an idempotency key
questions.explanation: Asynchronous Lambda invocations are retried a limited number of times. An on-failure destination keeps the events that still fail so they can be reprocessed. Idempotent handlers make replays safe. Longer timeouts or no retries do not keep the failed events.
rationales: Disabling retries loses even more events.
Timeout length does not help when the dependency is down.
This does not keep failed events, and EventBridge targets Lambda asynchronously.
Correct: failed events are kept and replays are safe.

questions.scenario: A public partner API on Amazon API Gateway is backed by a shared database. One partner's runaway integration recently sent bursts of traffic that degraded service for all partners.
questions.stem: Which approach BEST protects other partners while keeping the API available?
options: Remove the misbehaving partner's DNS access
Scale the database vertically to the largest instance size
Create API Gateway usage plans with per-partner API keys and throttling limits, and add an AWS WAF rate-based rule as an extra layer
Ask partners to add retries with no delay
questions.explanation: Per-client usage plans set throttling and quotas for each partner, so one partner cannot use up shared capacity. WAF rate-based rules add a coarser limit per source. A bigger database only raises the ceiling, and blocking DNS or retrying without delay does not solve the problem.
rationales: Partners resolve the public endpoint independently; this is neither enforceable nor targeted.
Vertical scaling does not isolate partners and raises cost.
Correct: per-client rate limits isolate noisy neighbors.
Immediate retries increase load further.

sources.title: Usage plans and API keys — API Gateway docs
